Lawsuit seeks to ban Trump Media from charging for early access to president’s posts on US policy
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump was sued in federal court Wednesday to stop him from making money off a new, paid service at his Truth Social company offering early, exclusive access to his posts on U.S. policy.
The lawsuit alleges the service offering paying customers sneak peeks of his posts about U.S. policy on war, tariffs and other issues violates the Constitution and that official announcements should be made available to everyone at the same time. The new subscription service rolled out earlier this month is charging Wall Street firms as much as $100,000 a month to trade off the market-moving posts before others.
“A president selling priority access to news he himself generates for the benefit of a private company he controls is so blatantly corrupt and unconstitutional that it would have been hard to even fathom just a few years ago,” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, a plaintiff in the case along with news outlet The Intercept.
Truth Social’s parent company, Trump Media & Technology, said selling fast access to traders is common in its industry, and that the plaintiffs are just trying to silence the president.
“Information from President Trump is disseminated by countless platforms and news outlets, many of which offer subscription APIs,” it said in a statement, using the acronym for the fast access service. “Now, left wing activists are trying to wrongfully weaponize the courts to censor him again and harm our shareholders.”
The early access service comes as the publicly traded Trump Media loses hundreds of millions of dollars each quarter and its stock has dropped below $10 from $62 shortly after going public two years ago.
The plaintiffs allege the service violates two parts of the Constitution — the First Amendment right to access a president’s comments on equal terms with other members of the press and public and the Fifth Amendment prohibitions on charging unreasonable conditions for government benefits.
The lawsuit asks that Trump Media be forced to end the new paid service, called Truth API, which offers access milliseconds faster.
Trump Media also benefits separately from a deal with Trump that gives its Truth Social six hours of exclusive access to his posts before he can distribute them elsewhere. The plaintiffs appeared to take aim at that, too, asking the court to stop him from “posting official government information exclusively” on his own site.
Trump is the largest shareholder of Trump Media, owning more than 40% of its shares through a trust.
Even before the new API service was started earlier this month, ethics watchdogs criticized Trump’s posting on Truth Social as a brash attempt to profit off the presidency, similar to other money-making venture s, including ones related to cryptocurrencies. Earlier this year, the president filed a required annual financial disclosure report that showed he took in more than a $1 billion last year from new crypto businesses that his administration regulates.
Among other moves since he was reelected, Trump’s digital finance company, World Liberty Financial, got a $500 million investment from a company tied to the government of the United Arab Emirates and sold hundreds of millions of dollars worth of special souvenir Trump meme coins to his fans and possible federal favor seekers, including a billionaire fighting a federal lawsuit that was later paused, then settled.
In addition to the president, the lawsuit filed in the Southern District of New York names his deputy chief of staff Daniel Scavino and his executive assistant Natalie J. Harp as defendants.

New indictment alleges Nick Reiner was lying in wait before killing parents Rob and Michele Reiner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

New indictment alleges Nick Reiner was lying in wait before killing parents Rob and Michele Reiner
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A Los Angeles County grand jury has indicted Nick Reiner on murder charges in the killings of his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, and adds the allegation that he was lying in wait before attacking them.
The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20, and it was unsealed Wednesday, when 32-year-old Nick Reiner entered a not guilty plea.
Rob Reiner, a director, actor and Hollywood luminary, and his wife, a photographer and producer, were stabbed to death in their home in the upscale Brentwood section of Los Angeles on Dec. 14. Nick Reiner was arrested within hours and charged two days later.
The grand jury indictment is a major step toward trial and allows prosecutors to skip California’s preliminary hearing process, where evidence is publicly aired.
Lying in wait means a suspect waited for or hid from victims in order to ambush them, and as an allegation it’s meant to show premeditation. A finding that he was lying in wait along with a murder conviction would make Reiner eligible for the death penalty, but prosecutors said they haven’t decided whether to seek it.
“This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement. “We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice.”
Unsealed indictment gives few new details in secrecy-shrouded case
The unsealed indictment reveals few new details in a case that has been shrouded in secrecy. It does not explain how or why Reiner was lying in wait. It also includes an allegation that he used a knife in the killing, but authorities have said previously that the couple was stabbed.
Prosecutors have said nothing about possible motives, and leaks in the case have been virtually nonexistent on both sides.
The Los Angeles County chief medical examiner told The Associated Press he would like to make their autopsy reports public, but a court order has prevented him from doing so.
Indictment released as Nick Reiner seeks trust funds
The indictment comes as Reiner is seeking unpaid money from a trust his parents established for him, saying he needs it to help in his defense.
Reiner said in a court petition that the trustees who oversee the funds have denied them to him without legal justification. The money was to have gone to Nick Reiner even if his parents were alive, legal filings say. The petition says the trust has at least $1.5 million in assets, but trustees would not share the exact amount.
“Nick loved his parents, and he is devastated by their deaths. But the facts about what did and did not happen to them are not at issue,” the petition says.
He is seeking to hire back high-profile criminal defense attorney Alan Jackson, who initially represented him before Reiner’s siblings would no longer agree to fund his defense and a public defender took over.
A hearing on the petition is set for next week.
The LA County Public Defender’s Office, which is representing Reiner, declined to comment on the indictment.
Grand jury process happens in secret
California prosecutors can charge a defendant and take the case through a preliminary hearing — a sort of trial in miniature where evidence is publicly aired and a judge decides whether it should be sent to trial — as recently happened with singer D4vd.
Or they can use a grand jury to go through the process in secret. They can also publicly file charges and later seek a secret grand jury indictment, essentially creating a new version of the case, as happened here and in the Los Angeles prosecution of Harvey Weinstein.
Rob Reiner had prolific career as actor and director
Rob Reiner began as an actor, starring in the TV sitcom, “All in the Family,” as Michael “Meathead” Stivic, the liberal son-in-law to a much more conservative and bigoted Archie Bunker, played by Carroll O’Connor. Reiner won two Emmy Awards for the role, and last month got a posthumous Emmy nomination for his work as a guest star on “The Bear.”
He became a prolific director whose work included some of the most memorable and endlessly watchable movies of the 1980s and ’90s. His credits included “This is Spinal Tap,” “Stand By Me,” “A Few Good Men,” and “When Harry Met Sally…” during the production of which he met photographer Michele Singer. They wed soon after and were married for 36 years.
Nick Reiner was the second of the three children they had together. He and his father co-wrote the script for the 2015 film “Being Charlie,” which was partly based on the son’s teenage struggles with addiction and homelessness.
His older brother Jake Reiner wrote in April that the experience of losing his parents and having his brother at the center of it was “a living nightmare” that is “too devastating to comprehend.”

Trump’s ‘energy emergency’ could fast-track massive expansion of Plaquemines LNG export terminal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
19:23:02 UTC
04:23:02 KST

Trump’s ‘energy emergency’ could fast-track massive expansion of Plaquemines LNG export terminal
Less than two years after opening, a liquefied natural gas terminal near New Orleans is seeking a multi-billion-dollar expansion under a new Trump administration “emergency” permitting process that shortens environmental review and may weaken protections for surrounding wetlands and waterways.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers granted Plaquemines LNG, on the Mississippi River between Myrtle Grove and Port Sulphur, fast-tracked permitting under a “ national energy emergency ” President Donald Trump declared last year.
The agency cut the public comment period from the typical 30 days to just 10, ending July 2, and is expected to move quickly to approve the expansion, which would allow the terminal to more than double in size, growing from nearly 590 acres to about 1,220.
That would make the facility the largest LNG export terminal in North America, according to its owner, Virginia-based Venture Global.
Environmentalists warn that the terminal’s expedited review could reduce scrutiny of dredging, in-water construction, and the filling of marshlands in a region suffering from rapid land loss. By the Army Corps’ estimates, the $18 billion expansion could damage up to 470 acres of wetlands and water bottoms in central Plaquemines Parish, about 25 miles south of New Orleans.
“Louisiana is already dealing with a coastal crisis,” said Matt Rota, a senior policy director with Healthy Gulf, a New Orleans-based environmental group. “Destroying 400 more acres in Plaquemines Parish is ridiculous. I don’t know how many acres they have left, but it’s not that much.”
Plaquemines has lost more than 250 square miles of land over the past 60 years to subsidence, sea level rise and erosion. The state’s Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority projects another 300 square miles — about half the parish’s remaining land — could disappear over the next 50 years. Much of Louisiana’s coast faces a similar threat. Since the early 1900s, nearly 2,000 square miles of the state have vanished, an area roughly the size of Delaware.
The Army Corps and Venture Global did not respond to requests for comment.
Hundreds of other energy projects could receive expedited permitting under the emergency declaration, which Trump said was necessary to maintain a “reliable, diversified, and affordable supply of energy” for the U.S. military and economy. Last year, the Army Corps identified more than 600 projects that could speed through the normal review process required by the Clean Water Act.
Streamlined permitting will likely accelerate the growth of an already booming LNG industry. More than 30 LNG export terminals are under construction or proposed in the U.S. Plaquemines LNG is the newest of four terminals in Louisiana, including Sabine Pass, Cameron LNG and Calcasieu Pass LNG, which is also owned by Venture.
LNG is natural gas chilled into a liquid for easier shipment overseas, where demand has surged as countries seek alternatives to coal and Russian gas.
The industry’s critics say shipping natural gas abroad conflicts with Trump’s stated rationale for declaring an energy emergency: boosting what he described as the “nation’s inadequate energy supply.”
“It’s hard to see how expanding an LNG export terminal is going to help domestic energy independence and reliability,” said Griffin Bird, a research analyst with the Environmental Integrity Project.
“This has nothing to do with energy security,” Rota said. “It sacrifices the Louisiana coast to enrich billionaires.”
Of the 833 billion cubic feet of gas exported from Plaquemines LNG last year, most went to Europe, with Germany receiving the largest share, at 19%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
The terminal is one of Louisiana’s largest industrial facilities, with 1.3 miles of river frontage, three ship berths, two gas-fired power plants, and nearly 30 miles of natural gas pipeline.
It’s also one of the state’s biggest polluters. Plaquemines LNG is permitted to release about 8.1 million tons of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases per year, according to company records. That’s equivalent to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of 1.7 million gas-powered vehicles.
The only industrial facility in Louisiana that emits more than Plaquemines LNG is CF Industries, an ammonia producer in Donaldsonville that released about 10.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023, the latest year available in the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas emissions inventory.
Those emissions, along with the carbon dioxide released when the LNG is burned for energy overseas, contribute to climate change, which is accelerating sea level rise and intensifying the storms that drive land loss in Plaquemines, Rota said.
“Burning more natural gas means we lose Plaquemines Parish even faster,” he said.
The terminal’s expansion would increase its production capacity from about 1.4 trillion cubic feet of gas per year to around 2.3 trillion.
It’s unclear how the expansion will affect emissions, but federal filings indicate the larger facility could produce at least 9 million tons of greenhouse gases per year. Venture plans to use carbon capture and sequestration technology to inject a portion of the terminal’s carbon dioxide underground.
Some Louisiana leaders welcome the expansion, saying it will spur economic activity and create jobs.
U.S. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, a Jefferson Parish Republican, celebrated the rapid development of the Plaquemines site.
“This was a cow pasture four or five years ago,” he told reporters during a tour of the facility in April. “Now it’s the most modern, the most efficient, the largest LNG export facility in the world, and they’re building another one just like it next door.”

A Kansas town will pay $850K to end a reporter’s lawsuit over a 2023 raid on her paper’s offices
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — A small Kansas town has agreed to pay $850,000 to a former reporter at its weekly newspaper to end her federal lawsuit over a police raid of the paper’s offices in 2023 that ignited a national furor over press freedom.
Now-retired Marion County Record reporter Phyllis Zorn said in her lawsuit that the raid violated press freedoms and protections from unreasonable law enforcement searches guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution. She also said it almost immediately led to health problems, causing the return of potentially life-threatening seizures that had been controlled for years with medication.
Zorn’s attorney, Randy Rathbun, and an attorney for the city Marion, Jennifer Hill, filed a joint statement Tuesday — the third anniversary of the raid on the newspaper’s offices — that Zorn’s lawsuit was being dismissed. It was among the lawsuits filed in federal court against local officials over the raids of the newspaper’s offices, the home of Publisher Eric Meyer and the home of a former City Council member.
Rathbun did not immediately return a phone message Wednesday seeking comment. Another attorney for the city, Scott Ufford, declined to comment about the settlement but confirmed the amount.
Marion Police Chief Gideon Cody said he was investigating whether the paper had committed identity theft or other crimes in accessing a local restaurant owner’s state driving record, but authorities who examined the raids said they were not legally justified. Meyer, Zorn and others saw the raids as retaliation for hard-hitting local coverage and efforts to gather information about Cody’s past in law enforcement.
The raids put a national spotlight on Marion, a town of about 1,900 residents about 150 miles (241 kilometers) southwest of Kansas City, and Cody later resigned. Meyer’s 98-year-old-mother, also the paper’s co-owner, who lived with him, died the day after the raids, and he blames stress from the raid at their home for her death.
Marion County agreed in November to pay a little more than $3 million to parties in the five lawsuits, including $600,000 to Zorn, to settle claims against its officials. While some of the remaining legal claims against the city and past and present officials have been settled or dismissed, some still remain, and a pretrial Zoom hearing is scheduled for Oct. 15.
Questions about Cody’s conduct after the state launched an investigation of the raid led two special prosecutors to file a felony obstruction of justice charge against him in state district court, alleging that he persuaded a witness, the local restaurant owner, to withhold information from authorities. He pleaded not guilty, and a trial set for the end of this month has been postponed.

Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreams after teen’s death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
19:21:11 UTC
04:21:11 KST

Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreams after teen’s death
Regulator says Discord failed to protect minors from violence, self-harm and suicide content.
Brazil has ordered social media app Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature across the country, accusing the platform of failing to protect children and teenagers after a 13-year-old girl died by suicide following a livestream in which authorities say she was encouraged to harm herself.
Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) on Wednesday gave Discord three business days to suspend its “Go Live” feature and other similar video-sharing tools. Discord itself will not be blocked, but those features won’t be available to users until the company can show it has put adequate safeguards in place for minors, said the agency in a statement.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Judge in Brazil orders Musk’s X to obey ban or face daily fine
- list 2 of 4Brazil lifts ban on Elon Musk’s X platform
- list 3 of 4US to impose new 25 percent tariffs on some Brazilian imports
- list 4 of 4The Global South’s digital future must not belong to Bezos and Musk
The regulator said it had found “robust evidence” that Discord failed to take reasonable steps to prevent minors from being exposed to content promoting violence, self-harm and suicide.
The order follows the death of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil last month. Authorities say that during a 45-minute Discord livestream, she was encouraged to harm herself and ultimately take her own life.
Five teenagers have been arrested in connection with her death. Police said the investigation also led them to another girl “who was about to commit suicide live on the internet”, but that the police operation saved her.
Alessandro Barreto, coordinator of the Brazilian Justice Ministry’s Ciberlab intelligence unit, described the case as a “terrible failure in moderation” by Discord.
“We witnessed truly outrageous acts being broadcast online,” Barreto said.
He said the 13-year-old had first been encouraged to kill an animal and, when she could not do it, was then encouraged to kill herself, “all of it broadcast live”.
“We used to see adults grooming minors. Now, what do we see? Minors grooming other minors to commit barbaric acts,” Barreto said. “Girls are being enslaved online and coerced into committing truly barbaric acts.”
Calls for Discord to be removed
Barreto said a 14-year-old boy arrested in connection with the case was “smiling as if he had just beaten a level in a game.” He added that the parents of most of the teenagers detained had been taken completely by surprise.
Following the girl’s death, Rosangela da Silva, the wife of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, called for Discord to be shut down and urged the judiciary to “remove this horrible network from the Internet”. Discord says it has more than 90 million daily active users worldwide.
But the ANPD said its concerns go beyond this case. The agency said Discord’s livestreams have repeatedly been used in connection with serious crimes and have put the physical and mental safety of minors at risk.
It also pointed to the way Discord’s livestreaming system works. According to the regulator, Discord cannot access the content of video streams while they are happening, meaning it cannot automatically analyse the video and detect violations in real time. Instead, the ANPD said, the platform relies on automated systems the agency described as flawed, as well as reports from users themselves.
Discord said in a statement to AFP before Wednesday’s decision that it was “cooperating with authorities in the investigation into this serious case”.
Brazil’s move against Discord is the latest example of the country taking a tougher approach to tech giants, particularly over their responsibility for what happens on their platforms.
In 2024, Brazil blocked X for 40 days, until the company complied with Supreme Court orders to remove accounts accused of spreading disinformation. The crackdown has angered United States President Donald Trump, who has accused Brazil of targeting American social media companies and cited that as one of the reasons for imposing tariffs on Brazilian goods.

British warship opens fire near Falklands to deter Argentina
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
20:17:22 BST
04:17:22 KST

HMS Medway carried out live machine gun firings at the edge of the Falkland Islands Conservation Zone during a four-day patrol at the end of July, British Forces South Atlantic Islands stated.
The patrol, designated Operation Southern Vigilance, ran from 26 to 29 July. The ship’s company fired mounted machine guns and worked through a man overboard exercise alongside an RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft, work the command describes as maintaining operational readiness.
According to BFSAI, the deployment demonstrated the UK’s enduring commitment to the Falkland Islands by maintaining a visible presence and a capable force, helping to deter potential adversaries.
The Falkland Islands Conservation Zone extends 150 nautical miles from the centre of the archipelago and was established in 1990 to manage fish stocks, principally squid, which underpin a large share of the islands’ economy. Licensing and enforcement within it fall to the Falkland Islands Government, with the Royal Navy providing the deterrent presence and the fisheries patrol vessel Lilibet carrying out routine inspection work.
HMS Medway is a River-class offshore patrol vessel commissioned in 2019 and took over the South Atlantic Patrol Task from HMS Forth, which held the role for several years after replacing HMS Clyde. The class displaces around 2,000 tonnes and carries a 30mm gun, machine guns and a flight deck able to take a Merlin, with an endurance suited to long independent patrols in remote waters.
The ship is the only Royal Navy vessel permanently assigned to the region. British Forces South Atlantic Islands also operates Typhoon fighters and A400M and Voyager aircraft from RAF Mount Pleasant on East Falkland, alongside an infantry company, Rapier’s successor Sky Sabre air defence and a radar station on Mount Byron.
Argentina continues to claim the islands, which it calls the Malvinas, and raises the question annually at the United Nations Special Committee on Decolonisation. The British position rests on the 2013 referendum in which islanders voted by 1,513 votes to three to remain a British Overseas Territory.
Photography from the patrol was taken by Corporal Braithwaite.

In another key primary test, a favored progressive is upset in Wisconsin governor's race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
19:16:24 UTC
04:16:24 KST

In another key primary test, a favored progressive is upset in Wisconsin governor’s race
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- David Crowley edged Francesca Hong by just 3,000 votes. He could become Wisconsin’s first Black governor.
- Progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan will face former TV sports reporter Michele Tafoya in the Minnesota Senate race.
WASHINGTON — In another major test of how far left Democratic voters in swing states are willing to go, moderate David Crowley narrowly defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong to become the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin.
The surprise result in Tuesday’s primary — in a closely watched swing state seen as a possible bellwether of Democratic sentiment — came after polls had shown Hong leading the field by double digits. With 95% of the vote counted, Crowley clinched the nomination early Wednesday by just 3,000 votes.
It was the second purple-state race between Democrats in two weeks to have an extremely narrow result, following the slim win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary last week. Polling also overestimated progressive performance in that race.
In the November general election, Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who was endorsed by President Trump. If Crowley were to defeat Tiffany, he would become the first Black governor in the state’s history.
The race had been closely watched as an example of the national fissure between progressive and establishment Democrats.
El-Sayed’s victory will put to the test in a swing state the broader strength of the progressive movement, which has found success in deep-blue places like New York City and Los Angeles.
“Hong’s candidacy is a sign of the broader trends in the party, with outspoken progressives and socialists emerging in some primaries and having real sway in the party,” said University of Wisconsin-Madison professor Barry Burden. “With Crowley, he has a more conciliatory approach ... that probably sits better with the average independent voter or moderate in the state who’s just looking to get some problems addressed.”
Crowley and his backers had undertaken an intense late-July sprint to persuade Democrats to coalesce around him. He suspended his campaign amid low poll numbers, then rejoined the race with less than a month before election day after establishment front-runner Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out.
“It was fast and furious very late in the campaign to try to build a movement in the party behind Crowley as the establishment candidate who is presumably more likely to win in a general election,” Burden said.
In another upper Midwest contest highlighting the choices confronting Democratic voters, progressive Lt. Gov. Penny Flanagan defeated center-left Rep. Angie Craig. Flanagan will face former television sports reporter Michele Tofoya, a Republican, in November for the seat held by Democratic Sen. Tina Smith, who is retiring.
As Democrats grapple with creating a party identity that will draw swing voters away from President Trump’s Republican Party in November and in 2028, a fierce debate has taken hold between the party’s factions — progressives who argue their approach is the key to the party’s fresh path forward, and moderates who fear that a far-left presidential candidate could cost Democrats the presidency in 2028.
Progressive candidates so far have fared well in blue strongholds such as Denver, New York and Minnesota this cycle, but they have struggled in Missouri and Wisconsin.
“Democrats of all ilk are winning elections all across the country,” said strategist Hyma Moore on Wednesday on CBS News, “and it’s very specific to what that state or that district needs.”
Moore said Hong’s loss was not “a setback for progressives,” arguing that she was a weaker political candidate than Crowley regardless of her ideology.
In his victory remarks Wednesday morning, Crowley rejected the framing of an intraparty conflict.
“We may not agree on every policy, we may not use the same labels, but we all want safe communities, strong schools, affordable healthcare, good-paying jobs and a brighter future for all of our children,” Crowley said.
Hong, a member of the state Assembly, ran into controversy late in the campaign with resurfaced social media posts in which she called for defunding the police and shared her negative opinions on Thanksgiving. Although she sought to retract or revise many of those comments in televised interviews, moderates and centrists seized on these points to argue against her electability.
“She had a whole smorgasbord of positions that were perfectly designed to repel voters in the middle that Democrats have to win,” said Kate deGruyter of the centrist Democratic group Third Way, which is funneling money into an effort to discredit democratic socialism ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Progressive candidates for governor in Wisconsin and U.S. Senate in Minnesota are making their final pushes ahead of Tuesday’s election
The race remained exceedingly tight until early Wednesday, when the Associated Press projected Crowley as the winner. In counties where Crowley was expected to dominate, such as Milwaukee, Hong performed better than expected. Although Hong won the city of Madison and areas with University of Wisconsin satellite campuses, the margin was too small to push her past Crowley, according to AP election data.
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) chose to publicly back Hong, but she was unable to secure key national endorsements from the two most prominent progressives in Congress, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).
Hong told her supporters Tuesday night, hours before she conceded, that regardless of the result, progressive politics would have to be reckoned with in Wisconsin’s electoral future.
“We have built something that will change politics forever,” she said. “I am so deeply grateful, to my core, for how hard you have all fought, and for what this fight, our movement, means for all of Wisconsin.”
Times staff writer Justine McDaniel in Washington contributed to this report.

Anti-Muslim hate speech targeting Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed surged twentyfold following his Aug. 4 win in the Democratic primary, according to a new study.
Findings of the Washington, DC-based Center for the Study of Organized Hate, as shared with Anadolu, found that posts naming El-Sayed along with anti-Muslim bigotry averaged 155 a day between June 1 and Aug. 3, then rose to 3,099 a day on Aug. 4-10, soaring 1,895%.
Those seven days accounted for 56.7% of all 38,280 Islamophobic posts targeting El-Sayed tracked since Jan. 1, with volume peaking on Aug. 5 at 6,923 posts in a single day.
Separately, the center tracked 409,640 posts promoting anti-Muslim bigotry on US social media company X in the country between June 1 and Aug. 10, with the platform's highest single-day total of the summer also seen on Aug. 5 with 11,883 posts.
The largest theme in the surge, the center said, involved posts describing El-Sayed as "an Islamic jihadist" and falsely linking him to Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Muslim Brotherhood. Other posts claimed he intended to impose “Islamic law,” recast campaign donations from Muslim groups as “terrorist financing,” or combined anti-Muslim conspiracy theories of a so-called "Islamist and communist" taking over the Democratic Party.
Some posts invoked the 2001 terrorist attacks to frame El-Sayed as foreign and hostile to the US, while others called for "remigration," meaning the mass removal of Muslims from Western countries.
The center said the pattern closely mirrored rhetoric it documented during Zohran Mamdani's successful run in last year's New York City mayoral election, pointing to a “stable repertoire” of tropes activated when a Muslim candidate becomes competitive or wins office.
Self-described ‘capitalist who understands how capitalism works’
El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in last week’s primary in a blow to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which spent more than $30 million backing Stevens.
He will face Republican Mike Rogers in November for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters, in a contest seen as pivotal to Democrats' hopes of retaking the Senate.
His campaign has centered on affordability, Medicare for All, and getting money out of politics. El-Sayed has also called for ending unconditional US military aid to Israel and other countries.

“But I do think about what it would mean about what our country is. You got people like Donald Trump and JD Vance and Mike Rogers, who want to define America as being smaller than she really is. I know America is big. It’s open-hearted. It is thoughtful,” he added.

However, they stressed that the data from registered party members reflect the preferences of "free" voters and do not take organized voting blocs into account, a particularly significant factor in Likud primaries.
One of the researchers' main conclusions concerns the latest reserved slots on the party list. According to the report, the reserved slots "saved" Haim Katz and Gideon Sa'ar and kept Israel Katz in the top 10.
Sa'ar was not ranked as a primary candidate in the poll. The researchers reached the conclusion as part of their simulation of the slate after the reserved slots were incorporated. Haim Katz, by contrast, ranked only 35th in the raw ranking among registered party members.
Party members back Ohana, voters prefer Barkat
On the question of Likud's leadership after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel Katz ranked sixth among registered party members, with 10.3%, compared with fourth place and 11.3% among Likud voters. The researchers attributed his weaker showing among party members to frustration over the security campaign. Following the reserved slot, Katz was placed fifth in the simulated party slate.
Sharp differences between registered party members and Likud voters were also evident at the top of the rankings. Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana led among party members with 73%, followed by Tally Gotliv with 70% and Boaz Bismuth with 69.2%.
Ohana also led among loyal Likud voters, but Nir Barkat ranked first among wavering voters and those who have left the party. Gotliv and Shlomo Karhi performed better among the registered party base, while Barkat, Yariv Levin, and Miki Zohar enjoyed greater support among the broader Likud electorate.
The divide continued in the contest over who should succeed Netanyahu. Ohana was the preferred successor among registered party members, with 22.9%, while Barkat led among Likud voters with 19%. Among party members, Gotliv ranked second with 15.6%, while Barkat was only fourth with 10.8%.
Party members want a fully right-wing government, voters more open to unity
The differences were even clearer when respondents were asked about the composition of the next government. Some 66.1% of registered party members said they would prefer the next coalition to be a "fully right-wing government," compared with 45.1% of Likud voters.
Conversely, 54.9% of Likud voters preferred a unity government with the center-right, compared with only 33.9% of registered party members.
The researchers said these findings, together with the differences in preferences for individual politicians, help explain the strategic importance of reserved slots as a tool for broadening Likud's electoral appeal beyond its registered membership base.
On the issue of military conscription, however, the picture was different. Clear majorities in both groups supported increasing the proportion of people enlisting in the IDF, even at the expense of Torah study and at the risk of a coalition crisis. The proposal was supported by 66.8% of registered Likud members and 80.4% of Likud voters.
The poll was conducted by Dr. Nimrod Nir of the Agam Institute between August 6 and 10 among 1,062 Likud members eligible to vote in the party primary, alongside more than 1,000 Likud voters.

Zelensky went to Belgrade for Serbian shells, Politico reports, and restated that Kyiv doesn’t recognize Kosovo’s independence. In Pristina, the ‘Free Ukraine’ banner came down the next day.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić in Belgrade on August 8. The visit, and Zelensky’s remarks about Kosovo during it, caused an uproar that is still being felt days later, Politico reported on August 12.
It was Zelensky’s first trip to Belgrade since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Serbia has taken a cautious line on the war: it condemns the invasion but, despite heavy pressure from the European Union, has not given up its economic ties with Moscow and has not joined the bloc’s sanctions. It sends humanitarian and energy assistance to Ukraine while formally refraining from military aid.
After the talks, Zelensky said he and Vučić had discussed “specific things that can add strength to our infrastructure,” as well as bilateral economic cooperation. Asked about Kosovo at a news conference, he confirmed that Kyiv still does not recognize Kosovo’s independence — just as Serbia does not recognize Russia’s annexation of Ukrainian territory.
We respect the territorial integrity of our partners, we respect international law, and therefore our position on … the unilateral declaration of Kosovo’s independence remains unchanged. We have always emphasized this, and Ukraine’s policy has not changed. Likewise, we are grateful to our partners for respecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, including, of course, Crimea’s status as part of Ukraine.
Zelensky’s words caused a serious stir in Kosovo itself. The next day, the enormous Ukrainian flag that had hung on a building in central Pristina since 2022 was taken down. “When Kosovo isn’t respected, the capital Pristina always reacts the same way,” Pristina Mayor Përparim Rama said. Kosovo’s foreign minister, Glauk Konjufca, said Pristina “takes note with regret” of Zelensky’s remarks but that it would continue to support Ukraine’s sovereignty.
The dispute over Kosovo’s status escalated further after Zelensky returned to Kyiv, now without his involvement. On August 9, Vučić said Serbia was prepared to consider rerouting the Ibar River, which runs through Serbian territory and replenishes the reservoir serving Kosovo’s largest hydroelectric plant. He called it a response to the Kosovo authorities’ demolition of ethnic Serb homes on the reservoir’s shore.
Albania — a longtime backer of Kosovo, where ethnic Albanians are the majority — then weighed into the public dispute. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama accused Serbia of living “in a political bubble” and refusing to acknowledge that it lost control of the region many years ago.
Politico suggested that Zelensky probably had little choice but to wade into one of the Balkans’ thorniest disputes, because he needs to keep weapons flowing from Belgrade. Serbia is a major producer of Soviet-standard ammunition, which Ukraine needs for the howitzers and tanks that do much of the work at the front. Kyiv’s Western allies cannot supply that ammunition.
Belgrade officially sends no weapons to Ukraine. In practice, Politico notes, Vučić supplies the weapons willingly and without much fuss. The Financial Times estimated in 2024 that Serbian ammunition worth 800 million euros had made its way to Ukraine since the start of the full-scale war. Formally, though, Serbia sells it only to its European partners, who then re-export it to Ukraine with no involvement from Belgrade.
As early as 2023, Vučić publicly confirmed that Serbia knew its weapons were ending up in Ukraine and had no intention of doing anything about it. “What’s our alternative? Not produce them? Not sell them?” he said at the time.
It was not until two years later, in May 2025, that Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service unexpectedly criticized Serbia because its defense companies were continuing to supply ammunition to Kyiv “despite the ‘neutrality’ officially declared by Belgrade.” The criticism had no consequences for Serbia’s relations with Russia: Vučić only said that he had discussed the matter with Vladimir Putin and had promised to order that contracts not be carried out if Belgrade learned that the end recipient of the weapons would be a party to the war.
After the Belgrade talks, Vučić insisted that military cooperation had not been discussed.

After ISIL lost its hold on territory it once claimed, coalition military operations ended in 2021.

Details
As UNN reported, on Wednesday, August 12, one of the year's main astronomical events — a total solar eclipse — will take place. In a narrow band passing through the Arctic and parts of Europe, the Moon will completely cover the Sun, briefly turning day into twilight.
Although the total phase was not visible in Ukraine, a partial eclipse could be seen in the western and some central regions.

New York cracks down on ‘predatory’ Polymarket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
19:02:19 UTC
04:02:19 KST

New York cracks down on ‘predatory’ Polymarket
New York City Council is investigating Polymarket, Kalshi, and other predictive market platforms for “deceptive and predatory” marketing practices, accusing the industry of encouraging gambling and insider trading.
Council Speaker Julie Menin notified Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, and Gemini Titan of the investigation on Tuesday. In a letter to Polymarket seen by Bloomberg, Menin referenced “troubling” news reports suggesting that the company and its competitors “target young adults – and thus potentially minors – with false, deceptive, and unconscionable advertising.”
According to the reports, Polymarket allegedly paid influencers to promote its platform without disclosure, produced videos showing fake trades on its site, presented losing bets as winners, and encouraged insider trading.
“Prediction markets aggressively entice consumers to bet and wager on sports, politics, culture, weather, and pretty much anything. We refuse to let New Yorkers, especially our young people, become collateral damage,” Menin said in a statement on Wednesday.
Prediction markets have snowballed into a $240 billion-per-year industry, counting the annual trading volume of Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, and Gemini Titan. By allowing customers to bet on politics and world events – for instance the likelihood that a world leader will be ousted by a certain date – they have reportedly become rife with insider trading.
A White House staffer has been investigated for allegedly making bets based on her advance knowledge of US President Donald Trump’s remarks, while a US special forces soldier has been arrested for using classified Pentagon materials to pocket $400,000 by correctly predicting the removal of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from power in January.
Suspicious trades surged during the US-Israeli war on Iran, with The Guardian counting more than $1 billion in “perfectly timed” wagers, including an $850,000 bet just before US strikes on Iran began on February 28, and roughly $950 million in oil futures hours before US Trump announced a ceasefire. Suspicion fell on Washington insiders, and the White House warned staff against insider trading in April.
The federal government has defended prediction markets against state-level oversight, arguing that event contracts are financial instruments and therefore different from traditional gambling. After New York Attorney General Letitia James attempted to shut down Kalshi for violating state gambling laws in July, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CTFC) stepped in this week and ordered the platform to remain operational in the state.
Responding to Menin’s letter, a spokesperson for Polymarket said that the company looks “forward to engaging with The New York City Council on this matter.”

Hospitality marketplace Supp facing Fair Work scrutiny

Hospitality marketplace Supp facing Fair Work scrutiny over contractor claims
In short:
Hospitality workers might be left short on entitlements like superannuation if their employer uses the Supp app to handle their pay.
The Fair Work Ombudsman is looking into the app. Supp's chief executive rejected suggestions the app deliberately misrepresents working relationships.
Think you might be affected?
You can make an anonymous report to the ombudsman's office if you think you're affected.
The Fair Work Ombudsman will scrutinise hospitality marketplace Supp, after a worker raised concerns it was misclassifying people who use the platform to find shifts.
Supp is branded as a "recruitment app that's made for the rush", and since 2017, it has been operating as a central hub for bars, pubs and cafes to advertise work.
Individuals can sign up to the platform and apply for shifts posted by businesses, with a description of the work and the hourly rate.
The Supp website refers to workers as "independent contractors" and says it is workers' responsibility to divide their payments to "meet their relevant taxation and superannuation obligations".
Rather than hospitality businesses paying workers through an ordinary payroll system, the Supp platform handles payment on their behalf.
Employment lawyer Fay Calderone told the ABC she is concerned this arrangement could be leaving workers without their correct entitlements, including to superannuation.
"One of the key legal risks in this area is assuming that contractual labels will be determinative," Ms Calderone, a partner at Hall and Wilcox, said.
"The mere fact that a worker holds an ABN or is described as an independent contractor does not determine their legal status."
The Fair Work Ombudsman spokesperson said it will make inquiries into Supp: "We are unable to comment on those further."
"We encourage any workers with concerns to contact us directly for assistance," the spokesperson said.
"The FWO also has an online anonymous report tool, including options to report in languages other than English."
Concerns about sham contracting in the gig economy, where employers say workers are independent contractors not employees, have been raised for years, with companies battling claims in court.
Supp rejects 'sham contracting'
The Supp website states that it has links to at least 15,000 venues, and more than 200,000 workers, across Melbourne, Sydney, Los Angeles and New York City.
One Melbourne-based hospitality worker has been using the Supp platform for more than three years. He requested anonymity as he still uses Supp for work.
He believes the type of work he has been hired to do reflects that of an employee, rather than a contractor.
"They'll be asking me to do whatever, [for example], you'll be behind the bar serving people," he said.
"They'll let you know if it's going to be mainly customer service or if you'll be in this area or that section."
Ms Calderone said there was a number of factors to take into account when determining if someone was a genuine contractor, rather than an employee.
"The question is not whether a worker enjoys some flexibility, but whether the arrangement as a whole reflects a genuinely independent business relationship [and] a number of factors are commonly examined," she said.
"Including the degree of control exercised over the worker, whether the worker can genuinely operate an independent business, whether they can delegate work to others and whether they bear any real commercial risk."
In a statement to the ABC, Supp's chief executive Jordan Murray said: "We reject any suggestion that Supp deliberately misrepresents working relationships or facilitates sham contracting".
"Supp was built to address two longstanding problems in hospitality: venues filling short-term gaps through informal networks like Facebook groups, often with very little transparency or protection around the transaction, and workers wanting greater visibility, choice and access to both additional income and permanent opportunities.
"Supp was designed to bring those transactions into the open with visible rates, digital payments, minimum rate protections, two-way reviews and a portable work history."
'I started to get a little more concerned'
In July 2022, the monthly minimum income threshold for compulsory superannuation was removed, meaning any employee over the age of 18 was now eligible for entitlements regardless of earnings.
Supp's chief executive told the ABC that it was not Supp's responsibility to pay superannuation.
"Supp is not the engaging business or employer in any engagement, and businesses using the platform are responsible for complying with their legal obligations to the people they engage," Mr Murray said in a statement.
Daniel McBurnie, who has been using the Supp platform since 2021, said chasing up unpaid superannuation contributions through individual businesses would not be worth his time.
"I've done a one-off shift at many venues and that one-off shift probably I've accumulated maybe just short of $20 super," he said.
"So for a one-off claim to go back and go through the process of disputing things and waiting for responses and then escalating it if you're not happy ... I go, well, why would I do this to myself?"
He is worried thousands of workers using the platform are missing out on building their retirement savings.
"As the app got more popular, and as it seems like more businesses were starting to use it, I started to get a little more concerned," he said.
While he initially used the app to pick up last minute shifts, he started to notice more regular shifts offered.
"I started seeing the same businesses every single week, every time I opened the app."
The Supp app shows some businesses have used the platform to fill thousands of shifts.
Even contractors may be entitled to super
Even workers legitimately engaged as contractors may still be entitled, in some circumstances, to superannuation contributions paid by businesses, Ms Calderone said.
"That is an area that is often misunderstood by both businesses and workers," she said.
"Even where a worker is properly characterised as an independent contractor for employment law purposes, superannuation obligations may still arise where the contract is wholly or principally for the worker's labour."

Angus Taylor plays a risky game in trying to capitalise on melon saga

analysis
Taylor is using the melon saga to mount an all-out assault on Albanese's character
Today marks six months since Sussan Ley was dumped by her colleagues.
She's been on an unusual journey of discovery since then.
After being defeated by Angus Taylor for the Liberal leadership and quitting parliament, Ley fulfilled a long-time dream of riding on Greyhound buses down the length of inland USA. She found a bleak interior and plenty of misery.
"Chains. Parking lots. Cheap builds. No trees. No spaces to gather," Ley wrote in The Australian Financial Review. "It was the underlying weariness. Everyone works hard. That part is true. But working hard is no longer enough."
Reflecting on the experience, Ley told 7:30's Sarah Ferguson of her great discovery: the extent of disconnection.
"This feeling of disconnection I found by the end of the trip really quite interesting, quite fascinating."
A problem of disillusion and disconnection
Ley wasn't deliberately sending a message to anyone in particular but it served as a powerful reminder. Political leaders need to stay focused on what really matters. The disconnected aren't interested in political games.
The dramatic shift in support away from the major parties in Australia this year points to a similar problem of disillusion and disconnection.
Much of this shift happened on Ley's watch. She carries at least part of the blame for weary voters walking away from the Liberal Party.
Ley was often criticised, including by her own colleagues, for whipping up issues that just didn't connect.
Issues like the prime minister's choice of T-shirt, Penny Wong's capacity to shed tears in public, or whether Kevin Rudd should be recalled as ambassador for upsetting Donald Trump.
Too much hyperventilating over the wrong issues. Not enough focus on the substantive concerns of disconnected voters.
Which brings us to the melons.
Taylor shifts direction
In his first speech as Liberal leader, six months ago today, Taylor vowed a "change or die" reset. Cost of living, immigration and Australian values would be his focus. In large part, he's so far stuck to those priorities.
This week, however, with the return of parliament after the five-week winter break, Taylor shifted direction.
He's gone after the prime minister's ill-fated and now infamous decision to appear on the satirical Bush Deep podcast where Anthony Albanese talked about the "melons" given to him by his Japanese counterpart.
The opposition leader has not been half-hearted in his pursuit. Repeatedly demanding Albanese apologise in Question Time, trying to move a motion in parliament to condemn the prime minister, accusing him of damaging relations with Japan.
The Coalition has even asked the Australian Federal Police to investigate who leaked a confidential note from Tokyo suggesting the Japanese government believed there was no "ill intention" behind the comments.
It's been a full court press from the opposition. And the government has been unable to shut it down, despite the efforts of various ministers from Tanya Plibersek to Katy Gallagher to defend the prime minister.
Having already issued an apology for his comments on the podcast about Kylie Minogue, Albanese has so far refused to offer another. He rejects any interpretation he was engaging in lewd jokes about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Japan, for its part, is trying not to stoke the issue further.
"We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported," ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki told the ABC.
Barnaby Joyce, himself familiar with the odd embarrassment or two, reckons there's no doubt what most people will make of it all.
"Turn the volume down and watch him [on the podcast]. You have a man in a T-shirt, with an empty bottle of bourbon in front of him, gesticulating with his arms, and anybody would say, 'I think I know what you're talking about there, mate,'" said the One Nation MP. "Imagine if for instance I had done that. It would be a riot."
Loading
Bipartisanship behind closed doors
Behind the scenes, Taylor and Albanese have been engaged in a rare level of cooperation this week.
They've been holding a series of personal meetings aimed at reaching bipartisan deals on gambling ads, forcing tech giants to pay for journalism, and reining in the NDIS. Both leaders have a pragmatic interest in squaring these issues away.
But in public, Taylor is using the melon saga to mount an all-out assault on Albanese's character. "He's full of hubris. There's no humility when he makes a mistake," the opposition leader told 2GB.
Choosing to pursue this may prove to be the right strategy. It's the sort of thing that can cut through and damage the prime ministerial image. Labor was devastatingly effective in going after Scott Morrison's character whenever they had the chance.
There is a risk for the Coalition, however, that weary, disconnected voters might not feel this is really the main game. They might feel there are bigger problems affecting their lives that deserve such attention.
Either way, Taylor is marking six months in the job this week with a slight detour from the plan he laid out at the start.

====================================================================================================

Torah dictatorship: How Israel’s ultra-Orthodox parties gained their influence – and why they risk losing it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:57:37 UTC
03:57:37 KST

Amid the unresolved situation in Gaza and the continued presence of Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election campaign is already in full swing. Most polls give neither the current coalition nor the opposition the 61 seats needed for a majority, meaning various smaller parties could once again determine the fate of the government — as they have many times in Israel’s history. For Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the key players are the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties, without which he has little chance of forming a majority. But the ultra-Orthodox are frustrated by the government’s failure to pass the promised law exempting most yeshiva students from military service, and as a result, their support can no longer be taken for granted. This time, the “kingmakers,” as Israel’s ultra-Orthodox parties are known, risk finding themselves on the losing side.
Knesset arithmetic
On the night of July 17, the 25th Knesset passed a self-dissolution law that officially ended its term — one of the most contentious in the country’s history, as it encompassed both the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack of 2023 and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran that followed in the three years since. The period was also characterized by deep internal divisions in Israeli society over Benjamin Netanyahu’s attempts at judicial reform and disputes regarding ultra-Orthodox military service. The current campaign to elect a new Knesset to grapple with these problems promises to be no less contentious.
Polls so far offer neither the parties in the governing coalition nor the opposition a clear path to a majority, though as of late July some polls gave the Zionist opposition parties — excluding the two Arab lists — a projected 60–61 seats. The governing coalition’s Zionist parties were averaging 34 seats without the ultra-Orthodox and 50–52 with them. However, the picture was somewhat better for the coalition in polls published by Channel 14, which supports Netanyahu: 45 seats without the ultra-Orthodox and 62 with them.
According to some polls, the opposition could win more than 60 seats; according to others, Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox could secure that many
The distinction between Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties is important, as both are considered part of the anti-Zionist bloc. Arab parties, naturally, do not consider themselves part of the Jewish national movement. Most ultra-Orthodox Jews, meanwhile, have rejected secular Zionism (the idea that Jews should achieve national self-determination through their own state). As the election campaign heats up, the most serious question concern cooperation between the potential winners and the non-Zionist parties of various stripes — namely, who is willing to sit with them in the same government and who is not?
Another debate revolves around who considers it permissible to form a government with Likud, led by Netanyahu, and who categorically refuses to sit at the same table as the current prime minister. There is also the reverse question: how stable is the opposition bloc, given diversity that ranges from the far-left Democrats to Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu?
In any case, public opinion polls are constantly shifting, and not all parties have even entered the race yet. As usual, new alliances emerge before elections, and unexpected coalitions may form. Some parties may fail to clear the electoral threshold, leading to a redistribution of seats. And after the election, politicians’ promises never to sit in a government with a particular party may be broken yet again. For example, Naftali Bennett, one of the leaders of the current BeYachad electoral list and a former prime minister, promised in 2021 never to join a coalition with Arab parties, but he later went back on his word, citing the interests of the state and society as his justification for doing so.
A parliamentary majority consists of 61 seats. After the election, the president consults with all the parliamentary factions and asks the lawmaker he believes has the best chance of securing the Knesset’s support to form a government and become prime minister. This is not necessarily the leader of the largest party. In 2021, for example, Bennett became prime minister even though his party held just seven seats — and even then, not all of its members supported the new government.
Moreover, a formal confidence vote can pass without 61 votes in favor. For example, the government formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid was approved by a vote of 60–59, with one abstention coming from a lawmaker of the Islamist Ra’am party. The party itself, meanwhile, made history by becoming the first Arab political movement in Israel to sign a coalition agreement with the Zionist camp by supporting the Bennett–Lapid government.
A party can also remain outside the coalition and receive no ministerial posts while supporting the government in confidence and budget votes. In the 1990s, for example, Arab factions helped keep Yitzhak Rabin’s minority government in power without joining it. But for a cabinet to function stably, it generally needs either its own stable coalition or guaranteed outside support. The Bennett–Lapid government, which lacked these requisites, lasted just over a year before announcing its dissolution.
Under the current political configuration, Netanyahu needs the ultra-Orthodox vote to have any hope of maintaining a majority. He may still find allies among smaller parties, but some of these categorically rule out supporting a government led by him or involving his Likud party — at least for now. However, they might agree to compromise in the event that Netanyahu agree to give up the premiership in the name of national unity.
“Kingmakers” – what the ultra-Orthodox want
The ultra-Orthodox are primarily interested in their own agenda, which involves state funding for their communities (including religious education), the sustained authority of rabbinical courts, and exemptions for yeshiva students from military service. They are willing to join forces with any party that best promises to satisfy their demands.
Attempts to reach an agreement on these issues began even before Israel declared its independence. In 1947, David Ben-Gurion, the country’s future first prime minister, promised to preserve the status quo: Saturday would be the official day of rest, state institutions would observe kosher dietary laws, marriages and divorces would remain under the jurisdiction of religious courts, and religious schools would retain their autonomy. In return, Ben-Gurion sought to secure the ultra-Orthodox’s support for the establishment of a Jewish state.
The situation changed dramatically in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 1977, the left-wing camp, previously led by Mapai and later by the Labor Party, lost power for the first time. In 1981, Likud and the left-wing bloc won almost identical numbers of seats — 48 and 47, respectively. Neither the right nor the left could count on forming governments exclusively with ideologically like-minded partners, and horse-trading with smaller parties began. The ultra-Orthodox proved particularly useful because, in Israeli political terms, they did not identify with either the right or the left, particularly when it came to the Arab-Israeli conflict and, above all, the Palestinian issue.
Today, the ultra-Orthodox camp is represented by two electoral lists but in fact consists of three parties: Shas, Degel HaTorah, and Agudat Yisrael. Since 1992, the latter two parties have run together under the United Torah Judaism list, which primarily represents Ashkenazi Haredim — descendants of Jews from Central and Eastern Europe. But the list contains two separate party structures, each subordinate to a different rabbinical council.
Agudat Yisrael (“Union of Israel”) consists primarily of Hasidic communities. The party was founded in Poland in 1912 as a movement of Orthodox Jews opposed to secularization and political Zionism. In Israel, the party’s influence is divided among several Hasidic courts, the largest of which have their own rabbis, educational institutions, and political representatives. Final decisions are made by the Council of Torah Sages, which includes leaders of influential Hasidic communities.
Degel HaTorah (“Banner of the Torah”) represents the Lithuanian, or Litvak, tradition. The party was founded in 1988 by Rabbi Elazar Shach after a conflict with the Hasidic leadership of Agudat Yisrael. Its leading religious authorities today are Rabbis Dov Landau and Moshe Hillel Hirsch. Their directives determine how Degel HaTorah lawmakers vote on key issues and which coalition they can join.
The two parties run together in elections because competing separately would put both at risk of failing to clear the 3.25% electoral threshold. Still, within United Torah Judaism, disputes over the allocation of seats, positions, and budgets are constant.
Shas (Sephardim – Torah Guardians) represents another segment of ultra-Orthodox society: Jews whose families originated mainly in the Middle East and North Africa. It was founded in 1984 by Rabbi Ovadia Yosef with the support of Rabbi Shach. One of the reasons for its creation was discrimination against Sephardim within the Ashkenazi system of religious schools, yeshivas, and political organizations. The party’s highest religious body is the Council of Torah Sages.
One of the clearest examples of the rabbis’ influence over the choice of prime minister can be found in the 1990 political crisis known as the “dirty trick.” Labor leader Shimon Peres secured a no-confidence vote against Yitzhak Shamir’s national unity government and attempted to form an alternative coalition with the ultra-Orthodox parties, but the deal fell apart after religious authorities intervened. Rabbi Shach opposed an alliance with the left, and two Agudat Yisrael lawmakers failed to show up for the decisive vote. Peres was unable to form a government, after which Shamir formed a new right-wing coalition.
For many years, however, the Haredim’s alliance with the right was not unconditional. In 1992, Shas joined Yitzhak Rabin’s government alongside Labor and the left-wing Meretz bloc. Labor had 44 seats, Meretz 12, and Shas six, giving the government a 62-seat majority. However, after Shas left the coalition, Rabin’s cabinet became a minority government and depended on outside support from Arab factions.
In 1999, Shas joined Ehud Barak’s center-left government, having by then won a record 17 seats. United Torah Judaism, with five lawmakers, also joined the coalition.
There have also been governments without the ultra-Orthodox. In 2003, Ariel Sharon opted for an alliance with the anti-clerical Shinui party, and in 2013, Netanyahu left Shas and United Torah Judaism in opposition, reaching an agreement with Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett instead. The most recent government without the ultra-Orthodox was the short-lived coalition that formed in 2021.
In the 25th Knesset, Shas and United Torah Judaism had a combined 18 lawmakers, and both remained key partners for the ruling coalition for most of the term. July polls projected the ultra-Orthodox to take between 15 and 17 seats in the October vote, but there is still no guarantee that they will support Netanyahu, who failed to keep too many promises over the past four years.
The ultra-Orthodox’s main grievance
The main complaint Shas and United Torah Judaism have against Netanyahu and their other coalition partners is the failure to pass a law that would guarantee exemptions from military service for yeshiva students (the bill never reached a final vote), who since 1948 have been granted deferments under the principle of “Torah is their vocation.” Initially the provision applied to only about 400 students, but since 1977 there has been no limit on their number. The provision had been enshrined in law several times, but those laws were struck down by the Supreme Court starting in July 2023, though the government subsequently issued a temporary order that yeshiva students not be drafted, hoping to pass a new law.
In June 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that the government could not grant such an exemption on its own and ordered the state to apply the general Military Service Law to the ultra-Orthodox. The army then began sending out draft notices — and later issuing arrest warrants — for conscripts who failed to report. By July 2026, some 72,000 Haredim aged 18 to 24 who were subject to the draft had not enlisted. The resulting arrests triggered mass protests within the community.
By July 2026, some 72,000 Haredim aged 18 to 24 were subject to the draft but had not enlisted
After nearly three years of war — in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, along with continued tensions in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) — the Israeli military is facing a manpower shortage that has placed an enormous burden on reservists. From October 2023 to the present, 27% of reserve soldiers have served a total of 150 to 300 days, while 20% have served more than 300 days. Against this backdrop, the idea that part of society is ignoring their obligation to service has sparked strong negative feelings.
The issue is not simply a demand to send all yeshiva students into the army immediately. Most Arab citizens of Israel are also exempt from the draft, while the IDF already has units adapted to the needs of the ultra-Orthodox, where special kosher requirements and gender segregation are observed. Supporters of the draft see this as proof that integration is possible, while most ultra-Orthodox Jews fear that mass military service would undermine their religious way of life. At the same time, there are concerns that adapting the army to accommodate ultra-Orthodox service could limit opportunities for female soldiers.
The issue, therefore, is much broader. Should the army adapt to the demands of the ultra-Orthodox community, or should the community adapt to the army’s general rules? Can military service be replaced with civilian service, and can that contribution to the nation truly be considered equivalent? And should a particular community be allowed to maintain near-total autonomy if the burden of its protection and funding falls on everyone else? Ultimately, the dispute over military service has become a debate over what the State of Israel should be and what obligations its citizens should have toward it.
In any case, as the election approaches, one element of this complex problem stands out: Netanyahu has alienated the ultra-Orthodox community. Moshe Gafni, the leader of Degel HaTorah, says the previous coalition arrangement will not be repeated after the election, promising: “Before forming any government, we will first pass a military draft law.” Technically, this is possible. The new Knesset can begin legislative work while the outgoing government remains in office, and the ultra-Orthodox parties could delay signing a coalition agreement until after the law they want has been finally passed.
Shas uses less forceful language and has not ruled out siding with the right-wing bloc, but the party’s fundamental demand is the same. Back in May, Shas leader Aryeh Deri said: “We will not join a coalition or government until we resolve the status of those who study Torah.”
The legislative blitz
Once it became clear that fulfilling the ultra-Orthodox’s main demand before the election was impossible, the Knesset entered what Israeli journalists called a “legislative blitz.” In the final days, lawmakers passed a series of laws demanded by the Haredim, who in return agreed to keep parliament working until a date that suited the prime minister by helping Netanyahu pass initiatives he and other coalition members needed. These included weakening the powers of the government’s legal adviser and reforming the media market.
The ultra-Orthodox secured a Basic Law on Torah study, albeit in a heavily watered-down version of the original proposal. Israel does not have a single written constitution — Basic Laws partly serve that role, so even a short declaration formally has constitutional status. The original version equated sustained Torah study with “meaningful service” to the state (that is, military service) and would have allowed it to be taken into account when allocating rights and benefits. This triggered a wave of criticism, including from within the coalition.
The ultra-Orthodox secured a Basic Law on Torah study, albeit in a heavily watered-down version of the original proposal
As a result, the substantive provisions were removed from the text. All that remained was a single provision: “Torah study is a fundamental value of the heritage of the Jewish people and the State of Israel.” For the Haredim, this amounted to historic recognition. Aryeh Deri called the vote “a victory for the Torah world,” while Gafni described it as the creation of “the state’s value compass.” But even within the Haredi community, questions arose as to whether the law had become a consolation prize.
A more effective measure was supposed to be a law suspending the arrest of Haredim who failed to report for military service after receiving draft notices. It barred the military police from detaining yeshiva students, initiating new criminal proceedings against them, or continuing cases already underway. The protection also covered those who reached draft age after the law took effect. Formally, the restrictions were set to remain in place until November 30, but given the election and the transition period, they could have remained in force until the end of January 2027. However, the Haredim did not have time to make use of the law. Less than 24 hours later, the Supreme Court suspended it.
Still, the Haredim did manage to secure some gains. The Knesset repealed the kosher certification reform adopted by the previous government and expanded the possibility of separate education for men and women at universities. Previously, special programs for Haredim existed primarily at the undergraduate level. Now the Council for Higher Education can authorize separate master’s and doctoral programs. At mixed-gender institutions, segregation is permitted in classrooms, and participation must be voluntary. Such programs will be available not only to Haredim but also to other students who cite religious beliefs. To secular Israelis, however, the law amounts to segregation and has further deepened the divide between the opposition and the coalition. For Netanyahu, though, this only works to his advantage, as it increases the chances that the Haredim will remain with him.
Against the backdrop of the heated public debate, the ultra-Orthodox do not have many options, as their agenda does not align with that of many other opposition parties. Asher Medina of Shas, for example, warned against an alliance with the left-wing camp, saying that its “only common denominator is hatred of the Haredim.”
But Israeli politics is known for its unexpected alliances and sudden twists. There are almost three months to go before the election, and the balance of power could change many times before then.

Poland, Boeing to launch Europe's largest Apache service hub
