Ex-Myanmar ambassador to UK on trial for trespassing in diplomatic residence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:01:51 UTC
03:01:51 KST

Myanmar’s ousted ambassador to the UK has gone on trial on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after being unceremoniously locked out of the embassy in 2021.
Shortly after Myanmar’s military seized power in 2021, triggering mass protests that spiralled into a civil war, Kyaw Zwar Minn was locked out of the embassy for declaring his loyalty to the deposed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
On Wednesday he appeared in a London court charged with trespassing at a diplomatic residence between May 2021 and November 2024. Kyaw Zwar Minn, who still lives at the ambassador’s residence in north-west London, has pleaded not guilty.
The former ambassador argues that the current president, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who plunged Myanmar into conflict and economic chaos, is illegitimate and had no power to ask him to leave the property.
Min Aung Hlaing’s pro-military party won a landslide victory in elections earlier this year that have been widely condemned as a sham. Min Aung Hlaing is wanted by the international criminal court for crimes against humanity against the Muslim Rohingya minority.
Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer, David Perry, told the court: “The military authorities could not lawfully terminate his licence at the address. Nor could they legitimately use the property.”
Prosecutors said Myanmar’s authorities instructed the former ambassador to “hand over state-owned properties” in April 2021, and that the Foreign Office also told him to leave the residence, but he did not comply.
They argue that his view of the Myanmar government – which is not formally recognised by most democratic countries, including Britain – does not provide a defence.
“Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed from that position means that he is guilty of the offence of diplomatic trespass,” the prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court.
Kyaw Zwar Minn previously told the Guardian he spent a night in his car outside the embassy in April 2021 after his then deputy, Chit Win, and a military attache, Soe Aung, locked him out of the building on the regime’s orders.
He said at the time that he no longer felt safe at the north London residence and had contacted the police after former staff delivered a letter ordering him to move. Friends and relatives in Myanmar had been forced into hiding fearing reprisals as a result of his stance, he said.
The 68-year-old became a diplomat under Aung San Suu Kyi after a long career in the army and has called the “Rohingya issue” very important. Before his removal as ambassador, he had been told by a source in Myanmar’s foreign ministry that his staff were spying on him.
He anticipated in 2021 that the crisis would lead to civil war. “You can see the military government is not going to step back,” he said. “More people will die and the economy is going to collapse. Then anything can happen in our country.”
The court case comes as the war enters its sixth year. More than 100,000 people have been killed and more than 5 million displaced, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
Aung San Suu Kyi, now 81, has been detained on a range charges since the military took power. She was previously held under house arrest for 15 years under a past junta, and was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991. After her election as state counsellor in 2015, she became a pariah for leading a regime that excused a genocide, jailed journalists and locked up critics.

A Ukrainian railway engineer spied on Lyman’s defenses for Russia using Google Maps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:01:41 UTC
03:01:41 KST

A Ukrainian court sentenced the former chief engineer of Lyman’s locomotive depot to 15 years in prison with property confiscation for helping Russia target the frontline city, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said on 11 August. Investigators report he sent a Russian handler the locations of Ukrainian positions intended for guided-bomb and artillery strikes.
Lyman blocks Russia’s northern route toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which are part of Ukraine's fortress belt in the Donbas. As attacks on supply lines intensify, information about Ukrainian positions can help Russia direct bombs and artillery. The case fits a broader pattern of Russian intelligence recruiting people inside Ukraine to locate targets. Russian services have used money and blackmail, including threats against recruits’ families, to secure their cooperation.
According to the SBU, the former engineer traveled around Lyman and its outskirts to record Ukrainian military bases. He marked possible targets on Google Maps, then sent screenshots to a handler in Russia through a messaging app.
The collaborator operated from basement
The agency said an acquaintance whom it described as a “DNR deputy” in occupied Donetsk Oblast connected him with Russian intelligence. The SBU said the man moved into an apartment building’s basement to shelter himself while directing Russian strikes on the community.
SBU officers detained him in Sloviansk in May 2026. The agency said a seized smartphone contained evidence of his reconnaissance and contacts with the Russian side.
The SBU did not identify the man, the court, or any specific strike enabled by his information.
How Russia turns locals into spotters
The Lyman case involved an acquaintance of the former engineer, but Russian services also use money, blackmail, and online platforms to find recruits. The SBU says minors may initially receive simple assignments, such as taking photographs or painting graffiti, before being directed toward more serious sabotage.
Other recruits have allegedly answered Telegram offers of “easy money.” These include a Zaporizhzhia man later convicted of building bombs and a Dnipro suspect accused of activating more than 1,000 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.
Ukraine has prosecuted similar cases before. In November 2024, a court sentenced another Russian agent to 15 years for guiding missile and drone strikes in Zhytomyr Oblast.
More recent cases remain at the allegation stage. The SBU has accused a Kharkiv Oblast man of installing hidden cameras near military sites and a Poltava student of mapping energy facilities while filming air-defense units.

ICE Is Getting Body Cameras. But Will They Help Hold Agents Accountable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:01:25 UTC
03:01:25 KST

All Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field agents will be equipped with body cameras by the end of the month, acting ICE Director David Venturella said. However, the footage acquired by the devices would only be released to the public if it is in “the best interests of the agency,” according to ICE. The policy raises questions about how body cameras are meant to be used in law enforcement, as well as whom they are meant to protect.
Venturella said in his statement last week that the body cameras would help the agency uphold its commitment to “transparency and accountability.”
However, a spokesperson for ICE tells TIME that the body cameras are needed because “the media and sanctuary politicians consistently spread smears about our law enforcement.”
This raises the question: Are the cameras meant to hold ICE agents accountable—or protect the agency?
White House “border czar” Tom Homan indicated that the cameras could be useful for both purposes, saying “body cameras are the way to go” to increase transparency between the agency and the public—but they can also provide insights about split-second behavior under high pressure in the field.
“I think body cameras let the American people know what that officer sees when he takes that action,” Homan said on CBS’s Face the Nation in July. On Fox & Friends Weekend that same month, he went further, saying that body cameras “exonerate more law enforcement than they convict.”
Who they ultimately benefit largely depends on how they are used—in theory and in practice, experts tell TIME.
“Body-worn cameras are only as good as their policies,” says Christopher Schneider, sociologist and professor at Brandon University.
The policies governing body cameras must determine not only when agents are recording, experts say, but also what happens to the footage the cameras collect.
Kirk Burkhalter, a New York Law School professor and former detective with the New York Police Department, believes it is a smart move toward course-correcting after multiple fatal shootings this year by ICE. He calls the rollout of body-worn cameras a “very important first step.”
Why did ICE start using body cameras?
Body cameras became a point of contention after two protesters were killed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers in Minneapolis in January. The deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti both led to disputes about what transpired and whether the use of force was warranted, leading DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to promise in February that agents would be equipped with body cameras going forward.
A policy regarding their use was established that same month, and Congress approved $20 million in funds for purchasing and operating ICE body cameras in April.
Read More: The Chaos and Cruelty of ICE
Body cameras had been issued to more than half of field offices by July, when agents shot and killed two people within the span of a week: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas, on July 7, and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 in Biddeford, Maine. Neither of the incidents were captured by body cameras, though The Intercept reported that the officers in Maine were equipped with recording devices that they were unable to use.
Members of Congress promptly called for stricter oversight.
“In shooting after shooting, we are told that there is no body-worn camera footage of the incident and asked to accept DHS’s account of the incident. Time and again, that account turns out to be a blatant falsehood,” a letter signed by dozens of senators on July 18 said.
But putting cameras in agents’ hands is just a start; they must also be recording when it matters.
When are ICE agents required to turn on body cameras?
The policy says agents should activate cameras “as soon as practicable” at the beginning of an enforcement activity and deactivate them once the activity concludes. Agents who fail to activate their cameras must provide a written explanation, but the policy does not spell out disciplinary consequences for failing to record an encounter.
This is not dissimilar from policies used by other law enforcement agencies, which also typically stop short of codifying disciplinary steps, Schneider says.
“You would think that if an officer was found after an investigation to have intentionally turned the camera off or not turned it on, to engage in misconduct or pretend, you would think they would be fired for that,” he says. “You won't find that in a policy.”
Phillip Atiba Solomon, professor at Yale University and co-founder of the Center for Policing Equity, says that comprehensive policy should not leave key questions unanswered, such as: “What are the consequences if you disobey those rules?”
“A piece of legislation without an enforcement mechanism is a polite request,” he tells TIME.
The policy does require “Field Responsible Officials” to provide operational training to their agents “at least yearly,” focusing on their handling of recordings, privacy compliance, procedures for redacting and sharing data, and civil rights considerations.
But knowing how to use the cameras is different from establishing how useful they actually are in the field.
How effective are body cameras in law enforcement?
Schneider says there is a presiding belief that the presence of body cameras will influence what transpires between civilians and law enforcement officers. Specifically, there is an assumption that they serve as a deterrent.
“The idea is that if a camera is on, of course the officer is not going to engage in misconduct or brutality, and of course people are going to comply with police,” Schneider says. “That's profoundly untrue.”
He points to the murder of George Floyd in 2020 as an example, since the police officers involved were wearing active cameras while the incident unfolded.
Studies show mixed evidence. Some found that body cameras reduce use-of-force incidents and civilian complaints. But when 70 such studies were analyzed together, they showed “no consistent or statistically significant effects,” according to the National Institute of Justice.
Part of the reasoning for this discrepancy, according to Solomon, is that people must believe that what they are doing is wrong in order for them to change their behavior when being observed. In a randomized controlled study that involved thousands of police officers in 2019, researchers wrote that “cameras did not meaningfully affect police behavior on a range of outcomes, including complaints and use of force.”
“Officers—who are not ICE but are regular municipal law enforcement—didn't think that what they were doing was a problem, so we didn't see significant reductions in use of force,” Solomon says of the study.
They must also believe that there will be consequences for their actions, he says. But the Trump Administration’s staunch defense of ICE in the aftermath of this year’s deadly shootings suggests that this component might also be lacking.
In addition to deterrence, body cameras also offer point-of-view documentation.
“The reason why it's so helpful is because it gives the vantage point of the law enforcement officer who's wearing the camera, and you can kind of see and hear what they see and hear,” Burkhalter says. This can give judges, juries, legislators, and the general public a clearer sense of why they responded the way they did at the time.
Read More: When ICE Kills, We Cannot Look Away
Without such video evidence, the public could be left with difficult questions about what exactly transpired in the critical moments of officer-involved fatalities.
When Silverio Villegas González was killed by ICE agents in September 2025 in Illinois, body camera footage captured by local police officers revealed key details about the incident. DHS claimed its officer was “seriously injured” during the altercation and feared for his own life. However, the footage later showed that the officer said his injuries were “nothing major,” undercutting his explanation of events.
Third-party video evidence was similarly instrumental in showing what transpired when officers shot and killed Good in Minneapolis in January. DHS claimed that Good was a “violent rioter” who had tried to run over agents with her car. It said that its officer then fired “defensive shots.” But cell phone footage captured by bystanders contradicted that account.
“The cameras dispel the rumor mill, preventing us from looking at some footage from someone's doorbell cam 50 feet away and trying to decipher what someone had in their hand or what they didn't have in their hand,” Burkhalter says.
Experts have acknowledged, however, that body camera footage is limited—for example, it does not show officers’ facial expressions and may miss key details that are just out of frame.
That makes how it is reviewed, edited, and distributed even more essential.
Who will have access to footage?
When deterrence fails, and use-of-force incidents take place, the footage is paramount in determining who is responsible and paving a path for justice. That raises the question of who has access to the footage and how it can be used.
ICE’s body camera footage will be immediately available to internal personnel and investigators, its policy says, but public access will be strictly restricted and controlled.
“Footage will be available as appropriate for official purposes,” a spokesperson wrote in a statement to TIME. “Body camera footage must be reviewed on a case-by-case basis due to privacy concerns for innocent bystanders.”
Burkhalter says that the agency’s approach aligns generally with existing law enforcement policies.
“I haven't reviewed all local law policies, but I can assure you that very few agencies have an administrative regulation that says we will release all body cam footage within ‘X’ amount of hours,” he says. “That would just be impossible, given most of those cases involve some type of criminal investigation.”
Policies vary by municipality. For the NYPD, for example, it is codified that body-worn camera footage will be released within 30 calendar days of a critical incident, which includes “incidents involving the discharge of a firearm by an officer that result in a member of the public being struck, as well as police use of force that results in serious injury or death.” Other cities require the police commissioner to personally sign off on the release of footage that may be of interest to the public.
The ICE policy says that when serious bodily injury or death in custody is captured on camera, ICE must “expeditiously review the footage,” and if it is determined it is in the “best interests” of the agency, then it must publicly release within 72 hours of the event or “as soon as operationally feasible.”
Given how the policy is written, and how ICE has operated in recent years, Burkhalter says, “I don't see … the agency releasing footage that is going to seriously harm their public image.”
The footage is also subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), giving members of the public another avenue to seek recordings regardless of whether the agency chooses to release them. But a FOIA request does not guarantee disclosure: Footage may be withheld or redacted under applicable exemptions, and requests can take considerable time to resolve.
Schneider’s concern is that, without more explicit guidelines about what acting in its own “best interests” means, the agency could be inconsistent and selective about releasing records. For example, it might prioritize the distribution of footage that puts the agency in a good light or supports the Trump Administration’s deportation agenda.
“Probably they're going to release some of those videos that involve undocumented immigrants who are armed and are also criminals,” he says. “Some people might start assuming because of what's being shared that, ‘Oh well, maybe all these undocumented immigrants are criminals and have weapons—because this is all I see.’”
Who else are the cameras watching?
The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other activist groups generally support the use of body cameras, but they have also warned that without good guardrails, “They risk becoming just another police surveillance device—and one with very real potential to invade privacy.”
Many municipalities require law enforcement officers to turn off their body-worn cameras during sensitive encounters, such as meeting with a confidential informant. ICE does not address such circumstances head-on, but it outlines exceptions for when body-worn cameras would not be worn or turned on, including when an agent is engaging in undercover activity; conducting interviews inside jails, prisons, or detention centers; and aboard commercial flights.
Solomon notes that privacy is one of his biggest concerns—especially because the Trump Administration has not ruled out the presence of ICE officers at voting sites in November.
Although DHS previously told election officials that ICE would not target polling locations, both Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Trump have since declined to categorically rule out a federal immigration enforcement presence at the polls.
ICE officers with recording devices could deter voters from turning out, he explains: “If you're not sure, or if you've got a record, and you just don't want to be on the grid, you are not going to the polling place.”
Those concerns come amid a broader debate over how law enforcement agencies use the data collected by surveillance technology. Recently, that has been expressed through a widening concern about the use of Flock cameras: automatic license plate readers that are cropping up in major cities in the U.S. Residents worry about the technology being used to identify and track people traveling to sensitive locations like protests and specialized health care facilities. There have already been reports from watchdog organizations that officers have used the cameras to stalk their romantic interests.
Solomon therefore expressed skepticism about equipping thousands of DHS field agents, across the country, with even more advanced surveillance tools.
“We are giving folks who have been tasked with terrorizing vulnerable communities the ability to further surveil those communities,” Solomon says. “That's not much of a step forward, if you ask me.”

Ex-Marine Robert Gilman tried to get out of a Russian prison by volunteering for the invasion of Ukraine. He got out on humanitarian grounds instead — so what does Putin want in return?

Ex-Marine Robert Gilman tried to get out of a Russian prison by volunteering for the invasion of Ukraine. He got out on humanitarian grounds instead — so what does Putin want in return?
Russia has released Robert Gilman, a 32-year-old American whom a court had sentenced to 10 years in a penal colony. Gilman was detained in Voronezh in January 2022. According to the Russian authorities, he kicked a police officer in the leg after being pulled off a train for causing a drunken disturbance. The court first gave him four and a half years, then raised the term to 10 over claims that he had attacked guards and an investigator behind bars.
Gilman said his troubles began with poisoned vodka. He said he remembered little about the incident with the police officer in Voronezh. He acknowledged drinking vodka and said something may have been added to it. There were at least five attacks on officers of the Federal Penitentiary Service and the Investigative Committee, Russia’s main federal investigative agency. One sent someone to the hospital. Gilman cited abuse in prison and attempts to keep his conditions from worsening.
Gilman’s family has insisted that he ended up behind bars solely because of his citizenship. His father, Vladimir Gilman, said in 2024 that his son had struck the officer accidentally while he was sick, had caused no serious injuries, and had still received a near-maximum sentence. The accusations of fights in the penal colonies and the pretrial detention center, he said, were the result of provocations meant to bring new charges against his son. He was convinced Robert had been convicted unlawfully so that Russia could later trade him for one of its citizens imprisoned in the United States, and he urged Washington to press for his son’s release.
Robert Gilman has Russian roots. According to his family and to Gilman himself, his parents are from St. Petersburg, he was born in Poland, and he had spent his entire life in the United States. He served in the U.S. Marine Corps and then taught English. He ended up in Russia in transit: he was flying to Moldova for work when he fell ill at the airport and had to stay to get treatment and replace his passport. Somewhere in the process, he got the idea of applying for Russian citizenship. In court, he spoke both English and Russian, and he once quoted, perhaps unwittingly, a meme well known to Russian speakers. “I really regret it. I was just walking toward success. And I find that from now on I will keep walking toward success,” he said in Russian.
Gilman asked to be sent to fight in the war against Ukraine, and he said staff at his pretrial detention center had put him up to it. At a hearing in April 2026, he abruptly announced that he wanted to be sent to fight in the “special military operation,” the Kremlin’s official term for the war. “My father served in Russia, his father served in Russia. My great-grandfather was a captain third rank and took two bullets at Stalingrad. So I believe I’m fully fit for service and am following in their footsteps,” he told the judge. She advised him to take the matter to a military enlistment office. Gilman replied that detention center staff had suggested he make the statement in court specifically. He had said earlier that he had pleaded guilty in the case involving the police officer because he had been promised a lighter sentence that never came.
Gilman’s family has long expressed concern about his health. A week ago, news broke that he might be dying. Global Reach, the human rights group that represented the family, said that Gilman had long been pumped full of unidentified drugs and that in June 2026 he had been admitted to the psychiatric ward of a civilian hospital in a state of dissociative stupor. He could not communicate, was being fed through a tube, and his life was in danger, the group told Reuters. The Reuters report also showed that U.S. officials were already working on the case: on July 23, Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised Gilman’s release with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Gilman was released soon afterward. On August 12 — six days after the Reuters report on the threat to his life — Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s special envoy, posted photos of Gilman and his family aboard his own plane. Witkoff has flown to Russia repeatedly for talks with Vladimir Putin. Gilman looks severely emaciated in the pictures, but he is conscious and smiling. After arriving in the United States, he was scheduled to be sent to a military hospital in Texas for a medical and psychological evaluation, Global Reach representatives told The New York Times.
Trump said Putin had released Gilman on humanitarian grounds and had asked for nothing in return. Ivor Bennett, the Moscow correspondent for Sky News, found that suspicious. “For now it’s a gift, but Russia will undoubtedly be hoping for something in return,” he wrote, suggesting that Moscow wants to win back Trump’s support in its negotiations with Kyiv. Dmitry Drize, a political commentator for Kommersant FM, also said the release could be groundwork for a new round of talks with Washington on peace in Ukraine.
Five more Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, according to Global Reach. One of them is Steven Hubbard, 73, who was detained in 2022 during Russia’s occupation of Izium, in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, and accused of taking part in Ukraine’s territorial defense. A Russian court sentenced him to nearly seven years in prison. Ukrainian prisoners who were held with Hubbard and later released have described how he was mistreated.

Greenland forces Trump-linked US oil firm to delay drilling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:00:41 UTC
03:00:41 KST

Greenland authorities have forced a US oil company connected to Donald Trump to postpone drilling wells in the Arctic territory, defying claims by the US president’s envoy that Americans could be extracting crude by next year.
Amid Trump’s imperialist threats, tensions have been rising on Greenland’s eastern coast after the oil company brought drilling equipment ashore in July without permission, drawing a “strong warning” from the government.
Just week before Greenland Energy intended to sink its first wells into the tundra, the government said on Thursday: “The necessary regulatory process cannot be completed, and the necessary approvals cannot therefore be obtained before the planned start of drilling.”
It said that during talks Greenlandic officials had expressed concern that the timetable was too tight to assess the environmental and social impact.
The authorities will have to decide whether to sanction drilling in a protected wetland that is home to rare birds and the muskoxen on which local hunters depend. At the earliest, drilling could now commence in the winter of 2027, the government and the company said.
That is a long way off the prediction made as recently as May by Jeff Landry, the hard-right Louisiana governor whom Trump named as his envoy to Greenland. He said after a visit that oil supposedly lying under Greenland could ease the energy crisis caused by the US attack on Iran.
Landry, whose stated goal is to “make Greenland a part of the US”, said: “We could have those barrels on production within 10 months or so.”
Robert Price, the Greenland Energy chief executive, who maintains that oil worth $1tn could lie under the remote Jameson Land region, said: “Greenland Energy remains committed to advancing its oil exploration programme responsibly and in accordance with Greenland’s regulatory process, and in full compliance with Greenlandic authorities.”
Price added: “We will use this time to refine our plans and deepen relationships with local communities, strategic partners and relevant authorities.”
Since a rich friend put the idea of acquiring Greenland in Trump’s head during his first term, the president has threatened to do so by buying it from Denmark, seizing it with military force or cutting a deal.
Shareholders in Greenland Energy had been hoping for a “Trump pump”, a presidential endorsement that could send the New York-listed stock rocketing. But on Wednesday the price fell by more than a third after the drilling delay was announced.
Price had said a ship bringing 300 containers of drilling kit would set sail from Canada for Greenland in September, with a first well to be sunk the following month. He told a community meeting – falsely – that Greenland had granted permission for the company to start landing equipment.
Greenland Energy’s British partner 80 Mile said in an update for investors on Wednesday that the delay was due to the need to “complete the permitting and regulatory approval process”.
80 Mile holds exploration licences granted before Greenland stopped issuing them in 2021, citing the climate crisis.
Greenland Energy, formed last year, has announced plans to spend $60m (£44m) raised from investors to fund drilling in exchange for a majority stake in the project.
Its representatives have said its oil venture is “not related to American annexation”, yet the company has established multiple connections to the Trump administration.
Phil McGraw, better known as the chatshow host Dr Phil, has a deal with Greenland Energy to “capture the mission of these modern-day wildcatters” for a documentary series to be broadcast on television and social media. He recently appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump, having served on the president’s religious freedom commission.
A US navy veteran who is working on Golden Dome, the missile defence plan for which Trump says controlling Greenland is “vital”, sits on Greenland Energy’s board. And Kenneth Griffin, a Wall Street billionaire who gave $1m towards Trump’s second inauguration, bought 9% of Greenland Energy’s shares in April.
Rod McIllree, 80 Mile’s boss, said: “While we are disappointed that the timing of the Jameson drilling programme has been impacted, the company remains fully committed to advancing this highly prospective project.”

Russia uses four main narratives regarding POWs and missing persons — CCD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:59:00 UTC
02:59:00 KST

Russia uses four main narratives regarding POWs and missing persons — CCD
Kyrylo Viktorov, head of the Department for Countering Information Threats to National Security at the Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD), reported this during a press conference at Ukrinform.
According to him, the study covered the period from January 1 to August 11, 2026. Using specialized software, analysts examined more than 94,000 publications from nearly 24,000 sources. The study covered both Ukrainian- and Russian-language segments of the information space, while the total number of views of the analyzed materials reached 419 million.
The Center's representative emphasized that not all of the publications analyzed contained destructive narratives. Analysts identified messages that Russia uses to carry out information operations, as well as the corresponding narratives and their objectives.
"The main pattern revealed by our analysis is that Russia often does not need to invent the event itself. It is enough to use a real event and impose the desired interpretation of it on the audience," Viktorov said.
According to him, the first main direction is the dissemination of claims that Ukraine allegedly does not want to return its prisoners of war. Russian and pro-Russian sources systematically promote the idea that Ukraine supposedly refuses to conduct exchanges, does not want to return certain prisoners, or is interested only in bringing back specific categories of servicemen.
"In this way, they try to shift responsibility for the difficulties or delays in the exchange process onto Ukraine, onto the Ukrainian side," the Center's representative explained.
The second direction, according to Viktorov, concerns manipulation of the issue of missing persons. Russian sources attempt to fill the information vacuum with their own explanations, including claims that the missing-person status is supposedly used to conceal the actual number of people killed or to avoid making payments to their families.
The third direction involves creating a positive image of Russian captivity. To this end, Russia uses videos and statements by Ukrainian prisoners of war that emphasize allegedly good treatment by Russia, an alleged unwillingness to return to Ukraine, or reluctance to go back to the front.
"A person who is being held captive cannot be considered a free participant in information communication, especially when we are talking about Russian captivity," Viktorov stressed.
He described the fourth direction as discrediting Ukraine by spreading fake information and disinformation about allegedly inadequate conditions for Russian prisoners of war, lack of medical care, poor food, beatings, or other forms of cruel treatment.
The Center's representative noted that this ultimately creates a distorted narrative: "Russia supposedly treats Ukrainian prisoners of war humanely, while Ukraine, on the contrary, allegedly treats Russians brutally."
He emphasized that these narratives are interconnected and have a common goal — to undermine trust in Ukraine. This includes undermining servicemen's trust in the state, families' trust in institutions responsible for searching for and returning people, citizens' trust in verified information, and international partners' trust in Ukraine.
Viktorov concluded that periods when public attention to the issue rises sharply are particularly favorable for such information operations — including during prisoner exchanges and negotiations, as well as when lists or new information about prisoners of war and missing persons emerge.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian law enforcement agencies currently have information on more than 114,000 missing civilians and military personnel.

Under new rules, countries affected by war will not be able to host Eurovision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:57:57 UTC
02:57:57 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Under new Eurovision rules announced Wednesday, countries affected by war or serious geopolitical instability will no longer be able to host the song contest if safety and security are at risk.
Eurovision said in a statement that its governing Reference Group approved the changes following its annual review and feedback from participating broadcasters after the 2026 contest in Vienna, ahead of next year's edition in Bulgaria.
"The Rules of the Contest now say the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," it said.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) may commission an independent security assessment and appoint an alternative host broadcaster if necessary.
The host broadcaster, it said, will organize the contest in its own right and will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member.
Under other revisions, starting next year, all competing artists must also be at least 18 years old on the day of their first rehearsal, up from 16, according to the statement.
Eurovision also clarified that lead singers must perform the main melody live. Pre-recorded elements and backing tracks remain permitted but cannot replace or unduly assist the lead vocal.
Eurovision Director Martin Green said the changes aim to strengthen clarity, artist protection, and safety while preserving the contest's “spirit and integrity.”

Russia Executed at Least 345 Surrendered Soldiers and Killed 375 Ukrainians in Captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:57:26 UTC
02:57:26 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Executed at Least 345 Surrendered Soldiers and Killed 375 Ukrainians in Captivity
Russian forces have executed at least 345 Ukrainian service members who surrendered and killed 375 Ukrainian citizens whose deaths in Russian captivity have been verified.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets made the statement during a press conference at Ukrinform focused on Russian disinformation concerning prisoners of war, exchanges, and people missing in action.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the ombudsman, the 345 documented executions involved Ukrainian soldiers who had clearly surrendered, including by laying down their weapons, raising their hands, or lying on the ground to demonstrate that they were no longer taking part in hostilities.
He added that Russian troops would inspect the surrendered soldiers and, in some documented cases, order them to remove their clothing before shooting them at close range.
Lubinets stressed that the killing of service members who have surrendered constitutes a separate war crime.
He also said that Ukraine has a separate list of 375 Ukrainian citizens whose deaths in Russian captivity have been verified.
“These are Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees who were verified as military or civilian detainees held by the Russian Federation. Some were also verified through the international verification mechanism of the International Committee of the Red Cross. All of them returned home on shields, meaning that the Russian Federation handed over the bodies of 375 Ukrainian citizens who had been tortured to death,” Lubinets said.
The ombudsman said Russia had established a system in which torture, humiliation, and unlawful convictions are used as instruments of war.
“We call this system the ‘Moscow conventions.’ This is not a legal term, but a definition of Russian practices of treating Ukrainians: under these ‘conventions,’ instead of protection there is torture, instead of medical assistance there is suffering, instead of justice there are show trials, and instead of returning home there are years of captivity or death,” Lubinets said.
According to the ombudsman, Ukrainian prisoners of war in Russia are subjected to virtually all forms of torture outlined in the Istanbul Protocol.
Lubinets said Ukrainian authorities had documented 695 forms of torture used against Ukrainian POWs and civilian detainees, as well as 860 cases of improper detention conditions.
He added that 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war had experienced torture, which he described as systematic in Russian detention facilities.
Against this backdrop, Russian forces have established a specialized combat brigade made up of Ukrainian prisoners of war and Ukrainians coerced into defecting.
Forcing prisoners of war into military service would violate international law governing the treatment of captives. The reported use of POWs for military purposes also follows broader patterns of coercion and abuse documented in Russian detention facilities, where Ukrainian captives have reported systematic torture, deliberate deprivation of food, and other forms of physical and psychological abuse.

Swedish court frees Russian tourists detained during camping trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:56:42 UTC
02:56:42 KST

A migration court in Stockholm has overturned a police decision to detain Russian citizens Semyon and Tatyana, who were recently detained during a tourist trip to Sweden. The court ordered both to be released immediately, according to a report by the Russian Antiwar Committee.
The court found no evidence in the case file constituting grounds for suspicion that Semyon and Tatyana had committed any crime. The ruling also said the Russians had cooperated with Swedish authorities and that police had failed to present convincing facts indicating that the couple had come to the country for purposes other than tourism.
“The mere fact of Russian citizenship and the fact that they speak Russian cannot be grounds for a detention decision,” the defense said in its complaint.
Police had insisted that Semyon and Tatyana posed a threat to Sweden’s internal security and might try to flee if released — arguments which the court found to be unsubstantiated.
The couple were detained on the morning of Aug. 6 while vacationing near the town of Furuvik. The Antiwar Committee previously told The Insider that Semyon and Tatyana had lived in Spain for the past five years and had come to Sweden as tourists. They were traveling with a tent, set up camp by the sea and went fishing.
A private home belonging to a person protected by the Swedish authorities was located near their campsite, something the tourists were not aware of, according to the Antiwar Committee. Security guards at the home called the police. Both the guards and law enforcement officers were reportedly drawn to the couple because they were speaking Russian and had two hiking walkie-talkies.
As The Insider previously reported, the Russians also could not clearly explain to the police why they had chosen that particular place to spend the night. They later told human rights advocates that they enjoy hiking and had decided to camp by the water.
After the detention, police ordered the couple deported, and Semyon and Tatyana were placed in a migration center. The Antiwar Committee said at the time that the decision to detain and deport the couple were based solely on three factors: their Russian accents, the walkie-talkies, and the tourists’ inability to convincingly explain their choice of campsite.
Margarita Kuchusheva, a consul with the Anti-War Committee, told The Insider that the case was not unprecedented:
“This is not the first case in which Sweden has recognized Russian citizens as a threat to national security. Unfortunately, anti-war Russians sometimes fall under these criteria as well. In this case, [they were] simply a pair of tourists who chose to go on a camping trip. Challenging such a status is extremely difficult, and it can seriously damage a person’s life, such as when one wants to apply for a visa.”
The Antiwar Committee added that Semyon (who works as a game developer) and Tatyana oppose Russia's invasion of Ukraine, do humanitarian work, and help teenage emigres adapt to life abroad.

25 years North Macedonian peace: reconciliation in sight?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:56:00 UTC
02:56:00 KST

25 years Ohrid Agreement: Is N. Macedonia's peace holding?
August 12, 2026
The guns fell silent in 2001, but North Macedonia is still grappling with the legacy of its ethnic conflict.
Twenty-five years after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended the fighting, ethnic Macedonians and Albanians live in peace, yet analysts say genuine reconciliation remains unattained.
The six-month conflict that erupted in February 2001 is often described as the final chapter of former Yugoslavia's violent breakup.
But unlike the wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it was contained before it could spiral into a larger tragedy, thanks in large part to a political compromise brokered by NATO, the United States and leading EU countries.
Agreement enters a new phase
Тwenty-five years later, the political order that emerged from the Ohrid Framework Agreement is entering a new phase.
When the conservative Macedonian VMRO-DPMNE party returned to power two years ago, the Democratic Union for Integration (DUI), the main ethnic Albanian party, went into opposition.
This development ended two decades of governing influence for Ali Ahmeti, who transformed himself from leader of the ethnic Albanian National Liberation Army (NLA) during the 2001 conflict into one of the country's most influential political figures.
Ahmeti, who swapped his guerrilla uniform for tailored black suits and white shirts after the Ohrid Agreement, now argues that ethnic relations have deteriorated over the past two years.
"Attacks on the official use of the Albanian language, the abolition of equitable and adequate representation, the weakening of mechanisms designed to prevent majoritarian rule and the promotion of a monoethnic concept of the state are serious signals about the direction in which the country is moving," he said in a statement marking August 2, North Macedonia's national holiday.
Balancing ethnic diversity and political stability
Home to a large ethnic Albanian minority, North Macedonia has spent much of the past quarter-century trying to balance its ethnic diversity within a stable political system.
According to the latest census, Albanians make up over a quarter of North Macedonia's population of 1.8 million.
For Bujar Osmani, a senior DUI official and former foreign minister, the key question is no longer how much of the Ohrid Agreement has been implemented, but whether its gains can be preserved.
"On the 25th anniversary of the Ohrid Agreement, the question is no longer only what we have implemented since 2001. The question is whether we will allow, within a few years, the dismantling of what has kept North Macedonia stable for two and a half decades," he told DW.
2001: A wound that has not fully healed
The legacy of the 2001 conflict runs deep.
The fighting claimed the lives of 72 soldiers and police officers, while the number of ethnic Albanian insurgents killed remains disputed, with estimates ranging from about 100 to several hundred. More than 170,000 people were displaced, including 74,000 within the country.
The Ohrid Framework Agreement that ended the conflict reshaped North Macedonia's political system, introducing power-sharing mechanisms designed to give minority communities a greater voice in decision-making.
Laws affecting sensitive issues such as language, education and national symbols require support not only from a parliamentary majority but also from representatives of minority groups.
While largely in line with European standards on minority rights, the arrangement did not end disputes over equality and representation.
"The agreement achieved a large part of its historic mission, but its essence cannot be declared complete," Osmani said. "Ohrid is not an administrative checklist that can be fulfilled once and then archived. It is a system of balance that must be respected continuously."
Macedonian majority also voices grievances
At the heart of the debate are differing views on Ohrid's legacy.
While many ethnic Macedonians argue that affirmative representation policies have created unfair advantages for Albanians, Albanian politicians say the real concern is the gradual erosion of rights secured under the agreement.
"There is discrimination that frustrates many in the Macedonian community because Albanians are often given priority in recruitment to meet representation quotas in the public sector," said Stojance Angelov, a police general during the 2001 conflict.
Angelov said such practices put ethnic affiliation ahead of qualifications.
Osmani rejects that narrative, arguing that recent government policies have weakened protections for Albanians that were introduced after the conflict.
"At first, all of this was concealed behind political propaganda, technical explanations and claims that it was merely modernization of the system. Today, as that noise gradually fades, it is becoming much clearer what is actually being called into question," he said.
Defensive nationalism on the rise
Domestic and international observers warn that years of political crises and disputes over national identity have slowed reforms and reinforced ethnic divisions.
Harald Schenker of the German peacebuilding organization Pro Peace says the Ohrid Agreement transformed North Macedonia's institutions, but not necessarily relations between its communities.
"Ethnic distance is increasing, the education system remains segregated, and the two communities understand each other less and less," he told DW.
According to Schenker, the agreement created new institutions and rules of governance but failed to foster reconciliation or a shared vision for the future.
"Each side maintains its own interpretation of what happened in 2001," he said. "Twenty-five years on, there is a need for platforms where people can discuss these differences openly. Different perspectives exist, but people need to talk to one another."
Stalled EU integration
At the same time, years of stalled EU integration have fueled uncertainty about the country's direction. Although North Macedonia became an EU candidate country in 2005, negotiations have still not formally begun.
After overcoming a decades-long dispute with Greece over its name, North Macedonia has faced new obstacles stemming from Bulgaria's demands relating to history, language and national identity.
The prolonged stalemate has not only frustrated reform efforts but has also deepened interethnic tensions, as the fading prospect of EU membership has removed one of the few unifying projects shared by both Macedonians and Albanians.
Against that backdrop, questions about North Macedonia's future remain closely tied to the legacy of the Ohrid Agreement. Next month, the country will mark 35 years since independence from the former Yugoslavia.
Osmani does not believe the country faces the risk of a new conflict but warns that ethnic tensions can build gradually.
"I do not believe citizens want a new problem," he said. "But ethnic tensions do not begin with conflict. They begin when one community gradually loses confidence that the system treats it as an equal."
Angelov shares that view.
"For me, the greatest achievement is that, whereas we once looked at each other through rifle sights, today I drink coffee with some of the veteran fighters of the Albanian NLA," he said.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

Austrian court convicts Belarusians over supplying Russian arms industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:54:46 UTC
02:54:46 KST

Austrian court convicts Belarusians over supplying Russian arms industry
VIENNA, Aug 12 - An Austrian court on Wednesday convicted two Belarusian cousins of violating export controls by supplying equipment to Russian companies that Austria's government says was used to make military items like engines for missiles and fighter jets.
The primary defendant, a 28-year-old man who has not been named, was the director of a Vienna-based firm that used a network of shell companies in third countries and faked end-user certificates to ship special metalworking tools and CNC machines, which can be used to make parts and tools, to Russia.
The other defendant was a 24-year-old woman who dealt with the company's accounts. Both were stakeholders in the company and pleaded guilty.
The man was handed a 21-month prison sentence, 19 of which were suspended, meaning he was released since he had been in custody since his arrest in May. The woman was given a 15-month suspended sentence. They declined to appeal against the ruling.
"I am truly sorry for the whole situation," the main defendant said. He and his cousin spoke briefly before declining to answer further questions.
He said he had acted at the instruction of his father and uncle, who both worked at an unspecified Russian company. The prosecution agreed he had not played a "leading" role in the scheme, which had been in place since 2022 and was recently exposed by the Austrian authorities.
Evidence seized during four raids in August last year indicated that industrial goods worth more than €3.3 million had been delivered to Russian arms manufacturers since 2022, the Austrian interior ministry said on Monday. REUTERS

'I think we'll keep it': Trump says US controls Hormuz, IDF believes blockade 'highly effective'
Unknown

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said the United States is in control of the Strait of Hormuz.
"The USA has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT! Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, their remaining soldiers are unpaid, the IRGC is decimated and fleeing, and their 'Leadership' is uncertain, at best!" Trump continued. "They have No Money - Their country is “shot.” All they have is FAKE NEWS and 300% INFLATION, and getting worse! Iran is all talk and no action, the Bully of the Middle East No Longer."
"Praise be to Allah!" Trump concluded.
Israeli officials believe blockade is wrecking Iranian economy
Israel is highly satisfied with the continued US maritime blockade of Iran, assessing that it is having a dramatic impact on the Iranian economy.
Two Israeli officials told The Jerusalem Post that during a Security Cabinet meeting about a week ago, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir told ministers: “The blockade of Iran is highly effective. The economic crisis there is getting worse.”
One of the blockade’s most significant effects has been on Iran’s ports and maritime trade routes. Because the Iranian economy depends heavily on those routes to import and export goods, raw materials, fuel, and other essential products, the blockade has caused sustained disruptions to port operations and supply chains.
The growing difficulty of exporting goods is also expected to worsen Iran’s shortage of foreign currency, making it increasingly difficult for Tehran to finance imports of essential products, including fuel, food, and industrial raw materials, even when those goods are brought into the country overland.
Experts estimate that Iran’s economy could contract by a staggering 5.6% this year, which would mark its sharpest decline since 1988.
As the blockade continues, declining revenues combined with rising import and reconstruction costs are expected to further limit Tehran’s ability to finance day-to-day government operations, rebuild damaged infrastructure, develop its military capabilities, and continue supporting its proxies.
Iranian citizens have largely remained off the streets since the protests in January, which were brutally suppressed by the regime and resulted in the deaths of thousands, and possibly tens of thousands, of people, with only isolated demonstrations taking place since then.
That relative calm has persisted despite annual inflation reaching 88.6%, according to Iranian authorities, while food prices have surged 130% over the past year. The rial has also fallen to a new low, losing approximately 20% of its value since the beginning of the war.
Israeli and US assessments are that the deteriorating economic situation will intensify domestic pressure on the Iranian regime. Long lines recently seen at gas stations are one indication of growing concerns over fuel supplies.
The Iranian government has sought to avoid cutting subsidies on basic goods, a step that helped trigger major waves of protests in 2017 and 2019. Nevertheless, Tehran has been unable to fully shield the public from significant price increases. The price of bread, for example, has risen by approximately 150%.
The assessment in Israel is that the longer the blockade remains in place, the greater the cumulative damage to Iran’s economy will become. That could set off a chain reaction in which worsening economic conditions place greater pressure on the Iranian public, which in turn increases pressure on the regime.
US has mine swept entire Strait of Hormuz, Trump tells reporters
Trump said on Monday that the United States controls the Strait of Hormuz and had swept the strategic oil waterway for Iranian mines.
"Look, the only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States Navy," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've mine-swept the entire strait."
 
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to six that day, compared with a 10-day average of about 11 vessels, shipping data showed, amid fading hopes of a peace deal between the US and Iran.
Four commodity vessels, including two empty oil product tankers, entered the waterway, data from Kpler showed on Tuesday. Two vessels - a small tanker laden with liquefied petroleum gas and another carrying residual fuels - exited the Strait, the data showed.
 
In pre-war days, about 130 to 140 ships typically transited the strait.
Iran fears economic sanctions more than military strikes, Trump's UN envoy says
Iran is more afraid of US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent than Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday.
“When they’re coming to the table with our negotiators, they are talking about cash, cash, cash. Because they’ll absorb the bombings," he said.
Trump also emphasized the economic pressure on Iran in a phone call with Axios on Sunday.
"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he stated.
One US official told Axios that during active warfare, Tehran can temporarily avoid dealing with the economic consequences of the fighting. But as strikes have paused, it is forced to confront the reality of its economic situation, with no solution easily available.
Leo Feierberg Better, Esther Davis, and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

In May, Syrian state TV reported Jordanian strikes on a drugs and weapons storage site in Suwayda province.
Jordan had previously carried out strikes on southern Syria targeting drug-trafficking networks.

Everyone wants to ‘tax the rich.’ In New York City, it’s getting complicated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Everyone wants to ‘tax the rich.’ In New York City, it’s getting complicated
NEW YORK (AP) — Across the U.S., calls to “tax the rich” have become potent political slogans. But even in Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s New York, getting the wealthy to pay more isn’t playing out as smoothly as supporters hoped.
What seemed at first like an easy idea — slapping a new tax on people who own luxury second homes in the Big Apple but live elsewhere most of the year — has instead created a lot of confusion in the city’s notoriously convoluted world of real estate arrangements.
“It seems very simple but the more you dig into it, the more nuances you look at, the more complicated it gets,” said Gary Bingel, a state and local tax expert and partner at EisnerAmper, an accounting firm.
It has also prompted pushback from both the city’s very wealthy and the merely moderately wealthy.
President Donald Trump, whose gilded Manhattan penthouse could be subject to the tax since his primary residence is now in Florida, said he was looking into whether federal intervention could “avert this disaster, before it is too late.”
A group of homeowners sued over the city’s rollout of the tax, arguing that officials had not done enough to figure out who would have to pay the tax and instead made it property owners’ responsibility. A judge temporarily paused the process this week, but the city moved to appeal, allowing the tax effort to continue until it’s sorted out in court.
Securing a new tax on multimillion-dollar second homes, known as pied-à-terres, was an early win for Mamdani in his quest to raise taxes on the city’s highest earners to pay for his ambitious liberal agenda.
The so-called pied-à-terre tax would levy a new surcharge on one-, two- and three-family homes valued at more than $5 million, as well as condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more, if those dwellings are not a person’s primary residence.
The idea, according to officials, would bring $500 million to the city’s coffers annually, paid primarily by bigwigs who get to enjoy city life but don’t pay city income taxes.
That’s where things start to get hairy.
It’s common for high rollers to place their properties in trusts, obscuring ownership while allowing the property to pass more easily to family members. Limited liability companies can similarly shield an owner’s identity, also making it hard for government officials to tell who actually lives in any given apartment.
From there, there are numerous arrangements that can complicate who would be subject to the tax. For example, letting a distant family member stay at a second home without formal documentation, or if someone owns one or more properties and rents them out, but the tenants don’t have documentation that the unit is their primary residence.
“Those situations make it difficult to prove people are in there,” said Mark Limardo, a partner at the law firm Herrick in Manhattan who focuses on taxes. “The concept is simple, but the ownership rules and the documentation rules have made it very complicated.”
Outcry and litigation
City Hall, for its part, argues that it shouldn’t be difficult to provide proof that someone actually lives in the city and says that its finance department is experienced in parsing tangled webs of paperwork.
Mamdani, no stranger to razzing wealthy people, debuted the tax with a video singling out hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin by standing outside a Manhattan penthouse the billionaire purchased for around $239 million. The clip sent Mamdani’s supporters swooning, but Griffin later said it was “frightening” that a public official would call attention to one of his homes, especially after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in the same neighborhood.
The city then published an expansive online list of property owners who it said could be subject to the tax, listing their names, addresses and property values. The list, which the city is legally required to publish, inflamed tensions between the mayor and the city’s wealthy, many of whom argued the roll amounted to doxing or public shaming.
The administration has mailed notices to a much smaller group — about 17,000 properties — that it suspected would be subject to the tax, telling them they could apply for exemptions. Mamdani announced the mailers in a celebratory social media post that read: “If you have a second home in New York City worth more than $5M, check your mailbox when you’re back in the five boroughs — because you’ve got mail.”
He later pushed back the deadline for exemption requests following public outcry from people who claimed to have received the letters in error or had trouble navigating the process.
Stewart Sterk, a real estate law professor at Cardozo School of Law in New York, predicted last week’s lawsuit wouldn’t be the last, saying he expected many of the targets of the tax to file individual cases over denied exemptions, given the vast number of apartments at play and the various arrangements people have connecting them to their properties.
“This is going to be a subject of litigation for quite a while,” he said.

Travis Kelce: Chiefs camp offers welcomed ‘sanctuary’ after closely watched wedding to Taylor Swift

Unknown Publisher

Travis Kelce: Chiefs camp offers welcome ‘sanctuary’ after closely watched wedding to Taylor Swift
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (AP) — Travis Kelce likes to call training camp with the Kansas City Chiefs his “sanctuary,” whether that be the quiet, hourlong drive north to Missouri Western State University or the solitude that he finds while living in college dorms for a month.
Such refuge was probably never more welcome than on the heels of this past summer.
It was just over a month ago that Kelce exchanged vows with Taylor Swift in a star-studded wedding that tied together one of the best tight ends in NFL history with the biggest pop star on the planet. At the intimate gathering in cavernous Madison Square Garden, Adam Sandler served as the surprise officiant, Stevie Nicks performed to a crowd of sports and entertainment icons, and fans lined the New York City sidewalks outside the historic venue hoping to catch a glimpse of it all.
“The wedding was the best night of my life,” Kelce said Wednesday, speaking for the first time at camp. “I appreciate everybody who came out and celebrated and had fun with us. That’s about all I got for that night. It was a crazy night.”
The guest list included actors Bradley Cooper, Zoë Kravitz, Hugh Grant and Ethan Hawke; models Gigi Hadid and Karlie Kloss; comic Chris Rock; film director Steven Spielberg; and plenty of NFL players, including retired quarterback Tom Brady and several of Kelce’s teammates with the Chiefs, like his best friend and quarterback, Patrick Mahomes.
The Swift-Kelce relationship began with his failed attempt at giving her a friendship bracelet at a concert. Kelce invited Swift to watch him play at Arrowhead Stadium, she took him up on the offer, and the rest of their courtship has been a celebrity fairy tale.
Right down to the nuptials at Madison Square Garden, which has always captured Kelce’s imagination, and where Swift has played to plenty of sold-out shows; she also turned up there to watch the Knicks play the Spurs in the NBA Finals in June.
“I always told myself I’d go for a playoff game when the Knicks were rocking, and my wife went when I was stuck in minicamp,” Kelce said with a wry smile. “It was kind of cool to live out my childhood dream to be in that venue. I can’t thank the owners of MSG enough for allowing us the opportunity to do that, knowing we wanted a private event.”
Besides the wedding, Kelce has been busy pursuing several business opportunities since the end of last season, including his decision to buy a small share of David Blitzer’s stake in his hometown Cleveland Guardians.
That puts him into rivalry territory with Mahomes, who owns his own small stake in the Kansas City Royals.
Yet on the field, the quarterback and tight end continue in lockstep, and never has it been more important for them to lift each other up. Mahomes is coming off a season-ending knee injury that required surgery in December, and Kelce is trying to prove that at age 36 — he turns 37 in October — he can still get it done in a young man’s game.
“I still got a lot of love for this game. I still think I can go out and play at a high level,” Kelce said. “I want to go out there and prove to myself that I can play at a better level than last year. I think that’s the biggest thing for me.”
There are few things that Kelce has not accomplished over 13 seasons on an NFL field. He’s won three Super Bowl rings, was voted first-team All-Pro four times, and he has been invited to the Pro Bowl each of the last 11 seasons.
He contemplated retirement prior to last year, but the fact that Kansas City had just been blown out by Philadelphia did not sit well with him. So, Kelce came back for another go-round, catching 76 passes for 851 yards and five touchdowns while playing in every game — numbers that would represent a career year for most tight ends.
The Chiefs scuffled to a 6-11 finish, though. And if Kelce wasn’t going out on a Super Bowl loss, he certainly wasn’t quitting after a season like that.
“The fact that we didn’t make the playoffs,” he said, “I moved on pretty quick.”
He moved onto wedding planning, to be sure. But also into preparing for the upcoming season, which most believe will be his last, one way or another. Kelce was ever-present throughout the offseason, whether it was voluntary workouts or mandatory minicamp, and he has been a constant source of energy during the hot, humid practices that are the hallmark of training camp.
“This is always going to be my sanctuary. I think St. Joe has a special place in my heart,” Kelce said. “You need to have these days. You need to have this time of grinding with the guys, being around them all day, starting to create that chemistry and standard for how we are going to do things. This year it’s ramped up even more.
“I think that’s a big thing,” Kelce added, “just enjoy these moments with these guys I’ve built this culture with.”

Morocco beefs up security at Ceuta and Melilla borders after online calls for new crossings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Morocco beefs up security at Ceuta and Melilla borders after online calls for new crossings
CASABLANCA, Morocco (AP) — Morocco said Wednesday it has beefed up security along its border with Spain as calls resurfaced on social media for mass crossings into the Spanish city of Ceuta, raising concerns of another surge, similar to the one last month when tens of thousands of migrants rushed the border.
Spain’s Civil Guard insisted that the border will remain closed and Defense Minister Margarita Robles warned against any new attempt at a mass entry into Spain’s North African exclaves.
Messages are circulating in Moroccan social media groups for a new rush on Ceuta’s border on Saturday. The source of the messages is unclear.
In late July, some 72,000 migrants swam or climbed over the border breakwater to reach the Spanish city, fueled by economic hardship and by false rumors circulating online about an open border. Nearly all have since returned to Morocco, but the surge had political repercussions around Europe.
At least 80 people died in the attempt, according to official tallies. Human rights groups have reported higher figures.
Would-be migrants are now also being urged to cross into Melilla, another Spanish autonomous city on the northern coast of Africa. Together, Ceuta and Melilla form the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.
The Moroccan Interior Ministry said in Wednesday’s statement that “all necessary measures have been taken to counter” any new “illegal crossing attempt.” It said the security monitoring is part of a “system of continuous vigilance — particularly in areas near the Ceuta and Melilla crossings.”
The Interior Ministry did not immediately respond to questions about the number of personnel deployed or the equipment being used.
Videos shared on social media show hundreds of police officers in riot gear deployed on the Moroccan side of the border, alongside water cannons and ambulances. Local news site Hespress said equipment for deploying tear gas and stun grenades had also been brought to the border.
A senior Moroccan diplomat previously said that more than 20,000 Moroccan security personnel are deployed along the border with Ceuta each day, at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. The diplomat was not authorized to speak to the media and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The Interior Ministry also said Moroccan authorities had arrested and were investigating “a group of people suspected of carrying out incitement activities.” It did not elaborate.
Robles, visiting Ceuta, said it was “everyone’s responsibility to deal with those who are directing these movements, including through social media,” and called “any aggression against Ceuta or Melilla … an aggression against Spain as a whole.”
“This must be absolutely clear: what happened cannot happen again,” she said.
Spain’s Civil Guard shared a message on social media seemingly aimed at migrants, in French and Spanish.
“Neither the border with Spain is open; nor will it be. There are new containment barriers. If you cross them, you will be returned. Don’t let yourself be deceived,” it said.
The Instagram post was accompanied by a photo of a containment barrier in Ceuta that was constructed in the immediate aftermath of the July 31 border breach.
___
Associated Press writer Suman Naishadham in Medinaceli, Spain, contributed to this report.

Occupiers execute at least 345 Ukrainian soldiers, another 375 die in captivity – ombudsman
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
20:49:43 EEST
02:49:43 KST

Ukrainian Parliament's Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said that 375 Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) and civilian hostages have died while in Russian captivity.
"We have a separate list; as of today, it includes 375 deceased individuals. These are Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian hostages who were verified… as having been detained by Russia; they were also verified through the International Committee of the Red Cross's international verification mechanism. And all of them returned home in coffins. In other words, the Russian Federation handed over to us the bodies of 375 tortured Ukrainian citizens who were verified as having been held in Russian captivity," Lubinets said at a press conference titled "Countering Russian disinformation. Exposing Russian disinformation regarding prisoners of war, exchanges, and missing persons" held in Kyiv on Wednesday.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, the ombudsman added that in August 2025, the repatriated bodies included the remains of five critically ill Ukrainian defenders from the Istanbul list. "That is precisely why we insist that the number one priority for repatriation is seriously wounded and seriously ill Ukrainian citizens. Instead of complying with the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law and urgently returning them, the Russians have failed to do so and continue to do so," Lubinets said.
He said Ukrainian prisoners of war, who had official prisoner-of-war status and had been verified by the ICRC, were killed in Olenivka. On the night of July 28-29, 2022, at least 53 Ukrainian prisoners of war were killed, and another 130 or so were wounded. "Verified Ukrainian prisoners of war were publicly executed in Olenivka. Each of them had been verified by the ICRC and had legally been granted prisoner-of-war status. And instead of returning them, Russia cynically orchestrated this terrorist act – a public execution," the ombudsman said.
In addition, Lubinets reported at least 345 known cases of killings and executions by the occupiers of Ukrainian soldiers who had surrendered.
"Since the start of the full-scale invasion, there have been documented cases of the killings and executions of at least 345 Ukrainian servicemen who, as shown in recorded videos, did everything they could to surrender. This means they laid down their weapons, walked out with their hands raised, lay down on the ground, and demonstrated that they were no longer engaging in combat. Russian soldiers searched them, made sure they had no weapons, removed their equipment – including any body armor they still had… After that, they forced them to lie on the ground and shot the Ukrainian soldiers at point-blank range," he said.
The ombudsman said he legally interprets this as the execution of Ukrainian prisoners of war. "According to the Geneva Convention, once a soldier has carried out all these actions, he automatically acquires the status of a prisoner of war," Lubinets said.
