Colombia declares three days of mourning after deadly earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:39:37 UTC
00:39:37 KST

Colombia declares three days of mourning after deadly earthquake
Hundreds are dead as rescuers race to find survivors of the magnitude 7.4 quake.
Colombia has declared three days of national mourning after a powerful earthquake killed more than 200 people as rescue crews race against time to find people trapped beneath the rubble.
The government said on Wednesday that flags would be lowered to half-staff at official buildings and Colombian embassies around the world “in honour of all the dead”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Search for survivors underway in Colombia’s earthquake aftermath
- list 2 of 4Colombia scrambles to find survivors after deadly earthquake
- list 3 of 4On the ground in Cali, Colombia’s worst-hit city after the quake
- list 4 of 4Woman rescued after 36 hours under rubble in Colombia
Monday’s magnitude 7.4 earthquake was the strongest to hit the country in a century. It flattened buildings and damaged roads across western Colombia. More than 100 aftershocks had been recorded by Tuesday afternoon.
The disaster is also an early test for President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office just three days before the earthquake. The first-time president came to power after a divisive election and is now facing the first major crisis of his presidency.
Government figures put the number of injured at 2,595 and the number officially missing at 195 although civilian-run databases suggested the number of people unaccounted for could be closer to 4,000.
The search for survivors has become increasingly urgent as the disaster enters its third day. Aid agencies said the first 48 to 72 hours are generally the most critical for finding people alive beneath collapsed buildings although people can survive longer if they have access to water and food.
Crews worked through the night in some of the hardest-hit cities, including Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo. In Pereira and Cali, rescuers used cranes, search dogs and heavy machinery while volunteers formed human chains to clear debris by hand.
In Cali, entire neighbourhoods appeared flattened with piles of rubble where blocks of homes and apartment buildings once stood and cars crushed beneath concrete and fallen walls. Residents have joined firefighters in searches for survivors, digging with picks, shovels and their bare hands and stopping periodically to listen for signs of life.
But the full scale of the destruction is still unclear, particularly in rural areas where little information has been coming out.
That includes Choco near the earthquake’s epicentre and one of the poorest regions in the country. Many communities there can only be reached by boat, through the jungle or by air. The region has also long been affected by violence between armed groups, making it even harder to reach remote areas.
The earthquake has put parts of Colombia’s health system under enormous strain. Part of the Hospital Universitario del Valle in Cali collapsed, forcing doctors to move patients into a parking lot and treat some people outside.
Colombians have mobilised to help. Thousands have brought food, water and other supplies to affected neighbourhoods while long lines have formed outside blood donation centres.
De la Espriella has declared a state of emergency and promised rent subsidies for families who lost their homes.
International help has also started to arrive. The United States has announced $15.5m in emergency aid, and the State Department announced on Wednesday that following a request from de la Espriella’s government, it was deploying urban search-and-rescue technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California, to help with the search effort.
The European Union has also pledged $2.3m, while Mexico has offered hundreds of search and health workers, and El Salvador said it would send two planes carrying 100 tonnes of aid.
But for rescue crews, the immediate focus remains searching the rubble.

Latvia 'forgot' about ammunition when buying anti-drone systems — new PM reveals strange incident
Latvian authorities previously acquired anti-drone systems without the necessary ammunition, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said, as reported by the Baltic news outlet Delfi on Aug. 12.
"They purchased the equipment, but forgot to buy the ammunition," Kulbergs said in an interview on the Leta news agency's program published earlier this week.
Kulbergs mentioned the incident during a discussion about drone incursions and the work of former Latvian Defense Minister Andris Spruds.
However, the prime minister did not disclose further details about the types of systems or agencies involved, declining to confirm whether he was indeed referring to those procured under Spruds.
The Kyiv Independent has reached out to Spruds for comment.
Spruds, from the Progressives party, stepped down on May 10 after then-Prime Minister Evika Silina said the defense chief "failed to fulfill its promise of safe skies" over Latvia when two Ukrainian drones strayed into the country's airspace.
Ukrainian drones originally intended to strike inside Russia have previously entered Baltic countries, as Moscow redirects their trajectory to neighboring NATO countries through jamming. The first major incident was recorded in Finland in March.
Spruds said that through his resignation he wished "to protect the Latvian army from being dragged into a political campaign."
The resignation triggered the Progressives' exit from the government and the collapse of Silina's cabinet. Spruds's party is currently the main opposition ahead of Latvia's parliamentary elections set for Oct. 3.
In the interview, Kulbergs also revealed that a new unified system involving the Latvian Defense Ministry and the Border Guard will benefit from Ukraine's expertise in drone monitoring and threat neutralization, saying that Latvia currently holds "no real substance" behind its claims of being a great power in the drone field.

USS Abraham Lincoln sailors tried to jump overboard amid extended deployment – reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:37:16 UTC
00:37:16 KST

Military families and Congress members are sounding the alarm about an intensifying mental health crisis onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, as its 5,000 sailors and marines endure a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran.
Two leading specialist military papers, the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, are reporting that there have been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard as poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach the breaking point. The crew is in its ninth month at sea, and has spent 250 days consecutively without making land – a record for an aircraft carrier in modern times.
Worried families vented their anxieties about loved ones onboard the Lincoln at an emotional town hall meeting with navy leaders in San Diego last Thursday, Stars and Stripes reported. One spouse among the 200 or so family members said that her husband had texted her that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”.
The families’ worries were expressed directly to navy leadership, represented at the town hall by the acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, and other top officials.
A woman at the meeting told Cao that the navy had “broken trust between us and the leadership”, the paper reported.
The Navy Times gave details of thwarted suicide attempts onboard the aircraft carrier during the current deployment. Annabelle Loma told the outlet that her husband had tried to jump overboard after his spell at sea kept being extended.
“He’s scared. He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out his 13-year career is ruined, just like that,” she said.
The paper quoted another sailor’s wife whose husband was involved in a separate incident onboard the Lincoln in which he prevented a fellow crew member from jumping, grabbing them and bringing them back on deck.
Mike Levin, a Democratic member of Congress from California, has sounded the alarm over conditions onboard the warship, which is in its fifth month of combat operations against Iran. He described the lot of the crew on X as “moldy showers, broken toilets, laundry down for weeks, long stretches with no hot water, a meal that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas. No soap, deodorant, or toothpaste.”
Jason Crow, a Democratic Congress member from Colorado who is a former army ranger having served in Afghanistan and Iraq, has warned that the strain on service members and their families on the Lincoln is “building week by week”.
The current crunch has been months in the making. The warship left San Diego on 21 November and was originally intended for the Pacific but was redirected to the Middle East once the US-Israel war with Iran began.
Since then, MS Now revealed, the 5,000-plus crew has had only two days on land, in Guam in December and Oman in July. The deployment was scheduled to end in May but has been extended a couple of times amid the ongoing war.
In April, there was a flurry of public criticism about dire conditions onboard the carrier. Photos emerged of poor-quality and rationed food, and there were reports of water shortages, moldy showers and broken laundry machines.
Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed the accounts as “more fake news”.
Levin responded to Hegseth’s remark this week. He said: “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”
The Guardian contacted the US navy for its response to reports of attempts to jump overboard. After this article was published, a navy official responded, saying that they were aware that “extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make”.
The official said that the health and wellbeing of every Lincoln sailor was a priority: “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship.”
Religious, medical and mental health professionals were available as part of a “comprehensive support network” that included “onboard deployment-resilience counselors and chaplains”. The official recognised that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but added that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC and healthy meal options”.
The mental health challenges faced by active-duty US navy personnel are well known. A study from last year looked at the unique stress factors faced by sailors on deployments and found the most common included loud noises, lack of rest, and inadequate mental and physical healthcare.
The researchers conducted a survey of deployed sailors and found that almost half complained that they were not receiving adequate help in coping with stress at sea. The study concluded that “given the high rates of military suicide, including within the navy, efforts to improve healthcare access on ships are urgently needed”.

Why You Need to Shape Your Brand Reputation Before AI Does It for You
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:35:38 EEST
00:35:38 KST

Alexander Storozhuk, the founder of PRNEWS.IO
Brand reputation directly influences the choices Ukrainian consumers make. According to Deloitte Ukraine, in 2025, reviews from other users were among the factors that helped 34% of respondents make a final purchasing decision. At the same time, 62% of Ukrainians do not buy products from companies whose sellers or manufacturers have not left the Russian market. Both figures show that price and product quality are not the only things that matter. What people know about a company and how much they trust it matter too.
For businesses, this means that negative information — from complaints about customer service to questions about a company’s ownership and operations — can affect sales before the brand has a chance to explain its position. Reputation management therefore cannot be a one-off crisis response used only when something goes wrong. It requires consistent work while the company is doing well.
This is often hardest to accept when a business is growing. Founders tend to assume that a stronger reputation will automatically follow rising sales. But that logic holds only until the first serious problem occurs.
4 Reasons to Strengthen Your Company’s Reputation Before a Crisis
Imagine that a cyberattack, infrastructure damage, or technical failure takes a banking app or online service offline. Customers’ first question will be: “What is happening, and are my money and data safe?”
A company that has already communicated openly about data protection, published its refund policies, and explained how it handles crises is more likely to be seen as a reliable business facing a temporary problem. If the company has remained silent until that point, complaints, rumors, and anonymous posts may quickly fill the information vacuum.
Building a reputation in advance helps address several fundamental business challenges that cannot be solved overnight.
1. Build a reserve of trust. A strong brand gradually accumulates goodwill among its audience. When a company with a history of transparent communication encounters a problem, customers are more likely to view it as an isolated incident rather than part of a pattern. Without that foundation, even a single mistake can reinforce doubts about the reliability of the entire business.
2. Stay top of mind. When people have a particular need, they rarely compare dozens of options. Their choice usually comes down to a few names they have encountered before. If a company starts telling its story only when it urgently needs sales, it will have to compete with brands that have spent years building a media presence. This presence creates recognition long before someone clicks the “Buy” button.
3. Appear in AI-generated answers. What ChatGPT, Gemini, and other AI services say about a company increasingly affects how people perceive it. According to the PACE Panel 2025 study, almost one in three Ukrainians already uses AI to search for information about brands. Even among people aged 45–64, one in four turns to these tools for this purpose.
Traditional SEO should therefore be supplemented with GEO — efforts to help AI services find, correctly interpret, and cite information about a company.
AI services can find even recently published pages. However, a single press release is rarely enough to create a complete and consistent picture of a brand. These systems compare information across multiple sources, which makes consistency, completeness, authority, and citability essential.
The sooner a company begins creating and distributing this kind of content, the more likely AI systems are to explain accurately what it does and why it can be trusted.
4. Reduce vulnerability to information attacks. Waves of negative reviews, fake posts, anonymous Telegram channels, and coordinated smear campaigns can all be used to put pressure on a business. In Ukraine, companies may also face false allegations concerning their owners, ties to Russia, tax payments or support for the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
A brand with little verified information available online is particularly vulnerable to the first wave of negative coverage. High-quality publications do not make a company immune, but they create a factual foundation against which people, journalists, search engines and AI agents can assess new allegations.
All four reasons have one factor in common: time. The sooner a business begins building its digital footprint, the less room it leaves for speculation and other people’s interpretations.
Preventive SERM: How to Strengthen Your Search Presence Before a Crisis
AI has not replaced traditional search, but it has already changed how people gather information. According to Deloitte Ukraine, 27% of Ukrainians used AI for work or education in 2025, an increase of 11 percentage points from the previous year. These services are also increasingly used to find product information, compare features, and identify the best offers.
For businesses, this means that during a crisis, conversations about a brand will take place not only on Google, in the media, and across social networks. People will also ask AI:
- “Why is Company X’s service not working?”
- “Will Company X refund my money?”
- “Is it safe to share my personal data with Company X?”
- “Who owns Company X?”
- “Has Company X left the Russian market?”
AI does not know the internal circumstances of a business unless the company has made that information public. It generates answers based on available sources, including the corporate website, media coverage, reviews, directories, social media, and other publicly accessible pages.
If the company has previously remained silent and recent complaints dominate the information available online, the resulting answer may be one-sided or repeat unverified claims. A company cannot control search results or AI-generated answers, but it can increase the likelihood that its position will be represented.
This is the purpose of preventive Search Engine Reputation Management, or SERM.
The practical principle is simple: do not wait for an angry customer or journalist to raise an uncomfortable question. Identify your audience’s main concerns in advance and answer them openly.
People may search for phrases such as “company name + reviews,” “company name + scam,” “company name + not issuing refunds,” “company name + owners” or “company name + Russia.” These searches cannot be prevented. At the same time, companies should not mechanically create articles with provocative headlines when no such risk exists, as doing so may create an unwanted association with the brand.
Start by reviewing actual search results, Google autocomplete suggestions, Search Console data, social media mentions, and answers generated by different AI systems. Ukrainian companies should analyze queries in Ukrainian, Russian, and English, as well as different spellings of the brand name.
They can then prepare materials addressing the audience’s genuine concerns:
- information about the owners and team;
- registration details, licenses and permits;
- payment and refund policies;
- personal data protection policies;
- explanations of the company’s operations in international markets;
- a service status page with information about outages;
- answers to frequently asked questions;
- authentic customer reviews;
- independent coverage in reputable media outlets.
These pages do not guarantee the top position on Google or a mention in an AI-generated answer. However, they give search engines, journalists and prospective customers verified sources to consult during a crisis.
Where to Start If You Have Never Managed Your Reputation Systematically
If your company has not yet taken a systematic approach to reputation management, begin with five steps.
1. Audit search results and AI-generated answers. Check what Google, ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models show in response to queries containing your company’s name. Look not only for errors and negative information but also for gaps in the available information.
2. Identify three to five sensitive questions about the company’s operations. For example: Why does the product cost this much? What happens if the service goes down? Who owns the business? How is customer data protected? Under what conditions are refunds provided?
3. Publish clear answers. Some information should appear on the corporate website, while broader explanations, expert columns and company stories can be published in reputable media outlets. Owned channels provide completeness, while independent sources add credibility.
4. Collect authentic reviews and respond to criticism. Do not publish only perfectly polished compliments. Neutral and moderately critical reviews often appear more credible, particularly when people can see how the company responds to problems.
5. Prepare a crisis communication protocol. Decide who will speak on behalf of the company, where updates will be published, how quickly the team must acknowledge a problem, and which facts should be released first. Once a crisis is underway, it is too late to design this process from scratch.
A strong reputation does not prevent mistakes. Data breaches, server outages, cyberattacks and leadership changes happen even to market leaders. But a digital footprint established in advance determines which sources customers encounter during the first hours of a crisis: the company’s explanation, verified facts or unsubstantiated rumors.
The difference between these scenarios comes down to the work completed before the company’s reputation was placed at risk.

Gulf oil spill fast becoming worst in years, agencies warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:35:11 UTC
00:35:11 KST

Gulf oil spill fast becoming worst in years, agencies warn
LONDON - A vast oil spill in the Gulf is quickly becoming one of the world’s worst in years after being allowed to spread almost unchecked for weeks, according to international agencies, satellite imagery and environmental groups.
The slick off the coast of Oman from a grounded tanker carrying Russian crude had reportedly reached the mainland on Aug 12, the UN’s shipping agency told Reuters.
The slick now covers an area of more than 2,000 sq km, said John Amos, an oil spill specialist who reviewed satellite imagery obtained by Reuters.
The Caroline Bezengi, carrying an estimated 800,000 barrels of Russian oil and under international sanctions, ran aground on June 30 at an Omani island that is part of a marine nature reserve.
The ship first reported difficulties off Yemen on June 8. Maritime sources said a blast appeared to have occurred aboard the Caroline Bezengi.
No party has claimed an attack, but the vessel was navigating two separate wars on its journey from Russia to India.
In April it sailed from the port of Novorossiysk on the Black Sea, a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war. Ukraine has carried out assaults on a so-called shadow fleet carrying Russian oil, which the Caroline Bezengi is part of.
It then passed through the Suez Canal at the end of May, ship-tracking data shows, before sailing past Yemen, where the Iran-aligned Houthi militants have entered a wider regional war between the United States, Israel and Iran.
A web of complex war- and sanctions-related rules governing shipping and oil spills is already hampering efforts to respond and could yet get in the way of halting an impending disaster, insurers and analysts say.
The IOPC Funds, an intergovernmental agency dealing with tanker spills compensation, told Reuters it would not be involved in clean-up costs because the incident was being treated as an “act of war” rather than a simple accident.
The 25-year-old tanker is also not insured by any recognised Western insurance provider.
“A nightmare scenario is there’s no adequate response to keep the worst from happening,” said the oil spills specialist Amos, CEO of SkyTruth, a nonprofit organisation aiming to strengthen environmental conservation through the use of satellite images.
Amos said that in this case, the vessel would “continue to break up under the steady onslaught of wind and waves and to lose the entire cargo and that could be a spill upwards of 40 to 50 million gallons.”
Amos said this would rival the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in sheer size.
The ship is similar in size and capacity to the Sanchi, an Iranian ship that collided with a freighter off China in 2018 in the world’s worst oil tanker disaster in decades.
Rapidly spreading slick
The spill, first detected by analysts in early July, has begun reaching the Omani mainland, the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) said.
“Oil is drifting offshore to the northeast of (Oman’s) Al-Qibliyyah Island, with some oil reported to be reaching the mainland. Oil spill contingency planning is in place,” an IMO spokesperson told Reuters.
The IMO said that seasonal monsoon conditions had limited access to the tanker and delayed salvage operations.
Satellite imagery shows it grounded at Al-Qibliyyah Island, part of a nature reserve that includes the Hallaniyat Islands, putting wildlife including endangered turtles, humpback whales and coral reefs at risk.
Oman said on Aug 10 the slick covers almost 400 sq km. It has not responded to Reuters requests for further detail or comment on the containment efforts, but said it had used booms to try to stem the spread.
Environmental agencies and oil spill specialists put it at up to several times that size, and say that the spread has accelerated dramatically since the beginning of August.
Greenpeace on Aug 11 reported a quickening spread.
“The affected area went from around 45 sq km by the end of July, to 150 at the beginning of August. And then within two days, it quadrupled to 600 by the 4th or 5th of August,” said Hanen Keskes, political campaigns lead for Greenpeace in the Middle East.
Amos’s assessment of 2,000 sq km means it has swelled by more than 40 times since the beginning of August.
He said that measures required, beyond the use of booms, including stabilising the vessel and transferring whatever crude oil was left onboard to another tanker.
“The longer we wait, the more damaged and decrepit that tanker gets, the more complicated and difficult and potentially dangerous that salvage operation is going to be,” he said. REUTERS

Latin America's rightward turn is reshaping its ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:31:14 UTC
00:31:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Latin America's rightward turn is reshaping its ties with Israel
The rise of pro-Israel diplomacy in Latin America is staggering. From renewing diplomatic relations to rekindling trade, newly elected right-wing leaders are more interested in forming strategic alliances than upholding international law.
This marks a departure from the political “pink-tide” that guided many Latin American countries in solidarity with Palestine after October 2023.
Nicaragua, Colombia, Mexico, Chile, Bolivia, Cuba and Belize all intervened in support of South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), while Colombia went one step further, placing a total ban on coal exports to Israel and terminating its bilateral free trade agreement.
On 31 January 2025, Colombia, Cuba, Bolivia, and Honduras also became founding members of The Hague Group. In response to Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank, they committed to “coordinated legal and diplomatic measures in defence of international law and solidarity with the people of Palestine”.
But in the aftermath of right-wing presidential victories, Bolivia and Honduras have both withdrawn from The Hague Group, and Chile and Honduras have returned their ambassadors to Israel.
The new president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, is ready to renew ties with Israel by ramping up security coordination, resuming coal exports, and withdrawing from The Hague Group.
This week, the new right-wing government also recognised Israel's claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which it captured from Syria in 1967, becoming only the second country to do so after the Trump administration in 2019.
“To learn about international experiences that have yielded results will be fundamental to strengthen our security policy and our penitentiary system,” De La Espriella posted on 10 August, days after entering office.
“Israel will find in Colombia a friend and a determined ally in the fight against terrorism and organised crime.”
In longtime pro-Palestine Venezuela, meanwhile, Israel and Caracas this week agreed to resume consular relations after diplomatic ties were cut in 2009. This comes in the wake of the US' military capture of Nicolás Maduro in January, marking a striking shift in Caracas' foreign policy.
A new alignment in Latin America
Bolivia and Honduras' withdrawal from The Hague Group on 4 March 2026 revealed the limitations of non-aligned movements in the absence of political will.
“The Hague Group was an important, organised response from states that were tired of waiting for countries in the UN Security Council to act,” María Alejandra Gómez, a legal researcher at Law for Palestine, told The New Arab.
At that time, the US had already utilised its veto power in the UNSC to block four ceasefire resolutions in Gaza.
“Every single state in the world is bound to prevent and punish genocide, regardless of what treaties they have signed,” she explained to The New Arab. “The Hague Group only did what it was obliged to do.”
Nonetheless, “the enforcement of international law is always subject to the political will of states, so if they change governments, they tend to change their stance,” Gómez said. “This is a structural problem with international law; it is not just about The Hague Group.”
In fact, months before their withdrawal, Israel’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Gideon Sa'ar and his Bolivian counterpart Fernando Armayo had already signed an agreement to renew diplomatic relations.
Similarly, on 3 June, Honduras and Israel signed an addendum to their pre-existing cooperation agreement. With a renewed focus on agriculture, water management, health, education and security, Israel’s Ambassador to Honduras Nadav D Goren called it “another milestone in the bilateral relationship between Israel and Honduras”.
Chile's turn towards Israel
On 3 August, the new right-wing governments of Chile and Honduras returned ambassadors to Israel nearly three years after they were recalled by former presidents Gabriel Boric and Xiomara Castro.
The appointment of Chilean Ambassador Gabriel Zaliasnik, a self-proclaimed “proud Zionist”, by President José Antonio Kast, was unequivocally denounced by the Palestinian community of Chile.
In June, they described the decision as “contrary to the national interest, incoherent with Chile's history of defending international law, and deeply offensive to the hundreds of thousands of Chileans of Palestinian origin”.
“Today, relations between Chile and the State of Israel have been normalised across all sectors,” Nelson Hadad, a Chilean lawyer and former ambassador to Iraq, Jordan and Egypt, told The New Arab. “The outlook is very bleak.”
In fact, “during a recent World Health Organisation vote, Chile, for the first time, abstained from supporting measures regarding public health and the delivery of humanitarian aid to Palestinians facing starvation in the Gaza Strip,” said Hadad.
Such pro-Israel foreign policy is particularly daunting in Chile, home to the largest Palestinian community outside of the Middle East and North Africa.
Last week, upon visiting relatives in Beit Jala, a Chilean-Palestinian named José Nicolás Khamis was detained at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv.
“He was interrogated for 36 hours without the right to a defence or to call a lawyer,” said Hadad. “Ultimately, he was accused of being involved in far-left, communist terrorist activities and was subsequently deported on national security grounds.”
These security concerns were "false and baseless,” said Hadad. As such, “this constitutes a serious violation of diplomatic reciprocity between the two nations and reflects a clear bias against Chileans of Palestinian or Arab origin”.
Enter 'El Tigre'
With even more vigour than his neighbours, Colombia’s President Abelardo De La Espriella, who calls himself ‘El Tigre’, has pledged to nullify his predecessor’s anti-Zionist legacy.
Before winning the elections in June, he proposed an “unprecedented offensive against organised crime in Colombia based on strengthening strategic alliances with the United States and Israel”.
Dubbed “a second Plan Colombia”, an homage to the 1999 US-Colombian military project to combat drug cartels and destroy left-wing guerrilla groups, it emphasises Israel’s value as “a leader in artificial intelligence applied to defence, drone surveillance systems, cybersecurity, and military training”.
After all, the State of Israel “is doing what must be done to defend its people,” declared De La Espriella during an interview in June. “And that is exactly what I am going to do to defend Colombia.”
Since then he has pledged to resume coal exports and leave The Hague Group, to withdraw Colombia’s intervention from South Africa’s case against Israel at the ICJ, to terminate plans to establish a Colombian consulate in Ramallah, and recognise the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
He has previously outlined plans to relocate the Colombian embassy to Jerusalem, flagrantly disregarding the city’s divided status under international law.
Unsurprisingly, one day before he entered office on 7 August, Gideon Sa'ar was right by his side.
“I had the privilege of meeting him in his office in Barranquilla,” wrote Sa’ar, describing their discussion about “the immediate establishment of diplomatic, security, and economic relations.”
“The golden age in relations between Colombia and Israel begins today,” he confirmed.
The battle moves beyond governments
Given former President Gustavo Petro's outspoken opposition to Israel, this realignment is momentous.
As co-founder of The Hague Group, Colombia and its keffiyeh-donning leader had highlighted the fundamentality of political will when enforcing international law.
His most brazen act of solidarity occurred at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in September 2025, when he proposed invoking UN Resolution 377 A, also known as Uniting for Peace, to “establish a peacekeeping force” to defend Palestine.
But “it was not just the will of the president,” pointed out Gómez, describing the impact of public pressure from activists and civil society. In fact, “it is not just about the states of The Hague Group. Activism all over the world will enable states to take more coherent action towards Palestine”.
Latin American domestic courts provide another essential avenue to uphold international law, regardless of a government's political position or a president’s personal interests.
“Their impartiality enables us to force governments to comply with their international obligations,” Gómez told The New Arab.
“For example, when the government of Argentina, under President Javier Milei, invited Benjamin Netanyahu to visit, the Prime Minister of Israel had to cancel his trip because Argentinian courts were [preparing] to issue an arrest warrant.”
Similarly, “in Colombia, we have something called the constitutional bloc which means that many international laws are considered to be incorporated into our constitution,” said Gómez. This gives them the same credence as constitutional laws, she explained.
Meanwhile, despite the difficulties, The Hague Group has continued to gain momentum. With 40 states in attendance at its most recent conference, this was the largest gathering since its founding.
“Participants reaffirmed the paramount importance of the Charter of the United Nations and the international legal order as the foundation of peaceful and just relations among states and peoples,” read the official statement.
With Colombia ready to withdraw, abandoning its role as co-chair, “The Hague Group must find ways to reinvent itself,” said Gómez.
In that process, “the role that activists and citizens will play in order for there to be more accountability in the international arena is going to be transcendental”.
Ana Maria Monjardino is an independent journalist and writer from London

Russian Warships, Submarines and Shadow Fleet Tankers Keep Britain’s Navy Busier Than Ever
British warships and helicopters spent significantly more time tracking Russian naval activity in July as Moscow maintained an elevated presence around UK waters and across the North Atlantic, according to Zona Militar on August 11.
Royal Navy patrol ships and aircraft devoted 21 days to monitoring Russian vessels during the month, up 25% from July 2025, according to figures released by the British Navy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The increase reflects a broader rise in Russian naval activity involving surface combatants, submarines, and vessels linked to Moscow’s shadow fleet.
According to Zona Militar, the patrol ships HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey, and HMS Severn were all involved in tracking Russian naval units during July.
They were supported by Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin helicopters configured for anti-submarine warfare, allowing the Royal Navy to monitor both surface ships and underwater activity across British areas of responsibility.
The Royal Navy also said the number of deployments triggered by Russian naval movements during the first seven months of 2026 was 25% higher than during the same period in 2025.
Among the vessels repeatedly monitored was the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, which crossed areas under British surveillance several times while escorting oil tankers associated with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet.
The heightened monitoring comes as Britain increasingly targets the maritime network Moscow uses to move Russian energy exports.
In June, the UK intercepted the sanctioned tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel. London has also sanctioned more than 500 vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
Russian Frigate conducts live-fire under British watch
One of the more notable encounters came on July 20, when Neustrashimy conducted live-fire exercises in international waters.
The Russian frigate notified nearby vessels in advance and asked HMS Tyne to move to a safe distance while the drills were underway.
The British patrol ship positioned itself approximately five nautical miles from the Russian vessel and continued monitoring the exercise.
According to the Royal Navy, Neustrashimy fired around 20 rounds from its main 100mm gun and also used its 30mm weapons.
HMS Tyne remained nearby throughout the exercise, gathering information on the Russian ship’s operations.
“A sustained presence and close cooperation with our allies meant HMS Tyne was perfectly prepared for this task, providing reassurance and surveillance while allowing other Fleet units to continue with their operational commitments,” Lt. Cmdr. Sam Fields, HMS Tyne’s commanding officer, said.
Russian warship escorts shadow fleet tanker
Neustrashimy was again tracked later in July, this time by HMS Severn during a three-day mission from July 23 to July 26.
According to Zona Militar, Severn took over surveillance duties in the North Sea from HMS Mersey while the Russian frigate escorted the tanker MV Vulkan from the Baltic.
The vessels continued through the Dover Strait before heading toward Ushant off the French coast.
The operation highlights the increasingly close connection between conventional Russian naval assets and tankers linked to Moscow’s shadow fleet, which Russia uses to move energy exports despite Western restrictions.
British frigate spends months hunting
At the same time, the Type 23 frigate HMS Somerset completed a four-month North Atlantic deployment focused on monitoring both surface and submarine activity.
The ship operated with advanced underwater sensors and a Merlin anti-submarine warfare helicopter from 814 Naval Air Squadron.
According to Zona Militar, the mission formed part of wider British operations to protect the country’s strategic nuclear deterrent while maintaining awareness of Russian submarine movements.
HMS Somerset returned to the UK on August 7 after traveling more than 26,500 nautical miles during the deployment.
“This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists for—to protect the United Kingdom and our allies wherever our interests are threatened,” commanding officer Matt Millyard said.
Millyard also highlighted the ship’s submarine-tracking missions and cooperation with NATO allies during the deployment.
The July operations show that Britain is increasingly dedicating both ships and aircraft to tracking Russian military movements across UK waters and the wider North Atlantic.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia has assembled an unprecedentedly large fleet of tankers, which have either begun or are preparing to transport nearly 8 million barrels of crude oil through the Northern Sea Route (NSR).

Russia’s “Spy Priests”: FSB Allegedly Uses Orthodox Church to Reach US Targets

Russia’s “Spy Priests”: FSB Allegedly Uses Orthodox Church to Reach US Targets
The Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) has systematically coordinated with Russia's FSB security service to identify and punish priests who oppose the war against Ukraine, religious scholar Sergei Chapnin alleges in a newly published book.
The findings were reported by the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo on August 12, drawing on Chapnin's English-language study, "Religious Communities Under Pressure: Documenting Religious Persecution in Russia 2022–2026."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Chapnin, a former editor of the Journal of the Moscow Patriarchate, wrote that documented cases reveal notable patterns of coordination between state agencies and church authorities.
That coordination, according to Chapnin's account, took several forms. Evidence gathered by state agencies—wiretapped calls and intercepted messages—surfaced verbatim in church court proceedings.
State-controlled media and church information services published nearly identical accounts of targeted clergy, deploying the same arguments to discredit them. In many regions, FSB officers personally visited local bishops to discuss priests who had taken, or might take, an anti-war stance.
After the invasion, the FSB sharply expanded monitoring of parish-level communications, social media groups, and correspondence among believers, Chapnin noted, allowing it to flag dissent early.
He also pointed to a declassified 2009 memorandum, recovered in part from the laptop of a church external-relations official and disclosed by journalists Andrei Soldatov and Irina Borogan.
In Chapnin's telling, the document authorized "coordination with the counterintelligence service of the FSB" and treated church representatives as intermediaries for reaching potential intelligence targets in the US. Enlisting them for operational work, it noted, required only the patriarch's blessing, with a dedicated church body coordinating contact with the security services.
Chapnin traced the arrangement to Patriarch Kirill, writing that one of the ROC leader's first initiatives after taking office was to restore cooperation with Russia's intelligence services.
The book cites the case of Archpriest Sergei Rybakov, former rector of a university church in Samara, who criticized the war online. In March 2023, Rybakov recounted, a local metropolitan warned him he was under FSB surveillance; by September, he had been barred from the ministry.
In another instance, seminary graduates Denis Popovich and Nikita Ivankovich, both ethnic Ukrainians, were accused in 2025 of plotting to kill Metropolitan Tikhon. A campaign to discredit them began in late 2022 via a Telegram channel that Chapnin linked to the Moscow Patriarchate and the FSB.
By Chapnin's count, authorities have secured at least 35 convictions against religious figures and believers since the full-scale invasion, with at least three more criminal cases under investigation as of June 2026.
At least 30 administrative cases were recorded for "discrediting" the army, 13 religious figures and organizations were labeled "foreign agents," five people were placed on "terrorist" lists, and 10 organizations were declared "undesirable."
The church imposed its own penalties on at least 38 priests, defrocking 17, barring 14 from ministry, and pushing seven into retirement. In all, the study documents more than 115 cases involving clergy, believers, and religious activists.
Meanwhile, assessments circulated in mid-2026 described ROC priests posted abroad as recruited by or affiliated with Russian intelligence agencies, including the FSB, casting the church's overseas parishes as instruments for espionage and pro-Kremlin influence across Europe.

Summer at USAFA: Academy Aims to Teach Airmanship to All
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:29:35 UTC
00:29:35 KST

Editor’s Note: This is the third and final article in a multipart series on military training during the summer at the U.S. Air Force Academy. The first, on Basic Cadet Training, is available here. The second, on Combat Skills, is available here.
AIR FORCE ACADEMY, Colo.—It’s a warm, windy morning at one of the busiest flightlines in the U.S. Air Force, and not a single officer or jet is in sight. Instead, dozens of 18-22-year-old cadets scurry around sleek, engine-less gliders as classic pop tunes blare from a speaker.
Every few moments, a prop plane takes off with a glider careening behind, pulled with battered tow rope, or the planes land, having successfully released a sailplane.
Across the runway, in an ops building, a dozen more cadets are strapped into simulators, soaring over a virtual replica of the Colorado landscape. Nearby, more cadets mill around the step desk, where an old-school “puckboard” displays names on the day’s schedule.
The Air Force Academy operates the largest glider program in the U.S., with more than 15,000 flights every year—almost entirely led and managed by the youngest instructor pilots in the Air Force. The enterprise is poised to get even busier as USAFA leaders drive toward their ambitious objective: to get every cadet serious time in the air.
70-Year Legacy
The USAFA glider program dates to the 1950s. Overseen today by the 94th Flying Training Squadron, participation levels have fluctuated over the years. There was a “Soar-for-All” program in the 1970s to give every cadet at least some time in a glider; today, about 500 to 600 members of every class—about half—take the Academy’s basic soaring class, 94th Commander Lt. Col. Curtis Holtman told Air & Space Forces Magazine during a recent visit. (The school also has a powered flight program, and as of 2018, about 70 percent of cadets participated in one or the other flying program.)
Now, once again, the academy’s is aiming to give every cadet a chance to fly.
Airmanship for All means ensuring all 4,000 or so USAFA cadets “obtain real flight experience,” said C1C Noel Migliaccio, cadet commander of the Operations Group this summer.
Some will do so in an expanded powered flight program, where cadets fly in T-53A Kadett II with a rated officer. But more will get that opportunity in one of USAFA’s 23 gliders, Migliaccio said.
Holtman said the program has evolved over time. “We in the 94th have actually kind of led … this over the last three years,” he said. “Three years ago, we were sitting right around 300ish cadets coming through. We’ve incrementally scaled that over the last two years to we’re heading into fiscal year ’27, we’ll push over 500 to 600 cadets through our basic soaring program.”
Changes to the syllabus helped. And with “access to cadet time, operating hour increases, things of that nature, then we can absolutely get to the 800 to 1,000 cadet throughput mark,” Holtman said. “If we can get to Airmanship for All through the soaring program, that is our end state objective.”
Cadet IPs
Each participating cadet gets eight flights—any less, Holtman said, and study shows cadets don’t get comfortable in the air. But some cadets get much more than those eight sorties.
After going through the basic soaring class, about 70 to 80 percent of participants apply to be instructor pilots. To be selected, they must pass an interview with a board of current cadet IPs, in which the candidate must teach the board members something to demonstrate their teaching style. The teaching topic is wide open—one cadet tought how to change a diaper, while another showed how to use a yo-yo.
Around 60 candidates are selected, after which they go through scores of flights to earn their “G” wings, then scores more as IPs. C1C James Callaghan estimates he has made more than 300 glider flights to date.
Holtman said the ranks of IPs will have to grow to achieve Airmanship for All, perhaps by an additional 10. Beyond teaching other cadets to fly, he says, IPs are also getting their first taste of life in an operational squadron. They rotate through different leadership positions throughout the year, conduct morning safety briefs, and run the step desk.
“Everything you see in this facility is what they are going to go see as soon as they go fly gray tails,” Holtman said.
The simulators cadets train on are the same immersive training devices that Air Education and Training Command uses at undergraduate pilot training, with virtual reality headsets and controls that mimic a real cockpit.
“If we can move the needle left, then we’re only preparing them better to have that high rate of fidelity transfer from what they have here to what they’ll go do in the future,” Holtman said.
Airmanship
Many academy instructor pilots have gone on to become full-fledged Air Force pilots. The halls of the 94th ops building are full of memorabilia from glider fliers who went on to Thunderbird pilots, general officers, astronauts, and more.
The skills developed in soaring build a strong foundation for future pilots—and future officers in any career.
“I think gliders are unique in that they really do build situational awareness and energy management, which are things that we’re gonna use throughout a career, no matter what platform we end up flying on when we graduate,” Callaghan said. “Those are values that take practice to build, and my bubble for both of those have increased exponentially. And then, on top of that, being an instructor pilot and being able to talk through your flying and get someone that has never touched an airplane before to basically learn how to fly has really helped with my communication skills.”
Not that flying a glider is the same as a powered aircraft, C1C Joseph Fitzsimmons said, but flying demands “soft skill and hard skills,” and gliders give cadets a jump start on the soft skills.
“The air awareness, the airmindedness, the task management skills, all of those are baked into us now, and we will be able to carry that into whatever experience we have in the Air Force, whether it’s aviation or just leading Airmen,” Fitzsimmons said.
Indeed, while the Airmanship for All program might inspire more cadets to want to become aviators, there are only so many slots for rated career fields like pilot, air battle manager, or combat systems officer. In USAFA’s class of 2026, almost 47 percent of graduates went into non-rated career fields.
In the Air
Whether they wind up becoming pilots, intelligence analysts, force support officers, or something else, cadets who go through the soaring program get to experience flying differently than most.
“I would argue that it is the most pure form of flying. Truly, you feel every bump of air, every input of the stick, every move of your rudder, you feel everything,” said Callaghan.
With the Academy located right on the windy edge of the Rocky Mountains, handling the glider requires vigilance and many small adjustments, Callaghan said. And because the gliders are so sleek, even flying while attached to the tow plane requires focus and touch.
It’s quiet aboard the glider—no engine roar, no ear-splitting whine. But there is maneuver, and glider fliers learn how to pull Gs and perform aerobatics. Some go on to compete, representing the Air Force Academy in competitions with other schools. USAFA cadets regularly bring home national championships.
The aerobatics come at the tail end of the eight sorties in the basic program—along with sick bags just in case cadets (or visiting reporters) can’t quite stomach 5 Gs.
“You feel everything about flying and build such an intimate connection with aviation,” Gallaghan said. It’s “flying in its purest form.”

Authorities in western Siberia’s Tyumen region have begun forcibly seizing and culling domestic pigs across several rural villages following an outbreak of an undisclosed disease, the local outlet 72.ru reported Wednesday.
As part of quarantine measures imposed Friday, disinfection checkpoints manned by police have reportedly been set up along Golyshmanovsky District roads to spray passing vehicles and prevent pork products from leaving the area.
Video shared by the outlet showed men in hazmat suits spraying vehicles and photographs of them inspecting pigsties.
Local veterinary officials reportedly refused to name the pathogen publicly, saying access to the information is restricted, while residents claimed it is being referred to as an “extraordinarily dangerous disease.”
According to 72.ru, local agricultural experts believe the outbreak is likely African swine fever, a viral disease with a nearly 100% mortality rate among pigs but harmless to humans.
Similar culls were carried out last September in the neighboring Vikulovsky District following an African swine fever outbreak, the outlet said.
Rural residents expressed anger about the forced confiscation of their pigs, telling 72.ru that the animals were injected and incinerated without clear documentation or specific compensation figures.
Local administration officials reportedly promised market-rate compensation during Monday’s town hall meeting, but warned that hiding animals from veterinary crews would carry steep fines.
An official added that residents in affected areas are barred from raising pigs for at least one year.
The incident follows a similar livestock culling after a pasteurellosis outbreak in the Novosibirsk region earlier this year. That quarantine, which triggered public protests, was lifted in June.

War on Iran: Phase II: Day 32
Tehran, Iran – Shortly after meeting China’s ambassador, Iran’s new security chief left no room for doubt about Tehran’s position after nearly six months of war with the United States.
“Iran’s message is clear: The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until the US ends the war and blockade, releases Iran’s frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Gaza,” Mohsen Rezaei said in a social media post late on Tuesday.

“Until all conditions are met, the Strait will remain closed,” added the former wartime commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
His defiant message was in line with conditions emphasised by his predecessor, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, and by newly appointed commanders as Iranian authorities maintain that they are willing and capable of continuing to stand up to their opponents in the US-Israel war on Iran.
In his first meeting as secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Rezaei sat down with a delegation led by China’s envoy to Tehran, Cong Peiwu, on Tuesday. With the 60-day period of the repeatedly violated MoU approaching next week, mediators such as Pakistan and Qatar have said they are continuing efforts to bring the two sides closer to a diplomatic solution.
Yet the rhetoric from Tehran has only hardened over the past week, with the IRGC indicating that it aims to take threats from the administration of US President Donald Trump, including to further strike Iran’s power plants and civilian infrastructure, more seriously.

Khamenei also selected Ali Abdollahi, head of the Khatam al-Anbiya joint wartime command, to lead the General Staff of Armed Forces.
Abdollahi is tasked with integrating the Khatam headquarters, which was formed during the eight-year war with Iraq in the 1980s to coordinate operations between the then-nascent IRGC and Iran’s regular army, with the general staff overseeing all armed personnel.

“The country’s borders are fully safe and impenetrable through the vigilance of border personnel and the backing of people living in border areas, including the brave people of Kurdistan, Sistan and Baluchistan, and Khuzestan,” he was quoted as saying by state media.
In the meantime, most of Iran’s population of about 90 million people continues to weather the worsening impact of war and uncertainty, as well as a tightening security grip at home.

Should You Let Your Dog Lick Your Face? 9 Animal Hygiene Questions, Answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:28:35 UTC
00:28:35 KST

You might be surprised to learn that Dr. Daniel Griffin, chief of infectious diseases at Island Infectious Disease Medical in Long Island, N.Y., lets his two dogs lick him.
He’s not delusional. “We know how dogs greet each other,” he says. “We know where that tongue has been.” But he lets his expertise take over afterward. Griffin diligently washes his hands after his dogs lick them, especially before picking up a slice of pizza.
That’s more or less the expert consensus: love the pet, wash your hands. Living closely with pets brings you closer to germs, but for most people, ordinary contact is low-risk. There are exceptions, however. Here, experts answer the face-licking question and eight others about hygiene and animals you might encounter.
Should you let your dog lick your face?
First, forget the thing you may have heard your whole life. “I used to hear, ‘Oh, dogs’ mouths are like 10 times cleaner than people’s mouths,’” says Kelley Steury, a veterinarian and clinical associate professor at the University of Nevada, Reno School of Public Health. “I don’t think that’s based in science.”
A dog’s mouth, like a person’s, is full of bacteria. One species commonly found in dogs, Capnocytophaga canimorsus, can occasionally cause serious illness in people. Most of the time, though, nothing happens. “It doesn’t really pose a problem,” Steury says. The trouble starts when saliva gets past the body’s defenses—through a bite or into an open cut, for example. In rare cases, the infection can progress to sepsis and become fatal.
The risk also depends on who’s getting licked. People being treated for cancer or taking immune-suppressing drugs are more vulnerable to severe C. canimorsus infection. So are people without a spleen and those with alcohol-use disorder. But for healthy kids and adults, the occasional lick is fine, experts say.
Official guidance takes the cautious route, though: Keep dogs away from your mouth and face, and don’t let them lick open wounds. Saliva is more of a concern when it reaches broken skin or a mucous membrane, such as the mouth or eyes. If your dog gets you anyway, wash the area afterward. And if you’re immunocompromised or don’t have a spleen, ask your doctor what precautions make sense. But the fact that dogs, like so many of our daily exposures, can carry germs is not “a reason to not own a dog,” she says.
What if your cat licks you?
A cat lick is usually a non-event, too, provided your skin is intact. Cats commonly carry Pasteurella multocida, but on unbroken skin, Steury says, it “pretty much will not be a problem at all.”
Experts are more concerned about bites. A cat’s teeth are narrow and sharp, so they often puncture instead of scraping the surface. “The tooth acts kind of like a needle,” Steury says, “and it’ll inject that bacteria into your deep tissues.” What looks like a pinprick can be a deeper wound than it appears.
If a cat bite breaks the skin, wash it immediately with soap and running water and see a medical provider, Steury says.
What should you do about a cat scratch?
“I definitely respect the claws of cats,” says Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist at the University of California, San Francisco.
If a claw catches you, wash your skin right away with soap and running water. The goal is to rinse the bacteria away before it settles in, not to disinfect. “Disinfectants don’t kill everything,” he says. “Running things are better than stagnant things in general.”
After that, pay attention to the area. Increasing redness, pus, or a fever over the next several days are all reasons to see a medical professional. So is a swollen lymph node on the same side of your body as the scratch, which can signal cat-scratch disease, a bacterial infection most common in kids. Location matters, too. Chin-Hong is extra cautious when a bite or scratch lands directly over a joint, where an infection can be harder to treat.
What if you have a fresh surgical site?
Coming home from surgery might be when you most want your furry friend on your bed. It’s also when experts want you to put a little distance between your pet and whatever is healing.
Dr. Ashley Drews, an infectious disease specialist at Houston Methodist, has seen patients develop infections after a pet licked an incision or surgical drain. “That’s not a good idea,” she says. Keep the site covered and your pet away from it.
Do you need to worry about the litter box?
Yes. Cats can shed Toxoplasma gondii in their poop, and the parasite can travel from the box to your hands to your mouth.
Yet the litter box isn’t the only way to get toxoplasmosis. The parasite can also turn up in soil, unwashed produce, contaminated water, and undercooked meat—especially pork, lamb, and venison.
“I think people are aware of the cat litter thing,” says Jill Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. Meat gets less attention. Roberts is so wary of undercooked pork that she skips thick cuts, which she worries are harder to bring to a safe temperature. “All I can see is Toxoplasma,” she says. You don’t have to give up pork chops, but you should use a food thermometer: Whole cuts of pork should reach 145°F. Once they come off the heat, wait at least three minutes before cutting or eating them; the meat’s temperature holds steady or continues to rise during that time, helping destroy pathogens.
While the pork chop may deserve more attention, the litter-box rule still stands. If you’re pregnant or immunocompromised, hand off the scooping if you can. If you have to do it yourself, wear disposable gloves and wash your hands afterward. Change the litter daily, too: The parasite takes one to five days after being shed to become infectious.
Can you catch your dog’s parasites?
Sometimes, but your dog’s diagnosis doesn’t automatically mean the whole household is next. When Griffin’s dogs had giardia, an intestinal illness caused by a microscopic parasite, he wasn’t panicking about catching it himself. “In general, it’s a different giardia that we get vs. dogs,” he says. The type that usually makes people sick isn’t the same type that usually infects dogs and cats.
Pay special attention during cleanup. Giardia can travel through tiny traces of feces on soil, water, fur, surfaces, and objects. Clean up dog poop promptly; keep up with veterinary care and parasite prevention; and clean the bowls, bedding, crates, and toys of a pet being treated for giardia. Your veterinarian may also recommend a bath to remove contaminated feces from its fur.
Always use actual soap and water after handling a sick pet or cleaning up poop. Sanitizer is helpful when it’s all you have, but it doesn’t remove dirt or every kind of germ.
Are your pets bringing ticks into the house?
Quite possibly. Your dog can come inside alone and still bring company. Dogs and cats can carry ticks indoors, where the ticks may disembark and choose a human for their next meal. Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious disease physician and assistant hospital epidemiologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York, takes the possibility seriously enough to pack fine-tipped tweezers for overnight trips to the country.
Ticks are remarkably good at hiding in plain sight. On people, they tend to hide under arms, behind knees, around the waist, and in the hair. On dogs, check the ears, under the front legs, and between the toes. Torres says many people who develop Lyme disease or another tickborne illness “have no recollection of ever being bitten by a tick or ever seeing a tick.”
After spending time in tall grasses or woods, make sure everyone gets inspected. “Check yourself, check your partner, check your kids, check your dogs,” Torres says. If you find a tick attached to your skin, remove it then and there; waiting for a doctor only gives it more time to feed and potentially transmit disease. Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp it close to the skin, pull upward with steady pressure, and then clean the bite and your hands. Finding a tick doesn’t automatically necessitate a trip to urgent care, but call your doctor if you develop a rash, fever, or other symptoms over the next several days or weeks.
What about backyard chickens and petting zoos?
Your pets aren’t the only animals capable of handing something off. More than 60% of known infectious diseases in people can spread between animals and humans, Steury says. The list of germs that can make the trip includes E. coli, Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, and Salmonella—none of which care whether the animal carrying them looks clean.
Backyard chickens deserve special mention, in part because more people are keeping them. A chicken can look perfectly healthy and still carry Salmonella. Steury’s rules for handling them are uncomplicated: Wash your hands afterward, and “don’t kiss them,” she says.
The same logic applies at the petting zoo, with the added complication that children are extraordinarily efficient at putting their hands in their mouths. Steury isn’t telling you to skip it; just wash everyone’s hands with soap and water on the way out, and keep fingers and pacifiers out of mouths until you find a sink. Hand sanitizer is a useful backup, but it isn’t an equal substitute.
When does an animal encounter require a same-day phone call?
If an animal bites you hard enough to break the skin, or if you’ve had a possible encounter with a bat, seek medical care immediately. For animal bites, wash the wound right away with soap and water, then call a health-care provider—especially if the animal was wild, a stray, or behaving strangely, or if you don’t know whether it’s been vaccinated against rabies, a fatal disease that affects mammals.
The reassuring part is that less than 10 people die from rabies each year in the U.S., largely because most pets are vaccinated and people who may have been exposed can get preventive treatment.
The bar for what counts as a bat exposure is even lower because people may not realize they were bitten. “People think, ‘Well, I think I’d know it if a bat bit me,’” Steury says, “but you may not.” Bat teeth are so small that their bites can be painless or barely noticeable. If you wake up with a bat in your bedroom, find one near a sleeping child, or think you might have touched one, don’t open the window and shoo it out before asking what to do, Steury recommends. Call animal control or your health department. If it can be safely contained, health officials can test it for rabies. If it’s already disappeared, call anyway; public-health officials can determine whether you need post-exposure vaccination.
Steury knew a veterinarian in Alabama who had an unnerving encounter. “A bat just fell out of the sky and fell on her neck,” she says. It tested positive for rabies, and the veterinarian needed post-exposure shots even though she’d already been vaccinated in the past.
Of course, none of this means treating every animal like a biohazard. It means knowing what calls for soap, what calls for a phone call or doctor’s visit, and what you can stop worrying about. As Chin-Hong puts it, “The benefits of pets outweigh the disadvantages.”

Search for Colombia earthquake survivors enters critical window
CALI/PEREIRA, Colombia – Colombian rescue teams raced on Aug 12 to find survivors still trapped beneath collapsed buildings two days after a powerful earthquake killed close to 250 people across the nation’s western valleys and coffee-growing region.
“We are in a race against time to save lives,” Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder told reporters, warning that less than a day was left in the critical 72-hour window during which there are far greater chances of finding quake survivors.
“We will keep working after this window, but it is important to rescue the most people we can in this day we have left,” he said, adding that rescue workers needed silence and order to detect survivors under the mountains of rubble.
Official estimates suggest the 7.4-magnitude quake, which struck the South American country just after 7am local time (8pm Singapore time) on Aug 10, also injured 3,770 people, destroyed more than 9,550 homes and impacted more than 30,300 families.
In Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city, 56 buildings collapsed, killing at least 95 people and injuring close to 1,000 others, according to data from Asocapitales, the country’s capital cities association.
Pereira, deep in the coffee-growing region and some 55km from the quake’s epicentre, counted at least 79 dead, according to Asocapitales. The mayor’s office said 300 people were missing.
First test for new president
Indira Meneses, 49, a nurse who lives with her two children and elderly mother, said the front of her home in Pereira collapsed, leaving them trapped inside. Their neighbours helped them get out, but they keep reliving the moment.
“I have five neighbours who died under the rubble,” Meneses said. “We’re waiting for local officials to help us rebuild and replace what we lost, but so far, no one has come.”
German Bahamon, the head of Colombia’s coffee federation, said ports in Buenaventura have paused operations while inspectors evaluate the impact of landslides on key roads, but “exports continue as usual, mainly through Caribbean ports”.
Colombia is the world’s third-largest coffee producer, and hundreds of thousands of families rely on the sector.
The earthquake struck just days after the inauguration of President Abelardo De La Espriella, who won a narrow victory against the candidate of the prior leftist government on a platform centred on less public spending and tougher security.
He travelled to the affected regions on Aug 11 and pledged aid to those who lost homes and businesses due to the quake. Several local mayors have announced nightly curfews, citing the possibility of looting.
“The earthquake will be the first test for the new Colombian president,” said Tiziano Breda, senior analyst for Latin America and the Caribbean at conflict monitoring group ACLED.
“De La Espriella ran on a platform to cut public finances, including defunding the state’s risk management unit,” he added. “This unit is currently at the forefront of the emergency response.”
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula rejected reports that the government had turned down international offers of aid, saying his office was coordinating the delivery of shipments that began arriving from Peru, Mexico and El Salvador.
The head of Topos Azteca, a Mexican search-and-rescue team, said in a video message that he had arrived straight from Venezuela, which suffered devastating twin quakes at the end of June.
Families await news
Rescue efforts in Cali were concentrated around seven buildings that might still hold survivors.
At the Torres del Limonar complex in the southern part of the city, residents formed long bucket brigades with soldiers, employees of the mayor’s office and others, handing down rubble from the peak of the debris.
Camilo Cano, a fire department official from Bogota, told Reuters that rescue efforts were more organised after police began restricting volunteers, which helped reduce noise and vibrations and allowed sensors to better detect movement under the debris.
He said the possibility of a serious aftershock posed risks to any large crowds, even as family members of those still trapped under the building waited anxiously nearby for news.
Some 30km north-east of Cali in Palmira, relatives of the deceased waited outside a morgue on plastic chairs under the shade of trees. An official called out the names of identified bodies via a loudspeaker.
Santiago Lloreda, 31, told Reuters he was at work when the quake hit his apartment, killing his mother and 13-month-old daughter Salma, who was too young to have a fingerprint registry and needs to be identified though DNA samples via Bogota.
“My daughter was a dream made reality,” he said. “My mother was the pillar of our family, she took care of everyone and always made you laugh ... she gave everything up to look after the baby. It cost her life but it made her so proud and happy.”
Ricardo, who did not share his last name, said he travelled from Miami to recover the body of his sister. He praised the efforts of doctors and neighbours’ solidarity.
“There are heroes in there helping return our family’s bodies to us as soon as they can,” he said, adding that his niece was awaiting surgery for fractures to her skull, jaw, leg and a collapsed lung.
“She’s alive. We know she’s going to get better,” he said. REUTERS

PSG looks for Super Cup success over Villa for first of six possible trophies this season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

Paris Saint-Germain retains UEFA Super Cup as Doué goal seals 2-1 win over Aston Villa
Paris Saint-Germain won the UEFA Super Cup for a second straight year by beating Aston Villa 2-1 on Wednesday thanks to Désiré Doué’s second-half goal in the annual curtain-raiser to the European soccer season.
Doué’s 61st-minute strike after running onto Ousmane Dembélé’s pass was initially ruled out for offside, only for the goal to be awarded following a video review.
Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s powerfully struck opener in the 20th was canceled out by a volley from Brian Madjo, a 17-year-old striker making his competitive debut for Villa days after getting approval to play following a dispute with FIFA over his registration.
It’s the first of a possible six trophies this season for PSG, which became the first team to win back-to-back Super Cup titles since Real Madrid (2016 and ’17).
The Super Cup is an annual early-season match between the most recent winners of the Champions League (PSG) and Europa League (Villa).
Referee was the Somali official barred from World Cup
The game in Salzburg, Austria, was refereed by Omar Artan, the Somali who was barred by the United States from officiating at the World Cup days before the start of FIFA’s tournament because of vetting concerns. U.S. officials claimed Artan had connections to terror organizations, though without providing proof.
UEFA responded by picking Artan — a referee judged the best in Africa last season — to take charge of the Super Cup in a powerplay by European soccer’s governing body amid its increasing disconnect with FIFA.
That disharmony has increased since, with UEFA leading the campaign to oust Gianni Infantino from the FIFA presidency over his recent — aborted — plan to sell an interest in the World Cup.
Artan was the first non-European referee to take charge of the Super Cup.
Another season, another trophy for PSG
After winning five titles last season, PSG is back on the trophy trail already — and could pick up a second in the 2026-27 campaign when it takes on Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday. That’s a match between last season’s league and cup winners in France.
Doué was one of the PSG players who only returned to training on Monday following the World Cup, but he was handed a start by coach Luis Enrique and proved to be the matchwinner.
The 21-year-old forward ran through unchallenged after latching onto Dembélé’s pass behind the Villa defense and curled a left-foot shot into the far corner. The offside flag was then raised but a check by the VAR showed that Villa right back Matty Cash was keeping Doué onside.
Artan awarded the goal after the review and Doué punched the air in delight.
Kvaratskhelia was PSG’s standout player of the first half and his goal was mesmeric as he cut in from the left and lashed a fierce, rising shot inside the near post.
Teenager Madjo causes havoc
Remember the name: Brian Madjo.
It was quite the debut by the powerfully built teenager who was born in north London, has played three friendly matches for Luxembourg, and now has decided to represent England.
Madjo joined Villa from French club Metz in January but FIFA blocked his registration because its transfer rules limit international moves by players under the age of 18. Villa appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport and it was upheld last week, allowing him to make his club debut as the youngest player to feature in a Super Cup.
He caused havoc at times for PSG’s elite center-half duo of Willian Pacho and Marquinhos and could have scored two or three goals before finally getting on the scoresheet by meeting John McGinn’s cross with a volley into the roof of the net.
Moments earlier, Madjo had bundled past Pacho and hit the post with a shot.
It was a fourth straight loss in the Super Cup for Villa manager Unai Emery, whose other losses came with Sevilla (twice) and Villarreal.
