Andrus Kaarelson: If we do not act fast investments will go to Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

Andrus Kaarelson: If we do not act fast investments will go to Latvia
Estonia's government has failed to attract foreign investment. Companies are choosing our neighbors instead. Now we cannot even distribute major investment support because there are simply no investors, Andrus Kaarelson writes.
Everyone who has been at the helm of the state in recent years should take responsibility. Our NIMBY culture ("not in my backyard") has grown beyond all reason. It is impossible to make any major energy or industrial investment in Estonia without years of disputes with a local municipality or even in court.
You cannot even build a poultry farm. A few years ago, when interest in building the Väimela large poultry farm faded, OÜ Lõuna-Eesti Talumuna leader Tõnu Vetik summed up Estonia's investment climate well: "It is not possible to build anything big in Estonia, whether wind turbines, poultry farms or pulp mills."
Investors are rational and prefer countries that welcome major investments instead of tripping them up at every turn. The state has had years to change this attitude. Officials talk about making planning easier, but real steps have been few and investor trust has not grown.
Problems with actually completing investments have been made worse by the unstable economic environment created after the 2023 elections. Constant and wide-ranging tax changes — always upward — have led foreign investors to look past Estonia. They prefer countries where taxes remain stable between drafting a business plan and completing an investment, so the plan still works.
This leaves Estonians poorer. Fewer competitive jobs mean lower wages and more unemployment. Unfortunately, the governing parties do not seem to understand this.
While neighboring countries are receiving foreign investments worth billions of euros, Estonia is trying to scrape together small investments to save what can be saved.
Recently we learned that the application threshold for support of up to €20 million — previously meant for companies investing at least €100 million in Estonia — was lowered by several tens of millions to €70 million. For defense industry projects it was lowered to €20 million, and for priority technology (which includes food production and renewable energy) to €30 million.
The government essentially admitted it has failed to attract major investments and now must lower the €100 million bar because applicants simply did not come. Under the previous conditions, the roughly €40 million available for support this year cannot be distributed. Major investment support should not be scattered randomly, and the government must start working seriously to find large investments.
This comes at a time when Germany's Rheinmetall alone is investing about half a billion euros in Lithuania, Finland is building data centers worth billions, and Poland is building a nuclear plant worth billions. Even Latvia received slightly more than €1 billion in foreign investment in 2025. Estonia's figure was nearly twice as low, between €500 million and €800 million depending on the source.
We should not forget that several Estonian entrepreneurs have made their biggest recent investments in Latvia or other nearby countries. These include Frankenburg's €10 million investment in the Ādaži rocket factory and Fibenol's decision to invest €700 million in a Latvian biorefinery.
Skeleton Technologies also did not choose Estonia. Last year it launched super battery production in Varkaus, Finland, and in late November opened supercapacitor factories in Germany and Poland.
Yes, Estonia still has more foreign investment overall than Latvia and Lithuania, but our lead has shrunk sharply in the past year. If the trend continues, our southern neighbors will soon pass us. To prevent that, Estonia's business environment must again become attractive to foreign investors. That requires breaking the NIMBY culture and ending constant tax hikes. Only then can our economy start growing strongly again.
Parempoolsed do not believe that high taxes and large subsidies will bring foreign investment to Estonia. The government has not created a competitive business environment in the past decade. Estonia lacks affordable electricity, fast internet access is still unresolved, and the state's erratic tax policy and heavy bureaucracy drive foreign investors away. It is high time to start improving Estonia's business environment.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

====================================================================================================

Jason Arday’s life may be a warped fantasy. But so is this conversation around DEI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:49:35 UTC
21:49:35 KST

Few stories have dominated discourse and headlines like that of Jason Arday. The University of Cambridge professor, now resigned, was accused of plagiarism, and appears to have made up an awful lot of fantastical stories about his life. But weeks into the affair, it feels that there has been an additional layer of reality-distortion: this time, by the rightwing press and in broader public discourse. This week, I try to unravel some of the falsehoods that have taken hold around the matter.
Debunking five myths around the Jason Arday discourse
The stories told by Arday about his life are outlandish, but so are some of the stories we are being told about Black people’s position in professional life. Increasingly, a number of fantasies are being spun by the media and wider public as they attempt to make an example of Arday.
Here are the most egregious:
1. Academia is dominated by DEI appointments
While Arday was in a senior position at Cambridge as the university’s youngest Black professor, he was still in a significant minority. The proportion of Black professors in the UK remains at around 1% of the total cohort. In the last academic year, only 75 of Cambridge’s 6,180 academics across all levels were Black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Authority. The university has serious questions to answer, but can this one case really be taken as a broader comment on the erosion of academic standards in favour of diversity? Arday was a high-profile appointment precisely because he was not the norm. For Black people, the path to academia is not a smooth ride greased by wokeness, but a bumpy one, hampered by persistent under-representation. And crucially, the percentage of Black professors in the UK has remained broadly static over the past few years, indicating that post-Black Lives Matter DEI measures, of which Arday has become symbolic, are actually not changing academia across the board.
2. DEI has taken over the world
Critics of DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inclusion; EDI in the UK) have framed the Arday case as evidence that diversity initiatives have taken over certain elite institutions and white-collar professions. Let’s zoom out a little, and survey what the real world looks like. In the UK civil service, there have been measurable improvements in racial diversity in entry-level roles – but diversity up the ranks remains largely unchanged. Sector statistics suggest that there is a glass ceiling firmly in place for Black civil servants. This glass ceiling also exists in media jobs: a recent survey of broadcast newsrooms found that journalists from all ethnic minorities are still locked out of top jobs. One respondent described their workplace as an “apartheid newsroom … You look left and there’s disproportionately too many people [of colour] because everyone’s on the lower rung. And you look on the other side, it’s like, [almost] everyone’s … white.” In 2015, Black journalists in the UK were “under-represented by a factor of more than 10”, a figure that has barely changed. The story is the same among Britain’s top firms, where Black directors remain under-represented, even as overall ethnic minority representation increases. In addition to this persisting lack of advancement, Black people now have to worry about a growing perception that they are “diversity hires”.
3. DEI is about race (and mostly Black people)
It’s striking just how much “DEI” has become a straight swap – a byword for “Black” in conversations about employment and representation. DEI is also about much more such as disability, class and gender. There is something instructive in how it has become collapsed into race, because it seems that it is only race that triggers outrage – the sense that these minorities are cheating their way in. The Arday case itself proves, rather than negates, the fact that resonant DEI themes go beyond race. One can see how his story weaves in all strands, and would not have been as compelling if it was one of a typical middle class professional. In Cambridge’s own announcement of the appointment, their narrative centred neurodivergence, Arday’s delayed speech, his class. He epitomises, the statement says, “the significant barriers that neurodivergent individuals, those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, and Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic people face when trying to build careers in the sector”.
4. Black people aren’t critical of DEI
The fallout around Arday has landed in the middle of a fraught and nasty public debate about DEI, which has pushed Black people into a particular rhetorical position. A post-BLM backlash has argued that attempts to redress systemic imbalances against people of colour are not only discriminatory, but unsafe. Donald Trump has legally challenged DEI initiatives in the US by executive order, and has gone so far as to blame air traffic accidents on DEI, due to the alleged lowered hiring standards under his predecessors. These interventions have created an environment in which it is impossible to have reasoned discussions about DEI, and its value, application, flaws and benefits. The Arday case is troubling on its own terms, but it also feeds into an image of a world held hostage by “wokeness”, one that has been amplified by motivated, cynical actors.
But there is a difference between rejecting such hysterical notions and universal denial that there is nothing to see here. Several Black analysts and writers (myself included) have long been critical of DEI. We have warned that a focus on “representation” over material change will do little to genuinely address the harms that Black people face due to their class, employment status, housing, policing and immigration. But it is the right, in politics and the media, that has dictated the terms of the debate.
5. We live in a meritocracy
Public discussion of Arday’s case would have you believe that elite institutions reward skill and aptitude alone. This is fiction. It is a mundane fact of life, for example, that US higher education admissions have a formal preference for “legacy students” who have family ties to a given university. Between 10% and 15% of Ivy League students are legacy, and are favoured in order to promote donations and alumni networks. In 2019 Harvard’s acceptance rate of legacy students was almost five times that of the general rate. These students are overwhelmingly white and wealthy. While things are not codified as such in the UK, one Cambridge student newspaper survey found that more than 27% of its undergraduates had an immediate family member who attended Oxford or Cambridge. One first-generation student recalled being asked in the first week which Cambridge college their parents went to. And the sort of informal networks that mean that a British royal and his sibling – the future king – can gain admission despite not attaining the results required, are evidence that there are systemic biases towards the connected, the rich, and the predominantly white circles from which they come. Yet that is not perceived by the same people scandalised by Arday. The outrage around perceived preferential treatment only seems to extend to certain demographics, which tells us a lot.
None of this is to say that Arday, and Cambridge, have not failed to live up to the academic standards required for such a role. But so much reality has been warped in the fallout, the story flattened into an account of a world in which Black people and their gullible enablers have created a society plagued by a fixation on identity, to the detriment of quality and fairness. Arday, by all accounts, appeared to tell many untruths. But we should be careful that in our eagerness to draw grand conclusions from his story, we don’t end up concocting another lie.

How are you handling the conversation around Jason Arday? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us at thelongwave@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Which countries have the best cyber security? Albania tops the global list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:49:25 UTC
21:49:25 KST

Estonia's e-Governance Academy ranks Albania and Czechia as the world's most cyber-secure nations, with major attacks often forcing the top-to-bottom overhauls that push smaller, easier-to-coordinate states ahead of larger powers like Germany and the US.
Albania has the world's strongest cyber defences, according to a global index that puts the Balkan nation ahead of tech powerhouses including Germany, the UK and the United States.
The ranking, from Estonia's e-Governance Academy (eGA), scores 155 countries and territories out of 100 points based on their readiness to prevent and respond to cyber attacks.
Its top two, Albania and Czechia, are not the names one might expect to top a global security league table.
Meanwhile, some of the world's largest economies rank surprisingly low. Germany sits in 13th place, the UK in 42nd and the US in the 31st — all trailing considerably behind Moldova, Jordan and North Macedonia.
At the bottom of the table are Micronesia, Palau and Timor-Leste.
The National Cyber Security Index (NCSI) is built from 49 indicators grouped into 12 capacities across three categories: strategic, preventive and responsive cybersecurity.
It covers everything from legislation and dedicated cyber units to crisis response plans and international cooperation.
As geopolitical tensions rise worldwide, cyber security has become a national priority for governments seeking to protect critical infrastructure, from power grids and hospitals to transport and financial systems, against escalating attacks.
Beyond the ranking itself, the NCSI also functions as an open database of evidence and official documents, helping governments identify gaps in their defences and build capacity where it's lacking.
Why is Albania top of the table?
Albania scored 98.33 out of 100 — a striking result for a country not typically associated with cyber security leadership.
It posted a perfect score across all its strategic indicators, including cyber policy, international cooperation, and education and research, and again across all preventive indicators, covering critical infrastructure protection, threat analysis and data protection.
Its only shortfall came under military cyber defence, where it scored two-thirds of the available points.
Every other responsive indicator, including incident response, crisis management and cybercrime enforcement, hit full marks. The gap traces to a single missing element: Albania has no published military cyber doctrine, the document that sets out the armed forces' rules for conducting cyber operations.
For Albania, the top-tier score followed a 2022 cyberattack by Iranian state hackers — so serious that Tirana severed diplomatic ties with Tehran over it — which forced a clean, top-down legal overhaul.
Rather than a setback, the crisis triggered rapid modernisation: legal frameworks were overhauled, defence operations centralised under the National Authority for Cyber Security and partnerships forged with the EU, the US and major tech firms. The government also moved to secure e-Albania, the digital portal that hosts 95% of the country's public services.
Czechia: Legislation and enforcement
Czechia matched Albania's score of 98.33, with a stronger digital development level than its Balkan counterpart.
Like Albania, it scored full marks everywhere except military cyber defence, where the same single gap applied: no published military cyber doctrine.
Its resilience rests on a centralised national strategy, close public-private coordination and a dedicated regulator, the National Cyber and Information Security Agency (NÚKIB), backed by EU and NATO alliances.
Czechia regularly updates its national cyber security strategy to address emerging threats, and imposes strict, tiered compliance requirements on critical sectors including energy, health and finance — pushing companies well beyond basic IT defences.
Canada: Strong, but two clear gaps
Canada ranked third with a score of 96.67. Unlike Albania and Czechia, its shortfalls were more varied and specific.
On digital enablers, Canada lost points because it has no nationally recognised electronic identification (eID) scheme for citizens to use in secure online transactions.
On crisis management, its gap was a missing operational cyber reserve — a formal mechanism to call on extra cybersecurity specialists during a large-scale incident. Every other category scored full marks.
The country's underlying strength lies in an integrated defence model built around the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, paired with deep public-private collaboration, a strong cyber talent pipeline and a sharp focus on data sovereignty.
Estonia: The pioneer
Estonia tied Canada on 96.67. Its gaps mirrored the pattern seen elsewhere: no formally adopted national crisis management plan for large-scale cyber incidents and,as with Albania and Czechia, no published military cyber doctrine.
Estonia underwent a similar shift after a 2007 assault widely attributed to Russia, though never formally proven.
The country pioneered a decentralised, whole-of-society model built on foreign data embassies and public-private partnership.
Its X-Road data exchange platform and KSI blockchain now underpin the digital economy, alongside heavy investment in public cyber awareness.
Finland: Strong across the board, one coordination gap
Finland rounds out the top five with a score of 95.83 and unlike the other four, it scored full marks on military cyber defence.
Its two shortfalls were narrower: no single body clearly tasked with coordinating national cyber awareness campaigns, and, as with Canada and Estonia, no operational crisis reserve.
Finland ranks first in the world on a separate measure, the Global Cybersecurity Index, reflecting its "Comprehensive Security" model, which brings together government, business and citizens.
That approach is sharpened by decades of vigilance living alongside Russia and one of the world's highest levels of digital literacy.
Energy and telecom operators work directly alongside the National Cyber Security Centre Finland to coordinate national defence.

‘I had planned to stay for life’: last villagers prepare to leave Cha Kwo Ling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:47:53 UTC
21:47:53 KST

‘I had planned to stay for life’: last villagers prepare to leave Cha Kwo Ling
‘There is no need for so many mega-events in Hong Kong to create something new ... better if we could retain something unique,’ resident says
Nestled within thick, verdant foliage in Cha Kwo Ling is one of Hong Kong’s last squatter settlements, where a handful of remaining residents are staying until a government deadline to move out for redevelopment of the area for public housing.
Mrs Lam, one of the last villagers living among the juxtaposition of makeshift metal dwellings and stone houses complete with wooden window frames, said she had until August 25 to clear her belongings.
“I’m going to miss my medicinal herbs so much,” said Lam, in her sixties, who declined to give her full name. She pointed to the plants at her door that she inherited after moving to the village more than a dozen years ago, saying she would not have space for them when rehoused.
The plants, such as Chinese fevervine, are a source of income for her as she dries them for medicinal use. Lam said that redevelopment work deprived her of space to regularly sun-dry them to keep the plants from moulding, causing her to forgo more than HK$400,000 (US$50,980) in potential earnings.
Her letters to the Chief Executive’s Office asking for compensation for her products have not yielded a substantial response so far, but she revealed her family of three had received just under HK$80,000 from the government for the forced relocation.
“Of course, it is a shame to have to vacate. I had planned to stay here for life,” Lam said, pointing out that she and former neighbours who had already left the village would regularly get together for dim sum.

By mid-month, the volume of oil stored on tankers in the region had returned to its lowest levels since February, but began to rise again by the end of July as inventories accumulated on vessels arriving in the area. Despite the partial resumption of production, total supplies from Persian Gulf countries in July stood at 23.9 million bpd, remaining 8.3 million bpd below pre-conflict levels.

In Russia’s Orenburg Region, restrictions on fuel sales have been introduced following a UAV attack on the Orsk Oil Refinery. Vehicles will be refueled based on even and odd numbers, and limits on the amount of fuel have also been introduced.
Fuel dispensing at all filling stations in Russia's Orenburg Region will be carried out according to even and odd numbers, depending on the vehicle's number. This was reported by Orenburg Region Governor Yevgeny Solntsev, UNN reports, citing DW.
Details
The day before, Solntsev reported a fire "at one of the industrial enterprises" caused by a UAV attack. According to the ASTRA Telegram channel, the target of the strikes was once again the Orsk Oil Refinery — PJSC "Orsknefteorgsintez" — one of the largest oil refineries in Russia, with a processing capacity of about 6 million tonnes of oil per year.
According to the Russian governor, filling fuel into canisters is also prohibited. Limits are being introduced on the amount of fuel dispensed. Petrol (AI-92, AI-95) will be dispensed in quantities of no less than 15 litres and no more than 30 litres per person. Diesel fuel will be limited to 60 litres in populated areas and up to 200 litres at filling stations on intermunicipal, regional and federal highways within the region. Ministry of Internal Affairs personnel and volunteers will be deployed at the filling stations.
We should add
In at least 12 regions, as calculated by the publication "7×7", filling stations are once again seeing queues for fuel lasting several hours. Journalists name Krasnodar Krai, and the Voronezh, Kaluga, Rostov, Ryazan, Tambov, Tula, Saratov, Smolensk, Penza and Ulyanovsk regions, as well as Primorye, among these regions.
Russian media note that restrictions on the amount of petrol dispensed to one person have also returned. On August 11, the Sochi administration announced that limits had been introduced at filling stations in the region "due to logistical disruptions in supplies." In addition, local residents and tourists were asked to "refrain from travelling by private vehicle where possible" in order to reduce the burden on filling stations.
A system of separate refuelling on even and odd days has also been reinstated in Lipetsk Region. It will take effect on August 13, Governor Igor Artamonov announced. At the same time, limits were introduced in the region — up to 30 litres of petrol at filling stations operated by the "Gazprom", "Lukoil", Teboil and "Rosneft" networks.
In addition, regions are reporting complaints about petrol shortages and the closure of some filling stations — residents of Krasnoyarsk Krai and Bashkortostan are talking about this. Rising prices are also being noted, as evidenced by some indirect signs — in particular, in the regions that Vladimir Putin visited in recent days.
In Krasnoyarsk, one day before Putin's visit, petrol prices at some filling stations of the regional network fell sharply (by 24 roubles per litre). The filling-station network itself attributed the price reduction to a "temporary improvement in logistics" and the "receipt of an additional volume of fuel directly from the oil refinery." However, immediately after the president's departure, prices returned to their previous level.
In Novosibirsk, which Putin visited next, his motorcade stopped (whether accidentally or deliberately is unknown) next to an empty filling station. Children were waiting there for the president, and he spoke with them. These images, filmed by Kremlin pool reporter Pavel Zarubin, were widely circulated by many media outlets. They show that the price display at the filling station was switched off.
Russian media note that there have so far been few reports from Moscow and St Petersburg. However, a Business FM subscriber said that she encountered a lack of AI-95 petrol at several Rosneft filling stations on her way to her dacha along Dmitrovskoye Highway.
We should add
The Russian authorities have not officially reported a new wave of the crisis. On August 11, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the fuel industry, held a meeting on the situation in the domestic market. Following it, relevant agencies, regional authorities and oil companies were instructed to "continue coordinated work to supply the domestic market with fuel," monitor price dynamics and guarantee the "uninterrupted delivery" of petrol to consumers.

Ukraine has updated its approaches to bullying and violence in schools — what is envisaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:43:52 EEST
21:43:52 KST

Ukraine has updated its approaches to bullying and violence in schools — what is envisaged
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Education has approved updated procedures for responding to bullying, introducing a single commission and clear deadlines. The fact of bullying is now established only by a court, and institutions must create their own prevention systems.
Ukraine is updating its approaches to preventing and responding to bullying and violence in educational institutions, the Ministry of Education and Science reported on Wednesday, UNN writes.
Details
"The updated Procedure for Responding to Cases of Bullying and the Procedure for Applying Educational Measures have been approved," the statement said.
The documents were updated in connection with changes in legislation on protecting children's rights. In particular, the approaches to defining bullying have been aligned with the Law of Ukraine "On the Protection of Childhood" and the nationwide system for responding to cases of violence and cruel treatment of children.
What is changing
The MES explained what has changed in the updated procedures:
-  A single commission has been introduced to consider cases of violence and bullying. From now on, instead of two separate response mechanisms in educational institutions, there will be a unified approach: one commission will consider all cases of violence and cruel treatment of children, including reports of bullying.  
-  A list of signs that may indicate violence has been established. These include economic pressure (including deprivation of property or obstructing access to educational services), psychological violence (insults, threats, humiliation, harassment, intimidation), unwanted verbal, nonverbal or physical behavior of a sexual nature (gestures, jokes, nicknames, distribution of material of an intimate nature), and any unwanted physical actions, from pushing to striking.  
-  Clear deadlines for responding to reports of violence have been established. The head of an educational institution must consider a report within one day of its registration. If signs of violence are identified, the head is required to immediately, but no later than within three hours, notify the National Police and the children's services. 
-  Only a court establishes the fact of bullying, not the commission. Instead, the commission assesses the circumstances of the case, identifies the child's needs, organizes the necessary support, and makes decisions guided by the principle of the best interests of the child. 
-  The range of people covered by the procedure has been expanded. Whereas previously the document applied only to participants in the educational process, it now covers the broader concept of members of the community, which includes students, employees of the educational institution, and other people involved in the educational process. 
-  Mandatory monitoring of the implementation of commission decisions has been introduced. If the measures determined do not produce the expected result, the commission must review them and, if necessary, adjust them. 
-  Children's rights during the consideration of cases of violence have been strengthened. The updated procedure guarantees a child's right to be heard in accordance with their age and level of maturity. The child's position must be recorded during the consideration, and the hearing takes place with the participation of the parents or their representatives and a practical psychologist or social educator (or without the parents, with their written consent). 
-  The criterion of systematic violence has been clarified. Violence is considered systematic if it is committed two or more times within 12 months from the day a report of the first case was registered or from the day it was committed, even if the first case was not officially reported. 
-  Every educational institution must create its own violence-prevention system. Educational institutions must approve internal regulations on preventing and combating violence, designate a person responsible for receiving and registering reports, provide various channels for submitting complaints, and keep records of all reports. In the near future, the MES will propose methodological recommendations to help implement these changes in practice. 
-  Reporting violence will become easier. Educational institutions must provide several ways to submit reports, including via email, telephone hotlines, or special boxes for written submissions. In addition, reports of possible cases of violence may be submitted anonymously. 
You can read the full text of the order at the link.

Ukraine strikes Novorossiysk, putting Russia's last Black Sea sanctuary within reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:43:23 UTC
21:43:23 KST

Ukraine’s strike on Novorossiysk demonstrates Kyiv’s ability to threaten Russian military infrastructure far beyond the frontline and challenges the assumption that shifting vessels from Crimea can keep them safe.
Ukraine has struck Novorossiysk, Russia’s main operational hub on the Black Sea, which has become Moscow’s last major naval base in the region after sustained Ukrainian attacks forced much of its fleet from occupied Crimea.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as a “unique operation” and said strikes on the designated targets had been confirmed.
He gave few further details, saying Ukraine had used Palianytsia jet-powered drones, Neptune missiles and unmanned naval systems to target air-defence positions, piers and port infrastructure.
“The occupation fleet and all the infrastructure supporting it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues,” Zelenskyy said.
He also posted a video appearing to show Russian air-defence activity over Novorossiysk overnight.
Novorossiysk and its naval base lie more than 300km from the frontline. Kyiv’s strike is significant because it suggests that Moscow’s decision to move much of its fleet eastwards from Sevastopol has not put it beyond the reach of Ukraine's forces.
By targeting the port that emerged as Russia’s principal Black Sea naval hub after its withdrawal from Crimea, Kyiv is seeking to show that Russia has no secure sanctuary for its fleet anywhere in the Black Sea.
Russian authorities didn’t not issue a full account of any military damage, although local reports described explosions and air-defence activity in the Novorossiysk area.
How Novorossiysk became Russia’s last Black Sea sanctuary
Novorossiysk has become increasingly important to Russia since Ukraine’s forced much of the Black Sea Fleet to leave Moscow-occupied Crimea.
For years, Sevastopol was the fleet’s principal base.
But Ukrainian missile and maritime-drone operations made the Crimean port progressively more dangerous, damaging warships and infrastructure and limiting Russia’s ability to operate in the western Black Sea.
Since 2023 Russian naval assets have been moved eastwards to Novorossiysk and other mainland ports.
The redeployment was intended to put the fleet beyond the range of Ukraine’s weapons. Kyiv is now seeking to demonstrate that distance offers only limited protection.
Novorossiysk matters not only as a naval base but also as a major commercial and energy-export port, handling substantial cargo traffic, Russian crude and petroleum products alongside military activity.
A sustained threat to the city could therefore create pressure beyond the immediate military target, disrupting logistics and maritime trade, affecting oil shipments and undermining the perception that Russia’s rear areas are secure.

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. The phenomenon of the Kalashnikov assault rifle, which has gained worldwide fame, lies in the personality of its creator, as well as in the weapon’s reliability, simplicity, and exceptional effectiveness, Alan Lushnikov, CEO of the Kalashnikov Group, said in an interview with TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:40:23 UTC
21:40:23 KST

Richard Tice has been accused by Labour’s Bridget Phillipson of mounting a “deeply chilling attempt to silence the free press” after he sent a legal threat to the Guardian over its reporting on his financial affairs.
Lawyers for Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, singled out a Guardian correspondent for her journalism about a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.
Tice is now suing the NCA, claiming that the information could only have come from an officer within the agency.
In a separate letter to the Guardian, Tice’s lawyers made clear they would be seeking disclosure of documents that they believe could reveal the details of sources.
In response, Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said it was an attempt to silence journalism. She said: “Rather than answer serious allegations, Richard Tice is now trying to harass those who have exposed them. The Reform deputy leader should drop this lawsuit [against the NCA] and come clean.
“Trumped-up legal letters targeting honest journalism are very revealing. Reform have zero regard for the cornerstones of British democracy: they’re unpatriotic and pathetic.”
The move was also criticised by the Liberal Democrats, anti-corruption and press freedom campaigners. The Lib Dem Cabinet Office spokesperson, Lisa Smart, said: “Weaponising the legal system to hunt down journalists’ sources is a desperate, bullying tactic. Tice has revealed what we all always knew to be true – Reform’s agenda is completely incompatible with a free and open democracy. They have proven once again that they are entirely unfit for public office.”
Susan Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Using legal threats to strong-arm journalists into disclosing their sources amounts to a deeply concerning attack on press freedom.”
Hawley said Tice would be better served being open about the legitimate questions being asked of him and Reform UK, rather than “trying to discredit those who have reported on them”. “Democracy depends on an independent press, and the government must get serious about introducing safeguards against abusive legal tactics.”
Phil Brickell, the Labour MP and chair of the all-party group on anti-corruption, said Tice had “questions to answer as to how money donated to Reform was reportedly routed through his companies”.
“What we now see is a contemptible campaign by Tice to detract from those public interest questions by threatening hard-working journalists and seeking to uncover their sources. It shows once again that the government must act to ensure that those seeking to expose wrongdoing are protected from the rich and powerful seeking to silence them.”
Tice and Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage, have been under intense scrutiny in recent months because of a continuing investigation by the Guardian into their financial affairs.
Separately, the Sunday Times has also published a series of stories about Reform’s funding.
The Guardian revealed in a series of detailed reports that Reform UK received a secret £1m donation via a fundraising vehicle run by Tice and that Farage received a secret £5m gift shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election.
The Guardian also revealed that these and other transactions were reported by bankers to the NCA over fears they could involve laundered money.
A “suspicious activity report” is not proof of wrongdoing, rather it is an invitation for the agency to examine the transaction to decide whether there are grounds to investigate it further. It is not the same as a crime report.
Farage and Tice have denied any wrongdoing.
Throughout its reports the Guardian has referred to financial industry sources.
Tice has suggested in a document filed at the high court that the Guardian’s award-winning City editor, Anna Isaac, could not have had sources at multiple banks.
In legal correspondence sent directly to Isaac, Tice’s lawyers suggested he was seeking to unmask sources based on his own assessment of the reporter’s work.
Farage has also issued proceedings against the NCA.
Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of the Index on Censorship, said it had the “appearance of an attempt to force a journalist to break the golden rule: that sources must be protected”.
“This has been vital public interest reporting by the Guardian. The sources of such journalism are sacred. If the facts are incorrect, then they can be challenged, but the sources should not be chased down. This appears to be a tactic designed to not only silence journalists but those who talk to them. It is a nasty tactic and we should all be concerned.”
Theo Bamber, the chief executive at the News Media Association, said: “Robust protection for journalists’ sources is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that reporters can scrutinise authority and hold the powerful to account on behalf of the people impacted by their actions and decisions.
“The use of legal threats by an individual or organisation trying to force journalists to disclose their confidential sources is an attack on this important principle, and one that must be resisted at every turn.”
A Guardian News and Media (GNM) spokesperson said: “Richard Tice’s legal threat against the Guardian appears to be a calculated attempt to deflect attention away from legitimate questions about his financial affairs and the funding of Reform UK.
“Instead of providing answers to those questions, he seems intent on intimidating journalists and seeking to expose sources. The Guardian will oppose these attacks on the freedom of the press and will not be deterred from public interest-driven investigations into politicians and the parties they represent.”

British journal retracts study on excess mortality after COVID-19 pandemic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:38:59 UTC
21:38:59 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The British journal BMJ Public Health withdrew on Wednesday a 2024 study on excess mortality after the COVID-19 pandemic, which had been frequently cited by vaccine skeptics, Austrian broadcaster ORF reported.
The BMJ Publishing Group announced the withdrawal, citing methodological flaws and noting that the study was "unbalanced," lacking in "accuracy," and containing "misinformation."
The study, which received a lot of attention online, particularly from vaccine skeptics, was published in May 2024 by a team led by Saskia Mostert of the Princess Maxima Center for Pediatric Oncology in Utrecht, Netherlands.
The researchers compared excess mortality data from 47 Western countries between January 2020 and the end of 2022, with the findings later cited by vaccine-skeptical outlets as evidence that COVID-19 vaccinations contributed to elevated mortality rates.
The research team reportedly did not establish a direct link between the elevated mortality rates and COVID-19 vaccinations. However, the researchers called on policymakers to release more detailed data to allow for a closer assessment of the effects of containment measures and vaccination campaigns.
The article was later accused of fueling unfounded criticism of coronavirus vaccinations, urging the BMJ journal to publish a warning and urging caution when interpreting the study.
The Princess Maxima Centre launched an ethics investigation, whose report was submitted to BMJ Public Health in May 2025 and later made public.
The ethics committee found no scientific misconduct or evidence of data fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism but concluded that the researchers breached two-thirds of the scientific integrity standards examined, including by giving disproportionate attention to COVID-19 measures and vaccinations while overlooking alternative explanations.
The BMJ later conducted its own investigation, noting that the article was withdrawn by the journal due to misinformation in the discussion about the possible causes of excess mortality.

The European Commission is reacting on the immediate needs of communities in Columbia and is providing €2.1 million in life-saving assistance. This funding will provide vital support to the most vulnerable. EU humanitarian partners on the ground will deliver health, water, sanitation and hygiene material, as well as shelter, food, protection and cash assistance.

The Commission also activated the Copernicus satellite mapping service immediately after the earthquake to support rescue operations on the ground and provide initial damage assessments.
The EU stands ready to provide further assistance as needs evolve on the ground.
President Ursula von der Leyen said:
'As search and rescue operations continue, the EU is supporting Colombia wherever possible. We are making €2 million available to support communities in the most affected areas. Following Colombia's activation of the civil protection mechanism, we are working to match aid to the needs on the ground. Esta es la solidaridad europea.'
Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, Hadja Lahbib said:
'In this very difficult moment, our thoughts are with all those affected by the earthquake. From the very first hours, the European Union has stood alongside Colombia, supporting rapid needs assessments so that first responders and urgent humanitarian assistance can reach the hardest‑hit communities. Today, we are reinforcing this effort with an additional €2 million in emergency support to help deliver life‑saving aid where it is most needed. Colombia can count on the EU's continued support as we remain ready to act further.'

Swiss retail sector grew in first half of year

Swiss retail sector grew in first half of year
Swiss retail sales rose in the first half of 2026, with turnover increasing by 2.6% compared with the previous year, according to market research firm NielsenIQ (NIQ).
Both main segments contributed to this positive performance. The food sector grew by 2.5%, whilst non-food slaes increased slightly faster at 2.7%. Online retail remained a key driver of growth, recording an increase of around 11% by the end of June.
Within the food sector, frozen products in particular recorded strong sales growth, whilst confectionery and snacks were also in demand. At the same time, fresh produce recorded “solid” sales growth.
According to Nielsen, non-alcoholic drinks were a key growth driver. Mineral water and sweet drinks were particularly in demand. Alcoholic drinks, on the other hand, were below the previous year’s level, with the wine category in particular showing weak performance.
In the non-food sector, leisure goods in particular drove sales upwards. Toys, World Cup sticker albums and fitness equipment were in high demand. E-bikes, on the other hand, continued to decline.
Home electronics and DIY also recorded significant growth. Air conditioners and fans, for example, sold well, as did charging stations for electric vehicles. In the home electronics sector, vacuum cleaners in particular were in high demand.
The fashion sector, on the other hand, stagnated. That said, swimwear, beachwear, summer footwear and football kit benefited from the summer temperatures and the World Cup.
The official retail figures from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) are calculated on a monthly basis only. The individual figures ranged from -0.5 to +2.1% and were therefore considerably lower. Whilst NielsenIQ primarily takes large retailers into account, the FSO figures also include the turnover of smaller retailers.

German Cabinet approves plan to grant more powers to spy services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:35:13 UTC
21:35:13 KST

German Cabinet approves plan to grant more powers to spy services
- Germany's Cabinet approved new measures giving intelligence services broader powers to hack communications and disrupt foreign threats amid rising cyber and hybrid attacks.
- The plan allows BND and BfV to access digital data, conduct active operations, and use AI tools, marking a major shift in Germany's security approach.
- Critics warn of civil liberties risks, but officials stress the urgent need as Germany faces real dangers from countries like Russia and Iran, with recent drone incidents highlighting threats.
AI generated
BERLIN – Germany’s Cabinet approved measures on Aug 12 to grant intelligence services new powers to hack communications and disrupt foreign adversaries’ operations to counter what officials say is a growing threat from cyber and hybrid attacks.
The measures, which have been under discussion for months, would allow both the BND – the foreign intelligence service – and the BfV – the domestic security service – broader authority to access digital communications, collect data and carry out active operations to thwart attacks.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the measures, which would incorporate artificial intelligence tools, would “revolutionise Germany’s security architecture”.
“We are transforming our intelligence services into genuine secret services,” he told a news conference in Berlin, saying that for the first time, the agencies would be given operational powers.
The measures, which would grant the BfV wide powers to collect data, have drawn criticism from some civil liberties groups.
Konstantin von Notz, from the opposition Greens party, supported giving expanded powers to the BND given the growing range of threats. But he said granting the domestic security services similar expanded powers was “a cause for concern in terms of the rule of law”.
Germany’s intelligence services, created after World War II when memories of the Nazi regime were still fresh, have traditionally had more circumscribed powers than the equivalents of allies such as France, Britain or the United States.
Germany faces ‘very acute’ danger, says top official
But amid warnings of rising threats from countries including Russia and Iran, there has been pressure to enhance their traditional role of information analysis with more authority to take concrete action to counter-attacks.
Nina Warken, head of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Chancellery, said Germany faced a “real, very acute” danger from hybrid attacks by foreign powers and could no longer rely on the intelligence services of allies for its security.
Last week, a suspected attack was avoided when a drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig airport in eastern Germany, while unidentified surveillance drones have regularly been spotted above military bases and other sites.
Under the plan, which must still be approved in Parliament, security services could interfere with attackers’ infrastructure, such as secretly disabling explosives to allow surveillance operations to proceed.
In cyberspace, they would have authority, under strict thresholds, to hack into attackers’ IT systems, copy or delete data, and disable tools used in campaigns by foreign states, including during specific threat situations such as large-scale cyber operations.
The draft also sets new rules for the use of state spyware in online searches and so-called source telecommunications surveillance.
Telecoms, digital platforms, transport operators and financial intermediaries could be ordered to hand over data, backed by fines and on-site inspections.
The measures would create more detailed legal bases for cyber investigations, and would centralise control under the Independent Control Council, an external supervisory body that currently oversees the BND’s signals intelligence. REUTERS

Trump Breaks Silence on Secret Plane Switch in Turkey Over Possible Iranian Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:35:11 UTC
21:35:11 KST

President Donald Trump has confirmed he secretly switched planes when leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month in an effort to evade a possible Iranian threat.
“It's only up to the Secret Service. I just follow what they'd like to do, so I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump told reporters late Tuesday at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane, equal safety, but they wanted me to do it, so I do it, I do what they say."
When asked about the nature of the “threat,” Trump acknowledged there had been one but said he “didn’t really ask too much about it,” adding that he receives “a lot of threats.”
The Washington Post first reported Monday that when Trump left Ankara, Turkey, on July 8 and headed to England, he boarded Air Force One in front of the media, before being transferred to a military aircraft via a catering truck in an effort to conceal his exact whereabouts. Several other outlets also carried the story citing unnamed U.S. officials as sources.
Video footage of the scene shows a Turkish airport catering truck, understood to be sheltering Trump inside, pulling away from Air Force One.
Journalists, alongside some White House staffers, traveled on Air Force One and were reportedly unaware of the President no longer being onboard.
The operation has come under scrutiny, sparking questions as to whether those left on the decoy plane presumed to still be carrying the President were at risk.
"I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump told reporters late Tuesday. ”Because that would be the plane, I think, that they would be more likely to go for."
Robert McDonald, who spent 21 years with the Secret Service, also pushed back on the idea that Air Force One and the people still aboard it may have been left exposed. “I would find it incredibly hard to believe that those two planes weren't escorted or with other assets from allies or the U.S. Air Force in the area,” he told TIME, adding that he doubted the people on the aircraft “were dangled out there and left to fend for themselves.”
Prior to leaving the summit on July 8, Trump had posted on social media that, for “old time’s sake,” he would fly out of Turkey on the older Air Force One instead of the newer, controversial Qatari-gifted aircraft, which had made its first international trip to the NATO event.
“To honor our brave men and women of the military, we are sending the brand new, and truly spectacular, Air Force One to Mildenhall Air Force Base, in the United Kingdom, to give them a chance to tour the aircraft,” he said.
When asked during a NATO press briefing why he wasn’t flying the new plane home, the President told reporters that the aircraft was being flown to a U.S. base to give service members a chance to see it.
In reality, the clandestine operation meant that, for a portion of time, the President’s real whereabouts were seemingly unknown to—and concealed from—the White House press pool.
Trump isn't the only President to execute a decoy mission
Although rare, a decoy maneuver such as this is not unheard of when it comes to presidential travel.
A similar episode occurred in March 2000, when former President Bill Clinton secretly switched to a decoy jet, with all of the markings of Air Force One, as he traveled to Islamabad, Pakistan for a visit marked by extraordinary security.
The switch was revealed when a Secret Service agent resembling Clinton stepped out of Air Force One upon touching down in Pakistan, while Clinton disembarked from the second aircraft.
However, at least one member of the White House pool was aware of the ruse: Susan Page, then-president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, who was covering the trip for USA TODAY.
Page this week broke her 26-year silence on the briefing that preceded the secret switch.
“They told me about the extraordinary security procedures being taken because of the dangers in flying there, including use of the decoy plane,” she told the Post. “Of course, the dangers threatened the journalists covering the trip as well as President Clinton.”
On why she chose to share her experience all these years later, Page explained: “I haven’t spoken about this episode before, because of the off-the-record ground rules of that discussion. But since more than a quarter-century has passed—and since the ruse became evident as soon as President Clinton disembarked in Pakistan—I think it’s OK for me to relay it now.”

Top Iranian commander visited Iraq to discuss disarmament plan: Source
Esmail Qaani, head of the IRGC’s Quds Force, held meetings over the Iraqi government’s plan to disarm armed groups and bring weapons under state control, source tells Al Jazeera.
Baghdad, Iraq – An Iraqi source from within the leading Coordination Framework, an umbrella for Shia Iraqi parties, has told Al Jazeera that the commander of the Quds Force in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, made an unannounced visit to Baghdad earlier this week.
The source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Qaani held behind-the-scenes meetings with Iraqi political and security leaders, as well as commanders of Shia paramilitaries, on Monday to discuss the Iraqi government’s plan to disarm the armed groups and bring weapons under state control.
“Tehran sent a message via Qaani … no handing over of weapons of the factions at the present time,” the source said, adding that Iran estimates that a new round of war could break out.
“The Iranian message stressed on finding a political compromise instead of sliding into confrontation between the government and the armed factions that refuse to hand over their weapons,” the source said, adding that Iraqi political parties oppose the use of force to implement the government’s plan.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is facing a mounting political and security crisis as a September 30 deadline to restrict all weapons to state control approaches. He told parliament that his government is eager to implement a 2024 deal made with the United States-led coalition’s military mission in Iraq to end its presence as combat forces by the end of September.
The Iraqi government’s push for a monopoly on arms and the disarmament of pro-Iran armed factions, as well as Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, were among the topics discussed during al-Zaidi’s visit to the US last month, his first foreign trip since taking office in May. Days after meeting US President Donald Trump, al-Zaidi also headed to Tehran, where he held talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
On Tuesday, al-Zaidi directed the parliament’s Security and Defence Committee to prepare a draft law to restrict weapons to the state in accordance with constitutional contexts. He warned that unregulated weapons represent the most dangerous threat to the state as they undermine the authority of the law and the standing of security institutions.
But while a number of armed groups have agreed to integrate into the state’s armed forces, the defiant stance of some powerful Shia paramilitaries, including Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, threatens to derail the government’s efforts.
In a meeting earlier this month, the State Administration Coalition – which includes the most prominent Shia parties, as well as some Sunni and Kurdish political parties – called for the necessity of restricting weapons to the state, and considered the entities carrying out activity that threatens the country’s security outside the official institutions to be “outlaws that must be fought”. The coalition hinted at applying the “Anti-Terrorism Law” to any armed activity after the expiration of the government deadline.
Other Shia leaders are said to be trying to de-escalate and defuse tensions. The head of the Hikma Movement, Ammar al-Hakim, is leading efforts to de-escalate and persuade the factions to move towards restricting weapons to the state during the remaining month of the deadline, a source told Al Jazeera.
Regional security equation
The head of the Iraqi Center for Strategic Studies, Ghazi Faisal, said the continued retention by the Iraqi factions of their arsenal could transform the issue into a broader security crisis.
“The factions’ use of Iraqi territory and their military capabilities as a platform to target neighbouring countries may push those countries toward a direct response or toward building joint security arrangements to confront the sources of threat,” Faisal said, adding that any new regional security alliances to protect the security of the Gulf and the strategic waterways may find themselves compelled to deal with the armed factions as part of the equation of regional security, not merely as Iraqi political parties.
“The most realistic way out is to firmly establish the principle of restricting weapons and to link the decision of war and peace to the Iraqi constitutional institutions alone, because a state that does not monopolise the decision to use force cannot fully guarantee its national security, according to him,” he said.
Baghdad witnessed last week a security escalation against the backdrop of armed factions’ threats to respond to the Saudi-US attacks that targeted Popular Mobilisation Forces sites late last month.
In a statement, the US Central Command said it had launched joint attacks with Saudi Arabia on July 28 “against Iran-aligned terrorists” that the IRGC had “directed to attack U.S. forces and Saudi energy infrastructure”. The kingdom’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also accused “Iran-backed terrorist militias” in Iraq of choosing “an irresponsible path of escalation” by carrying out drone attacks against Saudi Arabia.
However, efforts by the Iraqi government and political factions succeeded in containing the tension, opening a path towards de-escalation and diplomatic movement.

Saudi Arabia bets on defensive alliances to deter slide into war

Saudi Arabia bets on defensive alliances to deter slide into war
- Saudi Arabia is forming regional defence alliances, including a maritime coalition and a pact with Turkey and Pakistan, to deter attacks from Iran and its allies.
- The kingdom has faced increasing attacks on oil infrastructure and shipping, prompting limited military responses and joint US airstrikes against Iraqi militias.
- Yemen’s Houthis resumed attacks in July, challenging Saudi’s security and pushing Riyadh to seek a multinational coalition to protect Red Sea shipping and stabilise the region.
AI generated
RIYADH – Increasingly dragged into a war it did not choose, Saudi Arabia is building regional defensive alliances that it hopes will keep its enemies at bay and help it respond more robustly to attacks by Iran and its network of regional allies.
But nascent attempts to construct a multinational maritime coalition in the Red Sea, and the decision to bring Turkey into a defence pact with the kingdom and Pakistan, have so far failed to ward off attacks, analysts and diplomats said.
The kingdom’s own military responses to attacks from Iran, Iraq and from Yemen’s Houthis, who in July opened a southern front against the kingdom and have attacked Saudi shipping, have so far been limited.
Riyadh faces a dilemma: how to deter attacks and protect the ambitious economic vision it is pursuing without becoming entangled in a broader conflict in the region sparked by the war between the US and Iran.
As one Middle Eastern official put it, “Saudi Arabia’s problem is that the kingdom’s enemies know it wants to avoid war. They are abusing that.”
The Saudi government media office did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
“This is all very concerning and is exactly what Saudi Arabia wanted to avoid,” said Aziz al-Ghashian, a Saudi analyst and senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum.
“Iran and its affiliates think Saudi won’t respond. They understood restraint as basically an acceptance of being targeted and this is why it was very important for Saudi to find a way to deter them. The trick is how to balance it,” he said.
After the defence pact was signed, the Houthis again attacked oil installations in the kingdom.
Gradual escalation
Since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on Feb 28, Saudi Arabia has tried to absorb attacks, choosing to first pursue a purely diplomatic path before beginning limited military responses that were kept secret.
It reached a tentative calm with Iran around the time an April ceasefire with the US went into effect and emerged as a safer haven in the Gulf.
The past few weeks have jeopardised much of that.
The kingdom has faced damaging attacks on critical oil infrastructure from Yemen and Iraq, as well as on its shipping via the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
Two weeks ago, Saudi Arabia and the US launched joint airstrikes targeting Iraqi militias they said were involved in the attacks on the kingdom. It was the first retaliation announced by the kingdom during the war, and came despite the Saudis having sought to avoid being seen as a co-belligerent with the US and Israel.
Two days later, Riyadh announced its intention to lead a maritime defence coalition in the Red Sea.
Last week, it announced the joint defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in Mecca.
“This is Saudi Arabia’s way to signal to Iran that we are willing to go further up the ladder, of course (first that) of diplomacy before crossing the line of diplomacy to the other side,” said Yasmine Farouk, project director for the Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula at Crisis Group.
“The way I see this pact and coalition is (Saudi Arabia) incrementally reaching the final stages of de-escalatory and deterrence policies,” she said, while still noting the coalitions were “trial balloons” and joint military action was currently unlikely.
Mecca defence agreement
Announced at Islam’s holiest site and after Friday prayers, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence agreement carries the symbolic weight of Muslim nations pledging to defend each other as if they were one “ummah,” or Muslim nation, according to Sultan Alamer, a non-resident scholar in the Carnegie Middle East Programme.
But in practice, the roles appear less clear.
On Aug 8, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the pact was technically the same as NATO’s Article 5 and would require consultations between all parties to determine what sort of support to provide any attacked country, if they ask for any.
Islamabad under its pre-existing defence pact with Saudi Arabia had sought to avoid becoming engaged militarily with Iran or its allies and managed to do so despite Saudi Arabia facing hundreds of missile and drone attacks.
Iran has framed the agreement as a step away from reliance on outside powers, apparently a reference to the United States, and said it saw no reason to be concerned, “so long as it correctly identifies the enemy and the threat”.
The Yemen headache
On Saudi Arabia’s southern border, Yemen’s Houthis in July ended a four-year truce, declaring a naval blockade on the kingdom and firing on its oil infrastructure.
The Houthi attacks have shown the kingdom’s continued vulnerability to asymmetric warfare and revived memories of the 2019 crisis when Saudi oil production halved after Houthi drone and missile attacks that were planned by Iran, according to Reuters reporting.
Yemen is a particular sore spot for the kingdom, which led a military intervention in 2015 after the Iran-backed Houthis stormed the capital Sanaa, resulting in an international outcry over the high toll from war and famine.
With Yemen once again edging towards war, Riyadh this time wants the Yemeni government to lead any offensive that takes place, and has said a multi-national maritime coalition is needed to defend Red Sea shipping.
Invitations were sent out just a few days before the first meeting, several people who attended said, showing the urgency with which Saudi Arabia was approaching the mission.
So far, 14 regional countries have signed on, with more expected to join. Western diplomats say European nations are still deliberating whether to join, concerned about how far they would potentially become involved in a war in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia wants to announce its official formation as soon as possible, with meetings planned this week in Jeddah. REUTERS

How Wednesday’s solar eclipse could help scientists understand the universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:32:30 UTC
21:32:30 KST

Aysu Bicer
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
A solar eclipse sweeping across parts of the Northern Hemisphere on Wednesday is offering scientists and skywatchers a rare opportunity to study the sun, while also highlighting how eclipses have helped astronomers better understand the wider universe.
The Moon will pass directly between Earth and the Sun, with a total eclipse visible along a narrow path through Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain. Ireland will experience a partial eclipse.
Oisin Creaner, an assistant professor of astrophysics at Dublin City University who writes for Irish broadcaster RTE, said eclipses remain valuable scientific events.
“The more you think about eclipses, though, the more questions you have – these questions have fascinated astronomers from the time of Newgrange right up to today, when eclipses help us learn about the Sun and the fundamentals of the universe,” he said.
Unlike most eclipses, those seen from Earth can produce a striking coincidence: the Sun and Moon appear almost exactly the same size in the sky. The sun is around 400 times wider than the moon but is also roughly 400 times farther from Earth.
That alignment allows the Moon to block the Sun’s bright surface during a total eclipse, revealing its outer atmosphere, known as the corona.
“The close match in apparent size means that, during a total solar eclipse, we can see very close to the Sun without being blinded by its bright surface,” Creaner wrote.
Eclipses have also played a role in testing fundamental physics. In 1919, observations during a total eclipse showed that the apparent positions of stars near the Sun shifted in the way predicted by Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity.
The same basic principle of a transit is now being used far beyond our solar system. When an exoplanet passes in front of its star, the resulting dip in starlight can reveal information about the planet’s atmosphere and its chemical composition.
Creaner said such observations could eventually help scientists search for signs of life on worlds orbiting other stars.

41 nations call for advance warning on ballistic missile tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:32:09 UTC
21:32:09 KST

A 41-nation coalition has called on nuclear-armed states to provide advance notice of long-range ballistic missile tests, warning that unannounced launches could threaten regional peace and global security.
In a joint statement delivered at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva on Wednesday, the countries urged states to follow transparency measures under the Hague Code of Conduct Against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCOC).
The coalition said nuclear-capable missile tests conducted without sufficient warning and information can increase the risk of miscalculation, particularly for countries located near launch areas.
Coalition calls for 24-hour notice
The signatories urged countries testing intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles and space launch vehicles to issue notifications at least 24 hours before launches.
They said advance notices should identify the missile class, launch window, launch area and planned trajectory, along with clear warnings for ships and aircraft operating nearby.
The appeal follows recent missile tests in the Pacific, including China's reported launch of a strategic missile from a nuclear submarine after notifying several Pacific nations.
The coalition said standardised notification procedures would not restrict countries' military development or operational requirements but would instead improve confidence and reduce the possibility of dangerous misunderstandings.
China rejects criticism
China's Ambassador for Disarmament Affairs Li Chijiang rejected the statement, saying Beijing's legitimate defence modernisation should not be questioned.
He also defended China's advance notification of missile launches, arguing that its efforts should not be subjected to geopolitical calculations.
The 41 signatories include the United States, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada and Ukraine, among others.

A new data center in west London has been approved despite concerns over its demands on electricity and water supplies.
According to a report by the BBC, Hounslow Council’s Planning Committee voted in favor of plans for the facility on a 12.2-acre brownfield site at the Haslemere Heathrow Estate earlier this month.
The scheme requires an 80MVA high-capacity power connection, equivalent to the electricity needs of tens of thousands of homes.
The Greater London Authority (GLA) has warned that around 10 times the electricity capacity currently used by London’s existing data centres has already been requested in the grid connection queue.
Data centers house IT infrastructure, including servers, and are described by the government as underpinning much of the UK’s economic activity and innovation.
London is already home to the vast majority of the UK’s data center capacity, with 99 operational sites and 26 in the planning pipeline as of November last year, according to the GLA.
Ofgem has also identified data centers as a major driver of demand on the UK’s electricity grid.
Hounslow councillors were told that the new center would receive electricity from the National Energy System Operator via the Laleham Grid Supply Point, outside the borough. Planning officers said it would not use capacity earmarked for other developments, including housing.
However, questions remain over its impact on local water supplies.
Affinity Water told MPs in May that some data centers were seeking up to three million liters of water a day—equivalent to the peak demand of around 3,500 homes.
The GLA had previously warned that the scheme did not fully comply with the London Plan, citing concerns over transport and its high water and energy intensity.
Under the approval, the developer must submit a strategy to minimize operational water consumption.
The decision comes after Ealing Council approved a 52,000-square-meter data center at the former Honey Monster factory in Southall last month.
Both schemes remain subject to a Stage 2 referral to the Mayor of London.

British driver sets speed record in hydrogen-powered car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:30:36 UTC
21:30:36 KST

Retired RAF pilot Andy Green has set a world land speed record for a hydrogen-powered car, reaching 406.320 mph (653.908 km/h) at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah.
The 64-year-old drove the JCB Hydromax, a 9.75-metre car built by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The record, ratified by motorsport's governing body the FIA, was measured as the average of two runs and more than doubled the previous hydrogen combustion mark of 185.5 mph, set in 2004.
Green already held the diesel land speed record, set at Bonneville in 2006, and remains the only person to have broken the sound barrier in a car — a feat he achieved in the jet-powered ThrustSSC in 1997, at 763 mph.
The Hydromax runs on two hydrogen internal combustion engines producing a combined 1,600 horsepower, adapted from those used in JCB's construction machinery. They mix pressurised hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create power. "You burn hydrogen, water comes out of the exhaust. It doesn't get any cleaner than that," Green said after the run.
JCB hopes the project will strengthen the case for hydrogen in heavy industry. But hydrogen is only as clean as its source: the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels, and the green hydrogen the company has contracted to buy makes up a tiny fraction of global production.

Little surprise Beijing doesn’t want Western advice for its economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:30:10 UTC
21:30:10 KST

Little surprise Beijing doesn’t want Western advice for its economy
The lack of forceful stimulus is not policy paralysis, as foreigners assume – China simply operates on a different set of priorities
When a patient repeatedly refuses the same medicine, there are usually three possibilities: he does not understand the diagnosis, cannot afford the treatment, or does not trust the doctor. The same logic applies to economic prescriptions.
In the case of China, the first possibility is unlikely because Beijing understands what ails its economy. The reason it is not acting as expected is probably a combination of the other two scenarios, compounded by a more fundamental difference: China believes it is treating a different disease.
Western economists see weak consumption, a prolonged property downturn, deflationary pressure, a massive trade surplus and indebted local governments. Their standard prescription is to transfer more income to households, strengthen the social safety net and reduce reliance on investment, exports and manufacturing.
Beijing has moved in some of these directions, but not at the scale or decisiveness outsiders expect. This is wrongly interpreted as policy paralysis. A more useful explanation is that China is no longer optimising simply for short-term gross domestic product growth.
Beijing is preparing for prolonged strategic rivalry with the United States, as economist Tan Kong Yam and others have pointed out. Seen through this lens, China’s choices become less puzzling. Beijing is trying to reduce technological dependence, preserve industrial capacity and withstand a longer period of Western pressure. GDP still matters, but it is no longer the be-all and end-all of Beijing’s calculations.

ICJP letter to UK minister calls for sanctions on settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:28:51 UTC
21:28:51 KST

Breadcrumb
ICJP letter to UK's MENA minister calls for immediate sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
The International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) on Wednesday called for the UK to extend sanctions against all trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In a letter written to the UK's Middle East Minister, Labour MP Stephen Doughty, and seen by The New Arab, the ICJP welcomed his condemnation of settlement expansion and their illegality under international law.
The letter called on the UK government to "move beyond statements of concern and non-binding warnings directed at a limited number of organisations and address the settlement enterprise, and the economic relationships that sustain it, as a whole."
"We therefore urge you to use your position as Minister of the Middle East and secure targeted measures, without further delay, prohibiting trade with and economic support for illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory," it continued.
"Such measures should address not merely particular actors or transactions, but the broader commercial and financial relationship that contribute to the maintenance and expansion of the illegal settlement enterprise," the letter added.
"Sanctions are not a radical step–they are the bare minimum required to uphold international law, and the legal position on Israeli settlements is clear," Órlaith Roe, ICJP's Public Affairs and Communication Officer, explained.
"The question for the UK government is no longer whether it condemns settlement expansion, but what concrete measures it is prepared to take in response," she added.
The UK has frequently condemned the existence of illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside the accompanying rise of settler violence that is ongoing in the area.
On Monday, UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband held separate calls with both Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Moustafa.
In a statement released regarding his call with Sa'ar, Miliband said that he "raised the sharp escalation of settler violence and settlement expansion," adding that "Israel must crack down on violence in the West Bank."
Despite the words of condemnation and sanctions on individual settlers, Israeli settler violence has continued to grow, alongside Israeli government decisions to expand Israeli settlements, most notably the E1 settlement that threatens to split the occupied West Bank into two.
The expansion of Israeli state and settler violence, which has seen the forced displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, has been described by rights groups as a policy of state-sanctioned "ethnic cleansing".
ICJP noted in its letter to Doughty that the Israeli government approved 13 new settlements on 3 July, and £300 in funding for settlement expansion on 18 July, measures that "form part of an escalating effort to entrench Israel's unlawful settlement enterprise and create further irreversible changes on the ground."
It added that there was an expectation for the government to take further action, following a letter written by 140 Labour MPs to former Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper on 7 June which called for a ban on trade with settlements, and the announcement by the Charity Commission of an investigation into funding links between UK-based charities and settlements.
Roe told The New Arab that the ongoing changes on the ground in the occupied West Bank require immediate action from the British government.
"Sanctions have to be an immediate priority. With the E1 settlement tenders due to go live imminently, the window to prevent irreversible changes on the ground is rapidly closing," she said.
"This is also an important early test for Minister Doughty: how he responds now will set the tone for his tenure and show how seriously he intends to approach the UK's responsibility to uphold international law and prevent settlement expansion," she added.
Alongside pressure in the UK, the EU is also actively deliberating issuing of trade sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements, though efforts to push through bloc-wide sanctions have so far failed.
ICJP's own letter ended by saying that the implementation of sanctions on Israeli settlements would "demonstrate that the United Kingdom's stated commitment to international law carries real and measurable consequences."
