Five years on, international limitations weigh on Taliban-run Afghanistan as rights concerns persist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:20:21 UTC
21:20:21 KST

Share & more
Facing sustained international condemnation over its treatment of women and girls, Afghanistan’s Islamic Emirate government has spent five years under diplomatic, financial, and political pressure since Taliban forces entered Kabul on 15 August 2021 following the flight of former Western-backed President Ashraf Ghani.
The former government relied on international assistance throughout 20 years of US/NATO occupation from 2001 to 2021, including for 75% of its public expenditure in 2019. When the Taliban-led government returned to power, billions of dollars of the nation’s Central Bank reserves were immediately frozen and rendered inaccessible by the US and UK. Top leadership were placed under financial and travel restrictions and foreign aid was quickly slashed as nations cleared out their embassies.
One of the key stated intentions of these cutbacks and limitations was to pressure a government that keeps girls and women out of official schools and universities beyond the sixth grade, bars women from most government jobs, and is frequently accused of detaining activists and media workers on often unclear charges.
But the experience of the past five years shows that the consequences of these measures have fallen heavily on ordinary Afghans, while the Taliban's own policies have compounded the damage. The United Nations says at least 22 million Afghans, including 10.7 million women and girls, now need humanitarian assistance.
Even amid sustained international pressure, the Taliban government has made some notable gains in reconstruction and stabilising the nation’s currency, while continuing to face widespread criticism from rights groups for its treatment of women and girls.
Diplomatically, the Islamic Emirate has also made progress. Russia is still the only country to formally recognise the government, but Iran, Uzbekistan, India, the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and China have all developed closer ties with Kabul. These fall short of formal recognition but are increasingly seen by analysts as evidence of the Taliban’s growing de facto acceptance.
These ties have led to bilateral pacts, investment agreements, and diplomatic visits, but have yet to ease the bureaucratic difficulties faced by millions of Afghans looking to travel, study, and work abroad.
Anwar Mangal, an Afghan-American who moved to Oman in 2023, used the sultanate as an example of how non-recognition, even in friendly countries, can make the simplest of tasks more difficult.
Oman transferred control of Afghanistan’s embassy in Muscat to representatives appointed by the Islamic Emirate in 2024, but Afghans still have a hard time procuring even visitor visas.
“When I approached several universities to explore scholarship options for my cousins, I was told plainly that there are no bilateral education agreements in place” between Kabul and Muscat, and that any Afghan students studying in Oman were there as part of a “special USAID arrangement”, Mangal told The New Humanitarian.
That arrangement, he said, was a female-only programme that allowed dozens of Afghan women to study in Oman, but the Women’s Scholarship Endowment, as it was known, saw its funding terminated after the 2025 USAID cuts. “No one really knows what became of those [women],” Mangal said.
It’s not just Oman though. In the summer of 2026, a private business hung banners across Kabul advertising Turkish visas for $1,000 despite the fact that Ankara has hosted Taliban diplomats since 2023. Even New Delhi and Moscow, both of which have emerged as close partners of the Islamic Emirate, have yet to make good on promises of expanded visa programmes.
Frozen assets and bank wariness
The Islamic Emirate’s greatest diplomatic challenges lie in courting the Western countries that bankrolled the previous Islamic Republic government – which consistently ranked among the most corrupt governments in the world – as well as neighbouring Pakistan, which faced accusations of playing a “double game” between the Western-backed government and the Taliban during the US-led occupation.
In 2022, US President Joe Biden signed an executive order blocking roughly $7 billion in Afghan Central Bank reserves held in the United States and directing that $3.5 billion be set aside for the benefit of the Afghan people, while the other half remained subject to legal claims by families of victims of the 9/11 attacks. A New York federal judge ruled in February 2023 that the victims could not seize the $3.5 billion, a decision subsequently upheld by a US appeals court in 2025.
The assets remain outside the control of Afghanistan’s Central Bank, with the $3.5 billion allocated to the Switzerland-based Afghan Fund, where they are held and managed independently of the Islamic Emirate.
Meanwhile, financial restrictions and the disruption of Afghanistan’s banking links with the international financial system continue to complicate access to finance for businesses and investors.
US officials insist that a series of general licences allow investors and international aid groups to operate in Afghanistan without violating US sanctions. Business leaders say what happens in practice is very different: Banks remain wary of Afghanistan-related transactions, fearing the legal and compliance risks of inadvertently breaching sanctions.
A former USAID worker who advises a woman-run business in Kabul told The New Humanitarian she continues to face major issues with something as simple as transferring funds to pay workers in Afghanistan.
“I would say every other transaction still gets flagged by the banks,” she said, preferring not to publish her name. “That means that each time $25,000 just disappears into the banking system for at least two months and we have no way of tracing or tracking it.”
She said the business in Kabul may only employ a few dozen men and women, but made the point that one person in Afghanistan is often responsible for the financial well-being of an entire family, so a delayed payment can have an outsized impact on the lives of potentially hundreds of people.
“It leads to a lot of suspicions from the workers,” she said. “All they know is their wages get held up every few months.”
The impact of aid cuts
The decline in Western development assistance also remains a major constraint on Afghanistan’s economy. Donor governments have cited the need for greater coordination with Islamic Emirate authorities, as well as concerns over governance and women’s rights, in limiting their willingness to fund conventional development projects. The result is a growing gap between humanitarian assistance and the longer-term investment needed to modernise agriculture, healthcare, water management and other essential infrastructure.
Maisam Shafiey, advocacy and communications manager at the Norwegian Refugee Council, told The New Humanitarian the policy has left “vulnerable people of Afghanistan” to “pay the price” as systems and infrastructure continue to deteriorate.
He cited water management as a primary example of where development assistance can have a meaningful impact.
Kabul is predicted to become the first modern capital to run out of water, by 2030, but Shafiey said NGOs can’t just “keep delivering water with trucks” and hope to have a lasting effect.
Rather than abandoning development aid, Shafiey urged Western countries to pursue “pragmatic engagement” with the Islamic Emirate, working through relevant ministries and providing the technical assistance needed to plan and implement long-term projects.
Dejan Panic, Afghan country director for Emergency – an international medical NGO based in Milan, Italy – said a focus on humanitarian assistance above all has led to “a paradox”.
“Humanitarian funding,” he explained, “helped preserve essential services, but it could not fully replace the longer-term financing mechanisms that had supported the health system,” particularly in a country facing high levels of poverty, displacement, and malnutrition, alongside significant maternal and child health needs, chronic disease, disability, and limited access to specialised care.
The arrival of the second Trump administration and its drastic cuts to USAID funding further worsened an already precarious situation.
Shafiey told The New Humanitarian that the cuts had become a primary driver of the “deterioration of the humanitarian situation” in Afghanistan. He said his organisation “can only help 10% of the people in need” at present.
Panic said contractions in international funding had meant far more than simply scaling back humanitarian projects. Using the healthcare system as an example, he said aid cuts “can affect the ability of the health system to retain staff, maintain facilities, procure medicines and sustain referral networks.”
These are major blows to a health system that Panic said “had already become structurally dependent on international assistance” long before 2021, and where underfunded hospitals can be forced to treat hundreds of patients at a time following natural disasters.
Conflict with Pakistan, and the Iran war
Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have deteriorated sharply over the past year, with longstanding disputes over militant activity escalating into Islamabad declaring “open war” on its neighbour. Repeated clashes and Pakistani airstrikes have killed civilians, disrupted trade, and turned a historically important Taliban interlocutor into one of Kabul’s most serious security challenges.
Pakistan’s military killed or wounded more than 1,180 people, including women and children, in air and missile strikes across nine provinces between December 2024 and June 2026, displacing more than 29,000 families, according to Afghan human rights organisation Rawadari. The group also accuses Islamabad of damaging hundreds of homes, schools, health centres, mosques, and other public facilities.
Pakistan, meanwhile, maintains that its strikes target armed groups operating from safe havens on Afghan territory, rather than civilians. Islamabad has repeatedly accused Kabul of harbouring militants responsible for attacks inside Pakistan – a grievance that predates the Taliban's return to power and was also directed at the former Western-backed government.
For Elsa Chandio, a researcher at the Islamabad-based Center for Research and Security Studies, the deterioration of the relationship comes down to a single issue, security. She told The New Humanitarian that the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) group has adopted an “increasingly emboldened posture” since the Islamic Emirate’s return, which explains why “Islamabad’s concerns are legitimate”.
A report from a Pakistani think tank described 2025 as the country’s deadliest year in a decade, with 3,413 people killed in violence across the country. Pakistani officials have blamed much of the violence on the TTP, which they accuse of operating from and receiving support in Afghanistan. Kabul has repeatedly denied the allegations. The Islamic Emirate says Pakistan should address its own domestic problems, including longstanding grievances among its Pashtun and Baloch populations, rather than blaming Afghanistan. Speaking at a press conference in early August, Islamic Emirate spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said Afghanistan “did not initiate any such actions” and did not want relations between the two countries to deteriorate.
Since October 2023, when Islamabad enacted a mass deportation drive of Afghans, more than 2.5 million Afghans have returned from Pakistan, a figure that rises to almost six million if you include returns from Iran. Both the NRC and Emergency cited mass returns from both Pakistan and Iran as the primary humanitarian challenge for Afghanistan going forward.
The US-Israeli war with Iran has further complicated the situation. Iran, which has repeatedly offered to mediate between its two neighbours, is now embroiled in a conflict of its own, while the Gulf states and Türkiye, which previously hosted negotiations between the two sides, are grappling with the wider fallout.
That war has also added to the challenges facing Afghans.
Millions of Afghans living in Iran can no longer reliably send remittances – averaging about $129 a month – home to some of Afghanistan’s poorest communities.
The conflict is also driving up agricultural costs. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) says rising fertiliser prices will leave Afghanistan needing $38.3 million in additional funding to help up to 600,000 households procure fertiliser and certified wheat seed ahead of the winter planting season. Richard Trenchard, the FAO representative in Afghanistan, described the situation as “not a supply crisis” but “an affordability crisis” at a critical point in the agricultural calendar.
It is another example of how events beyond Afghanistan’s borders are having direct consequences for Afghans already struggling with poverty and hunger.

Inglorious Twelfth? Calls for grouse season to be banned to prevent wildfires and peatland damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:19:57 UTC
21:19:57 KST

Every year on 12 August, fans of traditional British cuisine flock to plush restaurants in Mayfair to dine on grouse served with bread sauce and game chips. But those hoping to find the small wild birds, sourced from the UK’s moorlands, may be disappointed.
Wildfires have been raging on moors across the UK, burning habitats and incinerating wildlife, after record-breaking heat turned the landscape into a tinderbox.
The intensive management of grouse moors involves the draining of peatland and the burning of the vegetation that grows on it. Environmental experts argue that doing this creates the conditions for wildfires as dry peat acts as fuel and smoulders for extended periods, making fires almost impossible to extinguish.
Because of this, the Green party in Scotland, where there are a large number of grouse shoots, has called for the Glorious Twelfth – the traditional start of the grouse shooting season, before which time the birds cannot legally be hunted – to be banned. The UK government recently banned the burning of vegetation on deep peat in order to preserve these habitats.
The climate crisis, caused by pollution from burning fossil fuels, makes every heatwave more likely and intense. The heatwave at the end of June was the most severe ever recorded in Europe and would not have been possible without human-caused global heating.
The chef Richard Corrigan, who owns Corrigan’s and Bentley’s in Mayfair, has always served grouse during his multi-decade career running kitchens. But this year they are in short supply.
He said: “I was hoping to get something on the 12th; it’s looking like it’s running a week and a half late. They will be smaller and fewer, which is fine and it is a treat. We should treat them with the respect they deserve. The hot weather hasn’t helped everything this year, that’s for sure.”
Corrigan will be finding it more difficult than some chefs to get birds for the table because he has become more particular about who he buys grouse from. “We now insist [birds] come from small estates rather than the large shoots, where dozens are shot at a time. I am not too sure I agree with the large shoots. I would rather people shoot wild animals for the table rather than shoot for the sake of having a day out.”
He also refuses to buy grouse from any moor that has been associated with raptor persecution – the shooting or poisoning of birds of prey to artificially boost grouse numbers. “Something that has really annoyed me is the killing of raptor birds on the estates. They are being poisoned by people on these estates. I would never buy grouse from those estates. We all know who they are,” Corrigan said.
The chef, who grew up in County Meath, Ireland, said the management of the moors had led to them being more susceptible to wildfires. “I was brought up in moorland, I am very aware of the heather and the turf, they need the wetlands to be restored to keep the moors in good shape. Some estates have taken it all a bit too far and have turned it into factory grouse shooting operations.”
While some will be serving their grouse with bread sauce and game chips, which are deep-fried, thin slices of potato, Corrigan is going to dish out a lighter option. “They will be on the menu barbecued with peaches and jalapeño. There is nothing better to eat than peaches from Provence and little spatchcocked grouse.”
Henry Harris, the chef-owner of Bouchon Racine in Farringdon, London, said he was keeping his fingers crossed that he would receive grouse this week from his supplier. “I will know today whether there’s been a problem,’ he said. “If they fly, they will be shot. If it is too hot, they will not fly. If the weather really is too hot, they tend to struggle to drive them up into the air, which will mean there are less birds out there.”
He added that he was concerned about the wildfires and their impact on moorland wildlife, including grouse. “People do expect us to serve it, it is very popular,” he said. “We had a queue for them last year.”
Unlike Corrigan’s untraditional peach and jalapeño recipe, Harris said he would be “serving it very traditionally with a slight Gallic twist, on a lovely piece of sourdough toast with a bit of paté, armagnac sauce, bread sauce and game chips”.
Ariane Burgess, the rural affairs spokesperson for the Scottish Greens, will not be joining the queue. She said the countryside should not be “managed as a playground for bloodsports”, and the moors of Scotland were “intensively managed so that grouse can be killed for entertainment”.
She said: “Scotland’s land is one of our greatest assets. It should be supporting thriving rural communities, restoring nature and tackling the climate crisis, rather than serving as a private playground for the wealthy few.
“The real glorious future for Scotland’s moors would be seeing wildlife flourish on them, peatlands restored and rural jobs created through the recovery of our natural environment.”

Iranian photojournalist faces 15 years in prison over images, reporting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

21:19:44 KST

Iranian photojournalist faces 15 years in prison over images, reporting
LONDON, Aug 12 - Acclaimed Iranian photojournalist Yalda Moaiery has spent much of her career documenting moments of dissent and the lives of women in Iran. The work has repeatedly brought her into conflict with the authorities, and on Iran's National Journalist Day on Saturday she learned she had been sentenced to 15 years in prison.
The sentence was handed down under a law enacted after a 12-day war between Israel and Iran in 2025, legislation that Iranian authorities say is intended to combat espionage and cooperation with hostile states.
When Moaiery arrived at Tehran's Revolutionary Court, she was not given formal case documents, she said. Instead, a friend accompanying her copied details from a charge sheet by hand. Rights groups say such procedures reflect a lack of transparency in Iran's judicial system.
According to the handwritten notes reviewed by Reuters, the accusations against her include giving interviews to media outlets deemed hostile by the authorities and providing photographs to organisations linked to the U.S. and Israel. Reuters could not independently verify the contents of the charge sheet.
In a statement provided to Reuters, Moaiery said the intelligence wing of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps raided her home during anti-government protests in January and confiscated her phone, laptop and other electronic equipment. She said IRGC officers returned after the U.S. launched air strikes on Iran this year and again seized her belongings.
“On this occasion, they took everything, including even the cameras I had owned since childhood," she said.
"I was subjected to several interrogations, and eventually my case was referred to Branch 33 of the Security Prosecutor’s Office and subsequently to the Revolutionary Court.”
The spokesman for Iran's United Nations Mission in New York did not respond to a request for comment on her case.
Roya Boroumand, executive director of the U.S.-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran, said that withholding case documents is an effort by the Islamic Republic to “silence" defendants and showed the judiciary "blatantly" acting as a state agent.
A CAREER CHRONICLING WOMEN'S LIVES IN IRAN
The handwritten document provided by Moaiery to Reuters lists accusations including “interviewing with networks hostile to the system” and sending photographs to entities in the United States and Israel that it describes as “hostile”.
Moaiery said she shared photographs showing damage from air strikes in Iran with CNN and appeared in an interview about her reporting in March 2026.
She has 10 days to appeal under the 2025 espionage law, half the time allowed under previous legislation.
Moaiery has previously been imprisoned for her work. She served two years in Gharchak Prison, a place that she had previously photographed.
In 2022, she spent three months in jail and was sentenced to eight years in prison for covering the nationwide “Woman, Life, Freedom” uprisings that erupted after the death of young Iranian woman Mahsa Amini in police custody. An amnesty later reduced the sentence, but she said the case continued to expose her to questioning by authorities.
Reporters Without Borders says 16 journalists have been detained in Iran this year.
Moaiery’s work has mainly focused on women. She photographed some of the earliest documented detentions of women by morality police, including a 2007 image showing two women sitting in white police vans, with tears streaming down their faces.
In 2017, she photographed a student protesting at economic conditions at Tehran University. The woman walks through tear gas, raising her fist in the air. The image was used by the Trump administration in its comments on human rights in Iran.
Moaiery said she remained committed to her work despite the prospect of further imprisonment.
“None of these sentences, however, has ever caused me to abandon my path, even for a moment. I have continued to document and show the realities of Iranian society,” she said.
“I don't have anything to lose. The regime took everything from me and the only thing that I still have is my truth and honesty as an observer.” REUTERS

EU's centrist coalition might fall short of a majority for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:17:45 UTC
21:17:45 KST

A new Europe Elects projection suggests Europe’s mainstream parties could lose their EU-level majority, reflecting the growing strength of right-wing and populist forces.
The next European Parliament majority may not be a centrist coalition, according to new data.
The three parties — the centre-right European People's Party (EPP), the centrist Renew Europe, and the centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) — which have formed a parliamentary majority since its creation would fail to secure one for the first time.
The seat projection was published on Wednesday by Europe Elects, an election data platform, which drew on voting intentions from each EU member state and modelled seat allocations based on each country's electoral law.
In recent years, Europe's mainstream political forces have been on a downward trajectory.
This latest projection marks a significant milestone: the centrist forces that have dominated European politics since the Second World War are, for the first time, projected to fall short of a majority at the EU level.
Parliamentary changes
The 2024 European Parliament elections already saw a significant shift in the political barycentre to the right, with right-of-centre parties gaining almost 60 MEPs, much of it driven by far-right, conservative and national-populist forces.
Europe Elects projects the S&D would suffer the largest loss, shedding 18 MEPs, followed by the EPP with 15 and Renew with nine. The Greens/EFA group, which has often propped up the parliamentary majority in the current term, would be further reduced, losing 14 seats.
Meanwhile, the hard-right Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) group, which includes Alternative for Germany, currently projected as the leading German party, would gain 19 seats.
The far-left group The Left is also projected to gain 19 seats, driven largely by leftist parties in France and Germany — a sign the political trend favours not just the right, but anti-establishment forces more broadly.
Still, most of the projected gains sit on the right of the chamber. Patriots for Europe (PfE), which includes Marine Le Pen's National Rally, is projected to gain 12 seats, driven by Spain's Vox and Austria's Freedom Party.
The European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), dominated by Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy, is due to remain largely stable, with three additional MEPs.
Group positioning
The hierarchy of political groups by size would largely hold, with the EPP remaining first, followed by the S&D, PfE, ECR and Renew. But the gap between the two main centrist forces and the largest right-wing group would narrow sharply, and Renew's position would be increasingly challenged by The Left.
The Greens/EFA group would slip behind The Left and the far-right ESN, becoming the smallest force in the Parliament — even as its votes become more pivotal than ever, since centrist parties would need the Greens more than at any point to form a majority.
One of the most significant shifts would occur within the EPP itself, where Spain's Popular Party and Poland's Civic Platform would become the largest national delegations, ending the German Christian Democratic Union's decade-long dominance of the group.
At the same time, the EPP would likely strengthen its position further, retaining the ability to form an alternative majority with right-wing parties, already a source of significant leverage for the centre-right group in day-to-day negotiations.
The ECR's standing could also be bolstered, having already gained significant institutional roles and legislative influence in the current term, potentially becoming more mainstream in the next.
Political trends
According to Europe Elects' director Tobias Gerhard Schminke, the latest projections confirm political trends that have defined the EU's electoral landscape in recent years.
"The first one that's often overlooked is that we see a fragmentation in the political system. So the EPP has about 21% support now in Europe. So, it will require a lot of political families to come together to form a majority," Schminke told Euronews.
He also pointed to eroding support for the political centre, part of a broader decline in consensus around liberal democracy, human rights and cooperation between European states within the EU framework.
Another trend he noted is that within the radical-right camp, forces like Meloni's Brothers of Italy and Le Pen's National Rally have reached a plateau, while most growth is coming from the more extreme forces gathered under the ESN umbrella.
The next European Parliament elections are not due until June 2029, and three years is a long time in politics. Parliamentary groups can also shift before or after elections, which inevitably affects the distribution of power in the chamber.
Still, if these trends hold through the next elections, they would further test the EU's unwritten cordon sanitaire: the agreement among mainstream parties to keep extremist forces from power.
"What we still see is an incremental increase of the radical right camp overall. And we're now at the point where it is difficult to ignore these parties when it comes to coalition dynamics, be it in the European Parliament or at the national level," Schminke said.

"Battlegroup South units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade, a mountain assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Nikolayevka, Slavyansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkovka, Pershomaryevka, Nikanorovka, Verolyubovka and Nikoaipolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 195 personnel, three armored combat vehicles, including a US-made Stryker armored personnel carrier and 21 motor vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup South over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 350 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 350 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy tank and five armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Center units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and four National Guard brigades in areas near the settlements of Dobropolye, Krasnopodolye, Belozerskoye, Annovka and Matyashevo in the Donetsk People’s Republic, Novopavlovka, Novonikolayevka and Petrovskoye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 350 personnel, a tank, five armored combat vehicles, seven motor vehicles and an artillery gun in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts 340 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted roughly 340 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup East units advanced deep into the enemy’s defenses and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of an assault brigade, three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Vasilkovka, Kolomiytsy and Ivanovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Shirokoye, Mirovka, Rybalskoye and Volnyansk in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 340 personnel, three armored combat vehicles and 17 motor vehicles in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 30 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 30 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades and a mountain assault brigade of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Orekhov, Preobrazhenka, Grigorovka and Yurkovka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
"Up to 30 [Ukrainian] military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 25 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and three electronic warfare stations were destroyed," the ministry reported.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian military airfields, fuel and energy sites over past day
Russian troops struck military airfields, fuel and energy infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army and enemy deployment sites over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces destroyed a patrol boat of the Ukrainian Navy and struck military airfields, fuel and energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army, sites storing attack unmanned aerial vehicles and their components, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 159 locations," the ministry said.
Russian air defenses intercept 1,061 Ukrainian UAVs, five HIMARS rockets over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,061 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and five US-made HIMARS rockets over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down six guided aerial bombs, five rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, five Neptune long-range missiles and 1,061 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet destroys eight Ukrainian naval drones over past day
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet destroyed eight Ukrainian naval drones in Black Sea waters over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"The Black Sea Fleet’s forces destroyed eight uncrewed surface vessels of the Ukrainian Navy in Black Sea waters," the ministry said.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 673 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 205,017 unmanned aerial vehicles, 669 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,551 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,769 multiple rocket launchers, 36,127 field artillery guns and mortars and 69,080 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

What is Zionism? Sabri Jiryis traces its origins and evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:17:06 UTC
21:17:06 KST

Breadcrumb
The Foundations of Zionism: Sabri Jiryis on the making of a colonial project in Palestine
"The Palestinians' adherence to their rights has never diminished. Their young generations recall history, are hostile to Israel and demand justice. It is not known when the chapter will come to an end - but the indigenous people have not forgotten their rights and will not give them up."
The Foundations of Zionism by Sabri Jiryis takes the reader on a tour of Jewish interreligious debates, from early Zionist settlers to the end of the British Mandate in 1948.
Jiryis, an 87-year-old Palestinian lawyer and writer fluent in Hebrew, with decades of activism, was the director of the Palestine Research Centre of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) in the 1970s and 80s.
His activism would lead to his being placed under administrative detention, or imprisonment without charge, by Israel before being exiled to Lebanon.
A major activist intellectual, his role as head of the Palestine Research Centre gave dispossessed people a chance to grow intellectually, academically and to explore their own history.
In 1982, Israel invaded Beirut and looted the Centre’s historical archives and this set Palestinian educational institutions back a step.
The Foundations of Zionism was originally published in two volumes in Arabic in 1977 and 1986, with the first volume first appearing in Lebanon and the second in Cyprus.
A single-volume, newly translated edition of the book will give English readers direct access to a towering work of historical writing.
Jiryis writes, "My encounter with Zionism began at a young age. As a child in my village of Fassouta, in the Galilee, I witnessed the Nakba of 1948 when I was 10 years old, and saw people from nearby villages in Lebanon… the question plagued me: ‘Who are these people? Why did they come here?"
Those two basic questions that animated the young life of Sabri Jiryis feel like the guiding motivation for producing this work.
What we find in the book is not a simple picture of what Zionism is and how history unfolded. Jiryis does not shy away from complexity, nuance and historically rooted analysis.
The Foundations of Zionism gets into the weeds of the debates Zionists had in the late 19th century and the 1940s, as well as the background for why they were happening.
The book begins by examining the development of Judaism before Zionism and the impact of European Christian persecution of Jews from the 15th century onwards.
Jiryis puts forward a well-documented case that Zionism is born out of European antisemitism — he examines the different manifestations of antisemitism in different places, regimes and ideologies and how this impacted Jewish life.
As Jiryis observes, events like the trial of the Jewish-French Army officer Alfred Dreyfus, falsely accused of treason, convinced many Jews that despite an era of equality and integration, their Jewish heritage would not be forgotten.
"The writings of many Zionist leaders and thinkers revealed a great disappointment with antisemitism, which prompted them to fundamentally reconsider their positions. In doing so, affected by the very racism inherent in anti-semitism, they adopted racist hypotheses of their own to counter it." They concluded that Jews needed to leave Europe and establish a country made up of fellow Jews.
A key takeaway from the book is that Zionism had several different beginnings in the late 19th century, and that the synthesis of these different parties was the source of constant tension.
In the chapter on Theodor Herzl, who authored The Jewish State and was an important Zionist leader, we find that many of his ideas were contentious among other Zionists.
"In his book, Herzl also called for drafting a constitution for the Jewish state, and suggested that this state should take the form of an aristocratic republic."
Herzl stated his position was explicitly against democracy in the new state. Herzl's involvement with the Zionist Congress, which brought together various pro-Zionist factions, drew scrutiny, as he was often accused of being insufficiently practical.
Herzl was opposed to the settlement of Jews in Palestine before receiving political support from regional powers.
Some, including the Lovers of Zion faction, wanted a movement to embrace Jewish settlements that were taking place at the time.
There was also suspicion that Herzl was willing to settle for any land, regardless of its location, and that he lacked commitment to the Palestine project.
Reading these arguments and how they evolve later on offers us a trace of what Israel would be formed out of.
The Foundations of Zionism introduces English readers to an important Palestinian intellectual as he dissects and makes sense of the history of Zionism.
It will challenge many to take the intellectual work of Palestinians seriously and offer piercing insight into how they make sense of the world around them.
The book dispels myths and unveils the history and trajectory of Zionism. Essentially, reading is for anyone looking for a deeper understanding.
Usman Butt is a multimedia television researcher, filmmaker and writer based in London who read International Relations and Arabic Language at the University of Westminster and completed a Master of Arts in Palestine Studies at the University of Exeter

Cambridge agrees to hold independent inquiry into Jason Arday appointment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:15:54 UTC
21:15:54 KST

Cambridge University’s leadership has bowed to internal pressure for an independent investigation into its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor, with its vice-chancellor admitting the affair has damaged the institution.
Prof Deborah Prentice said she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case” but described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour.
Senior Cambridge academics had called for the university to hold a fully independent inquiry into the circumstances around Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology of education, after the details of his career and life story were exposed to intense scrutiny.
The university initially defended him as the “victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility” but he resigned last week after a series of his claims were called into doubt.
In a letter to staff, Prentice said: “I know there is anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case … We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.
“That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge.”
The university did not supply any details of the investigation’s membership or its terms of reference.
Prentice said the investigation’s findings would be used to review Cambridge’s appointment process for senior roles, and that its education faculty bore some responsibility for Arday’s selection. She also highlighted that Arday had held positions at Durham and Glasgow universities before applying to Cambridge for a professorial chair.
“As you are fully aware, appointments to senior academic roles, as in the case of the faculty of education and Jason Arday, are currently led at department level,” she said. “I note that Durham and Glasgow universities have announced that they are also investigating the circumstances surrounding the appointment of Jason Arday to academic posts there.”
However, academics at Cambridge said Prentice’s description of the appointment process was “nonsensical”, and Arday’s appointment had been made by a separate board of electors chaired by a representative of the university’s leadership.
While Glasgow has announced its own investigation into Arday’s selection, Durham University declined to endorse Prentice’s comments.
A spokesperson for Durham said: “Since the recent emergence of questions relating to the circumstances surrounding Jason Arday’s appointment to a chair at Cambridge University, we have looked into his appointment to a junior academic role at Durham in 2019. He was appointed following a standard, competitive recruitment process in which he met published criteria for the role.
“He left Durham over four years ago and no longer has any formal association with us. Allegations about plagiarism in his PhD did not surface until after he had left Durham.”
Prentice also recognised the effect of the controversy on other black and minority ethnic academics at Cambridge, after some had described the atmosphere as toxic.
She said: “In light of the focus on this troubling case and the widespread commentary around it, I want to be very clear that we do not need the outcomes of an investigation to clearly and loudly affirm that our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community.
“This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge.
“The desire for quick answers and rapid responses is understandable, but we need to allow these reviews to complete their work effectively so we can learn from any mistakes and, where needed, improve our processes.”
Prentice joined Cambridge from Princeton University in 2023, several months after Arday’s appointment.

Mortgage rates finally stop rising, causing demand to trickle back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:13:45 UTC
21:13:45 KST

After five weeks of gains, mortgage rates fell very slightly last week. That was enough to bring a bit of demand back to the market.
Total mortgage application volume rose 3.6% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 6.77% from 6.81%, with points increasing to 0.67 from 0.65, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
"Mortgage rates declined slightly last week as oil prices dipped briefly on the hopes of a sustained resolution to the war in Iran," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release.
Applications to refinance a home loan rose 5% for the week but were 22% lower than the same week one year ago. Rates were 10 basis points lower one year ago.
"As refinance incentives have dwindled with rates at current levels, the average loan size for refinance applications was down to its lowest level since July 2025," said Kan.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 3% for the week and were 1% lower year over year. August is typically one of the slowest months for home sales, but this year appears to be even weaker than last year, due to stubbornly high home prices and less certainty in the overall economy. The supply of homes for sale has also not improved meaningfully.
Mortgage rates moved slightly higher to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. Rates could move more decidedly, depending on the results of the monthly consumer price index, set for release Wednesday.
"This is one of the most important pieces of monthly economic data as far as rates are concerned," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "There's no way to know how it will impact rates ahead of time--only that a large deviation from expectations is likely to result in a larger-than-average move higher or lower."

Parts of Spain were briefly plunged into darkness on Wednesday as a solar eclipse that began in Iceland and the Arctic progressed across the continent. It was the first total eclipse to be seen from mainland Europe in two decades. Read our blog to see how the event unfolded.

🎥 Solar eclipse plunges large swathe of Spain into total darkness
On Wednesday evening, millions of Europeans and enthusiasts from around the world gazed up at the sky in wonder as a rare total solar eclipse took place over northern Spain.
FRANCE 24's correspondent Sarah Morris has more from Segovia, Spain ⤵️
Parts of Spain plunged into darkness for two minutes
A large part of Spain switched from daylight into total darkness as the Moon covered the Sun, as thousands of spectators across the country looked on.
The total eclipse lasted less than two minutes in Lodoso, near Burgos, to the delight of thousands of people observing the phenomenon using special spectacles for safety, an AFP journalist at the scene said.
📸 Start of partial eclipse in several regions of Spain
The partial solar eclipse reached several regions in northern Spain, AFP journalists at Burgos, Tarragona and Colmenar Viejo near Madrid noted.
Several hundred people including many visitors from abroad and all wearing special protective glasses, gathered to watch the phenomenon in a field at Lodoso, near Burgos, an AFP journalist said.
Total solar eclipse plunges cloudy Iceland into darkness
The total solar eclipse plunged western Iceland into darkness, though heavy cloud cover blocked thousands of curious onlookers from seeing the sun disappear behind the moon, according to an AFP journalist.
Total darkness swept over Keflavik, some 50 kilometres (30 miles) southwest of the capital Reykjavik, at 5:47pm.
A total solar eclipse, which will briefly plunge part of Europe into daytime darkness, began over a remote region of the Arctic, the Russian space agency Roscosmos said.
The rare astronomical event started at around 1700 GMT at the northernmost tip of mainland Russia and is set to cross the northern hemisphere, passing over Greenland before moving across the Atlantic Ocean.
A total solar eclipse begins in the Arctic on August 12, 2026 as seen on Icelandic broadcaster RÚV .
🎥 Preparations ongoing in Spain for total solar eclipse
Across a swath of northern and central Spain, millions of people will have some of mainland Europe's best views of the celestial spectacle.
FRANCE 24's correspondent Sarah Morris reports from Segovia, Spain ⤵️

📸 Tourists and residents are getting ready for the eclipse in Segovia, Spain
On Wednesday evening in mainland France the sky will be mostly clear, offering perfect conditions for observing the total solar eclipse.
At around 8pm, when the sun will momentarily be obscured by the moon, temperatures are expected to remain “very high across many regions, particularly in the west, often ranging between 30 and 35°C, and between 25 and 28°C along the English Channel”, according to the national weather forecaster.

Tartu University Hospital cutting back departments seeing fewer patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:13:00 UTC
21:13:00 KST

Tartu University Hospital cutting back departments seeing fewer patients
Some employees at the hospital fear layoffs, but the hospital's management says staff will initially be offered the opportunity to take up other positions.
Several employees at Tartu University Hospital say there is anxiety and uncertainty among staff over how work will be organized in the future, amid fears of layoffs. Some employees have even taken out legal expenses insurance out of concern that they could lose their jobs. Although no official notices have yet reached the maternity ward, staff there are prepared for the possibility that 14 people could be laid off. One daytime midwife position was already eliminated in the spring.
Saima Hinno, a member of the hospital's management board, confirmed that work arrangements are being reviewed and positions will be eliminated if necessary, but said she could not say whether layoffs would take place or how many people they might affect.
"I can't give a specific number at the moment because, on the one hand, some reviews are still underway, while in some cases people have already moved to other positions. Whether the number ends up being that high, lower or higher, time will tell, as will the funding model we have been given. We also can't keep more people in positions than we have the funding or volume of treatment to support," Hinno said.
Hinno did not specify which other positions and departments could be affected by the restructuring. She said, however, that demand for staff has increased in the mental health field. The hospital is therefore also offering employees the opportunity to move into positions where there is a greater shortage of workers.
"We can talk about specialist nurses and whether they need additional training, more experience or further studies, because that would allow them to provide services for which there is greater demand. Layoffs are always subject to discussions between both sides and must be justified, because presumably there was a need for a position before and now that need no longer exists. Employees are always offered work they can do within the scope of their qualifications or with additional training, and we will certainly offer that," Hinno said.
So far, maternity ward employees have been offered the opportunity to work as operating room nurses or move to the hospital pharmacy. Many, however, would prefer to continue working in the profession for which they trained and maintain their professional qualifications.
According to a board member of the Estonian Midwives Association (EÄÜ), the decline in the number of births has not actually reduced midwives' workloads, as the profile of the average person giving birth has changed over the years, making deliveries more complicated.
"A midwife's work in a maternity ward certainly can't be assessed solely by how many births they actually attend. You also have to consider how much midwifery care each person giving birth may need overall. If we eliminate one position, regardless of where maternity care is provided, the workload of the colleagues who remain will certainly increase significantly. It may also be that some issues only become apparent once the changes are actually implemented. If staffing is reduced and there is a very large amount of work within a very short period of time — maternity care is an emergency healthcare service — unfortunately, not all of the consequences can be foreseen," EÄÜ board member Käthlin Vahtel said.
Neither North Estonia Medical Center nor the Women's Clinic at East Tallinn Central Hospital is planning similar changes to positions or layoffs.

Palm oil to cool data centres? Malaysia explores option as water demand surges
However, the proposal has raised concerns that it could lead to an expansion of palm plantations and create an environmental burden
Researchers at the Malaysian Palm Oil Board (MPOB) are developing a palm-based liquid to cool computer servers without relying on copious volumes of water, as the country grapples with high resource demands to support its rapidly expanding digital infrastructure.
The new approach – termed the Sawit EcoTherm technology by the government agency – is nearing commercialisation.
As of January, data centres were using 28.68 million litres (7.6 million gallons) of water a day, according to the National Water Services Commission.
But the palm oil technology has raised the question of whether a green solution for data centres would create new pressures further down the supply chain. Experts say this hinges on where palm oil sources are derived and if existing plantations can meet demand or result in more land clearance.
Noor Khairin Mohd, a MPOB senior research officer, said the coolant research had been tested in an operational environment, with a licensing agreement being finalised with a local manufacturer.

Poland unveils first warship under major naval modernisation programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:09:56 UTC
21:09:56 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed.
The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences.
“Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity.
Na terenie PGZ Stoczni Wojennej w Gdyni prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki, @PremierRP @donaldtusk oraz wiceministrowie @MON_GOV_PL @magdasobkowiak i @pawelbejda uczestniczą w uroczystości chrztu pierwszej jednostki programu „Miecznik”, fregaty wielozadaniowej – przyszłego ORP Wicher. pic.twitter.com/X2ftjoKTLZ
— Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026
The ORP Wicher, a medium-sized warship designed for escort, air defence and other fleet protection duties, is the first of three multi-role frigates based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design being built under Poland’s Miecznik programme, the largest modernisation project in the history of the Polish Navy.
It is due to be launched on Thursday in a complex manoeuvre involving its transfer and controlled launch from a semi-submersible barge. Shipyard officials have described the operation as one of the most demanding engineering projects undertaken by Poland’s shipbuilding industry.
The three frigates are intended to form the core of Poland’s surface fleet and will replace Poland’s two current Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates, which were constructed in the 1970s and transferred from the US Navy in the years 2000 and 2002.
Ahead of Wicher’s launch, leading Polish officials attended the naming ceremony in Gdynia, including Tusk and Nawrocki, who are normally bitter rivals but have sought to present a more united front when it comes to national defence.
“There can be no arguments or disputes when it comes to our country’s security,” said Tusk, who declared that Poland was seeking to play a role in “determining not only its own future, but also the entire region and Europe”.
Nawrocki, meanwhile, said that the modernisation of the Polish navy “sends a clear message that we will develop our armed forces in every theatre – on water, on land, and in the air”.
Both leaders also hailed the fact that the new frigates are being built in Poland itself, helping bolster the Polish shipbuilding industry.

The contract for the three frigates was signed in 2021 between Poland’s state Armament Agency (AU) and a consortium led by state-owned defence group PGZ, with British defence firm Babcock and other foreign partners also involved.
The project was initially valued at about 8 billion zloty but had risen to around 15 billion zloty by the end of 2023 following amendments.
Construction of the second frigate in Gdynia’s military shipyard began in May 2025, while work on the third began in April this year. The programme is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2031.
Swedish defence giant Saab has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Polish state defence group PGZ.

The ships are more than 140 metres long and are based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design, developed by Babcock and adapted to Polish military requirements.
The frigates will be equipped with British CAMM and CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles, naval guns and anti-ship missiles capable of striking targets at ranges of more than 200 km.
Their missions will include protecting shipping lanes and critical energy infrastructure and taking part in NATO naval groups.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on a major defence procurement spree. It now has the highest relative defence budget in NATO and is also the alliance’s largest arms importer.
In recent years, Poland has also increasingly oriented itself towards the Baltic region, forming closer economic, energy and military ties with allies around the sea.
Last year, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership on defence and economic ties. They subsequently held their first ever bilateral military exercises in the Baltic.
As part of its naval modernisation programme, Poland has selected Sweden’s Saab as the supplier for three advanced A26 stealth submarines in a deal worth around €4.5 billion.

Russia Amasses 6,200 Kamikaze Drones for Armada Assault on Ukraine, HUR Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:08:52 UTC
21:08:52 KST

Russia has accumulated about 6,200 Geran kamikaze drones of various versions for large-scale attacks against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian military intelligence.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) provided the estimate to the Ukrainian defense news outlet Militarnyi, saying the figure reflected Russia’s stockpile as of August 2026.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Limited production capacity prevents Russian forces from maintaining the highest rate of drone launches continuously, the intelligence agency said. Moscow therefore has to build up large reserves before carrying out particularly intensive attacks.
During Russia’s largest strikes, between 600 and 1,000 drones could be launched in a single attack, according to HUR.
When Russian forces are replenishing their stockpiles, they typically launch about 150 to 200 drones at a time. That number can reach approximately 300 in some attacks.
Russia has set new records for the number of drones launched against Ukraine this year, using between 6,000 and 6,500 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in some months, Militarnyi reported.
The reported stockpile could allow Moscow to conduct several large-scale attacks, although the precise number would depend on how many drones Russia deploys in each barrage and whether it continues manufacturing additional drones during that period.
The term “Geran” covers several Russian versions of the Iranian-designed Shahed kamikaze drone. Russian forces use the drone in attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, often launching them alongside missiles and other types of drones in an attempt to overwhelm air defenses.

Vigor unveils its newest Maneuver Support Vessel for U.S. Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:08:46 UTC
21:08:46 KST

- Vigor Marine Group unveiled the USAV Craney Island, the second Maneuver Support Vessel (Light) built for the U.S. Army, scheduled for fall delivery.
- More than 300 workers at Vigor's Vancouver, Washington facility built the vessel alongside more than 40 Washington state-based companies and additional suppliers nationwide.
A boat built to carry a 70-ton battle tank through the surf rolled off an assembly line in Vancouver, Washington, and the U.S. Army is counting down to delivery this fall.
Vigor Marine Group unveiled the USAV Craney Island, the second Maneuver Support Vessel (Light) built under a program designed to replace the Army’s aging landing craft fleet, the company announced, describing the vessel as carrying next-generation capabilities meant to improve payload capacity, maneuverability, speed and operational flexibility over the class it replaces.
The Maneuver Support Vessel (Light), known by its shorthand MSV(L), exists to retire a landing craft that has been hauling Army equipment ashore since 1959, a boxy, flat-bottomed vessel commonly nicknamed the “Mike Boat” for its official designation, the Landing Craft Mechanized-8. That aging fleet has kept the shallow-water beaching capability the Army needs to move heavy equipment from ship to shore in places without developed ports, but decades of service left it increasingly outmatched by the weight and speed modern battlefield logistics demand. Vigor built Craney Island using an all-aluminum hull design paired with waterjet propulsion, a lightweight construction approach that keeps the vessel maneuverable in shallow coastal waters while still delivering the payload capacity needed to move some of the Army’s heaviest vehicles.
Francesco Valente, CEO of Vigor Marine Group, framed the unveiling as validation of years of work by the Vancouver workforce that built the vessel.
“We are proud to reach this important milestone with the unveiling of Craney Island. This is a critical milestone for both the U.S. Army and for our skilled Vigor Marine Fabrication workforce in Vancouver, where this journey began years ago. Today reflects the dedication of our employees, suppliers and Army partners who have worked together to refine this next-generation vessel. Our goal is to support our customer’s mission by completing quality work safely, and today we celebrate achieving that on behalf of the U.S. Army,” said Valente.
More than 300 skilled workers at Vigor Marine Fabrication’s Vancouver facility, led by Vice President and General Manager Mark Norris, contributed to building Craney Island, drawing on trades including aluminum welders, electricians and mechanics who specialize in the kind of precision fabrication national security vessels require. More than 40 Washington state-based companies contributed to the effort as well, alongside additional suppliers and partners spread across the Pacific Northwest and the broader United States, a distributed industrial footprint that Vigor says has directly supported growth in family-wage manufacturing jobs in the Vancouver area.
Craney Island did not emerge from a blank design. Vigor launched the program’s prototype, the SSG Elroy F. Wells, in 2022, and has spent the years since working alongside the Army to test that vessel across the Pacific Northwest and in Hawaii, gathering real-world performance data under actual operating conditions rather than relying solely on computer modeling or dockside testing. Craney Island incorporates the lessons learned from that testing period, combined with what the company describes as expert craftsmanship from its local workforce, resulting in what Vigor calls a first-of-its-kind capability for the Army built around a sophisticated all-aluminum design paired with advanced propulsion systems and electronics.
The vessel’s design centers on features built specifically for the demanding job of moving armored vehicles between ship and unimproved shore. Its drive-through configuration, with ramps at both the bow and stern, lets vehicles load and unload without needing to turn around inside the craft, a detail that speeds up operations during time-sensitive amphibious missions. The combination of lightweight aluminum construction and waterjet propulsion gives the vessel a shallow draft suited to littoral operations, the term for missions conducted in the near-shore waters where larger, deeper-hulled ships cannot safely operate, while still delivering what Vigor describes as significant payload carrying capability and unparalleled maneuverability compared to the legacy fleet it replaces.
The company’s Vancouver facility has now entered full-rate production of MSV(L) hulls, the manufacturing phase that follows initial prototype and early production work, while simultaneously continuing fabrication of a separate vessel class, the Combatant Craft Medium, of which the yard has already produced more than 30 units for other military customers. That dual production track underscores how central the Vancouver facility has become to a specific segment of American naval shipbuilding, one focused on smaller, specialized craft rather than the large surface combatants that typically dominate headlines about the state of the U.S. Navy’s shipbuilding industrial base.
Vigor tied the Craney Island unveiling directly to a broader federal policy push, noting that the skilled workforce building these vessels represents an important piece of the nation’s maritime industrial base and supports military readiness through the delivery of advanced, high-quality vessels.
The company said those capabilities align with the objectives of Presidential Executive Order 14269, Restoring America’s Maritime Dominance, a directive emphasizing the need to strengthen America’s shipbuilding capacity and maritime workforce after decades of decline in domestic commercial and military shipbuilding relative to competitors like China and South Korea.

Not doomed but very risky: airBaltic’s financial troubles deepen as S&P cuts credit rating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:08:00 UTC
21:08:00 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic is facing mounting financial pressure after S&P Global Ratings cut its credit rating to CCC- from CCC+, warning that the carrier may need as much as 170 million euros in additional capital.
Despite the downgrade, the airline says it is continuing normal operations and working to strengthen its finances.
For years, airBaltic has operated on a financial knife-edge. The carrier has invested heavily in a fleet of new Airbus A220-300 aircraft and expanded its network, but those investments have yet to consistently translate into profits. The airline has posted annual losses in four of the past five years, with 2023 the exception.
The picture has not improved this year. airBaltic reported a loss of 70 million euros in the first quarter, while its second-quarter results have yet to be released.
Higher fuel prices following the war in Iran have added to the pressure, further weakening the carrier’s financial position.
S&P’s downgrade to CCC- puts airBaltic deep in speculative, or “junk”, territory. The rating indicates that the agency sees the airline as highly vulnerable to adverse business, financial and economic conditions and considers the risk to its ability to meet its financial obligations to be very high.
S&P said airBaltic’s existing cash and other financing sources are insufficient to reliably cover its upcoming financial obligations, leaving the airline dependent on external financing and support.
The agency had previously supported its rating in part on the assumption that the Latvian government would provide assistance if needed. It now sees less certainty that government support would be sufficient or arrive in time.
Uncertainty surrounding Latvia’s parliamentary election in October is adding another layer of risk.
Airline seeks changes to bond terms
airBaltic has also approached bondholders seeking changes to the terms of bonds due in August 2029, according to S&P.
The airline is proposing to suspend cash interest payments for two quarters. Interest due in August and November would instead be capitalised, meaning it would be added to the outstanding debt rather than paid to investors in cash.
The carrier is also asking for a temporary waiver of a requirement to maintain at least 25 million euros in cash in its bank accounts. That would allow it to use those funds for its operations.
S&P estimates that higher fuel costs mean airBaltic will need at least an additional 120 million to 170 million euros in capital.
The downgrade has raised concerns among investors.
Vytenis Šimkus, an investment strategist at Swedbank, described CCC- as an extremely low rating. S&P considers ratings of BBB- and above to be investment grade, while CCC- sits near the bottom of the speculative-grade scale.
“The risk that the company will be unable to meet its financial obligations is increasing,” Šimkus said. “That does not mean the company cannot meet its obligations, but there is a significant risk that it will encounter financial difficulties.”
He said more radical solutions may be needed to address the airline’s financial commitments.
The rating also carries a negative outlook, meaning the situation could deteriorate further if current conditions persist, Šimkus said.
The market is already pricing in substantial risk. According to Šimkus, airBaltic bonds with a 100-euro face value are currently trading on the secondary market for about 30 euros.
“These are definitely risky bonds,” he said, adding that investors should closely examine the airline’s financial position.
Because airBaltic is a state-owned company, government policy will play an important role in determining its future, Šimkus said.
“If it were not a state-owned company, the rating would probably be even lower,” he said.
Still, Šimkus said the situation was not beyond repair. The Latvian government could assume additional obligations, while the airline could seek a strategic investor, potentially from one of Europe’s major airlines.
“The situation is not ultimately doomed, but the risks are high,” he said.
airBaltic says it is operating normally
In a response to LRT.lt, airBaltic emphasised that S&P is an independent credit rating agency and that its assessment is based on information available to it and assumptions applicable at a particular point in time.
The airline said it is continuing normal operations.
“airBaltic continues normal operations. The company’s priority is to strengthen its capital structure and ensure sustainable operations, independently of extraordinary state support,” the airline said.
The carrier added that it is implementing a new business plan approved by the Latvian government July 30. The plan is intended to strengthen airBaltic’s financial foundation and ensure its long-term sustainability.

Ivan Hinovski: Bulgaria’s еnergy sector is currently keeping the region afloat

Ivan Hinovski: Bulgaria’s еnergy sector is currently keeping the region afloat
Bulgaria’s energy system is operating under optimal conditions, says Bulgarian Energy and Mining Forum Chairman Ivan Hinovski
Wednesday 12 August 2026 13:18
Wednesday, 12 August 2026, 13:18
Ivan Hinovski
PHOTO Stefan Kunchev
Font size
Fuel prices have stabilised for now, as the market awaits any new shocks, energy expert Ivan Hinovski, chairman of the Bulgarian Energy and Mining Forum, told the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR).
“It has become common practice to expect shocks. However, we can say that we are in the best position in Europe because we are a fuel producer and our prices are relatively low. Our market is not experiencing any shocks and is not under pressure at the moment”, Ivan Hinovski said.
Ivan Hinovski recently warned that critically low water levels in the Danube River are threatening the cooling system of Bulgaria’s Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant. In an interview for the “12+4” programme of the BNR’s Horizont channel, he explained:
Kozloduy NPP
PHOTO Ministry of Energy-archive
“The Danube’s water level is crucial for the safe cooling of the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant, but it has stabilised over the past few days. Analysts have even reported a slight reversal in the trend, with the level rising by a few centimetres. There is still a safety margin. Kozloduy is a stable nuclear power plant when it comes to external cooling risks, as it was designed with such risks in mind. We still have a reserve of at least 10–15 centimetres in the Danube’s water level before any gradual shutdown of Units 5 and 6 would have to begin. I believe it will not come to that”, said Ivan Hinovski.
“The future Units 7 and 8 should have closed-circuit cooling towers'', the expert said. However, according to him, this approach has both advantages and disadvantages.
Kozloduy NPP
PHOTO BTA- archive
“It is safer because it does not depend on local fluctuations in the Danube’s water level, including temporary rises and falls. On the other hand, however, it requires more electricity for cooling, which means that the cost of electricity generation will be higher than with an open-loop system”, the expert explained, adding that the current conditions in the river will make the closed-loop system the preferred choice.
“Several days ago, the expert called for the coal-fired power plants at Maritsa East 2 and Bobov Dol to step up production. According to him, the plants are already taking advantage of the supply deficit in the region:
Ivan Hinovski
PHOTO BTA-archive
“At present, Bulgaria’s energy sector is helping to keep the region’s energy system afloat. We are exporting huge amounts of electricity, mainly to Romania, Serbia and North Macedonia, because we have managed to keep the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant operating at full capacity. In addition, the crisis in the region has prompted us to put almost all coal-fired power plants into operation. So, the mobilisation I spoke about has taken place”, said Ivan Hinovski.
According to Ivan Hinovski, Bulgaria does not have an energy strategy but has flexible energy investors. Regarding the role of photovoltaics in the stability of the grid as a whole, he said:
PHOTO Radio Vidin-archive
“Photovoltaics have their role as a modern technology and as an innovation. But Bulgaria went too far. The country made a major mistake by allowing a completely liberalised investment regime for photovoltaics.”
Ivan Hinovski pointed out that Bulgaria is currently a leader in photovoltaic energy storage systems, particularly battery storage. “This summer, based on applications for grid connections, we will reach 19,000 megawatts”, the expert said, adding that Bulgaria’s energy system is currently operating on an extremely optimal schedule for investors, the industry and the energy sector.

Taiwan power semiconductor makers see growth as AI pushes up power requirements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:04:45 UTC
21:04:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s power semiconductor makers are seeing stronger demand as the rapid growth of AI computing drives data centers to adopt higher-capacity power systems.
Panjit International Inc. reported consolidated revenue of NT$1.45 billion (US$44.9 million) in July, up 30.98% from the same period a year earlier. Revenue for the first seven months reached NT$8.8 billion, an annual increase of 16.46%, according to CTEE.
Eris Technology Corp. posted July revenue of NT$291 million, up 29.78% year-on-year and marking a new monthly record. Revenue for the first seven months totaled NT$1.78 billion, an annual increase of 19.02%.
The stronger performance comes as AI data centers adopt new power architectures to support increasingly powerful servers. Nvidia is developing an 800-volt power architecture for its next-generation AI server systems, while Microsoft is also working to redesign power systems from the electricity grid to individual server racks.
Industry sources said higher-voltage systems can reduce energy losses during power conversion, but they also require components that can withstand higher voltages, switch electricity more efficiently and operate reliably under greater heat loads. This shift is expected to benefit suppliers of power semiconductors, which are used to control and convert electricity within power systems.
AI servers can also experience significant changes in power consumption, making protection against sudden voltage increases particularly important. The trend could increase both the number and cost of power components used in each system, while raising technical requirements for suppliers.
Panjit has expanded beyond diode production into a broader range of power semiconductors. Its product lineup includes 650-volt and 1,200-volt silicon carbide diodes for server power supplies and industrial power systems.
Eris is gradually expanding its product portfolio to include power transistors, electrostatic discharge protection devices and silicon carbide products. Together with subsidiary Yea Shin Technology Co., which provides access to wafer manufacturing, Eris covers wafer production, packaging, testing and sales.
