Partial solar eclipse draws crowds across Germany
Millions of people across Germany have watched a partial solar eclipse, with largely clear skies offering good views as the moon covered around 85% to 90% of the sun.
Large crowds gathered at parks, observatories and viewpoints around the country, while many others stopped to watch from streets, balconies and open spaces.
In Munich, large numbers of people gathered in the Olympic Park to watch the eclipse.
Hundreds also headed to the Großer Feldberg in the central state of Hesse, while in Berlin around 3,000 people gathered near the planetarium in Prenzlauer Berg, according to police. The crowds caused some traffic disruption.
In the eastern city of Dresden, at least six hot-air balloons were spotted above the city, giving passengers an elevated view of the event.
Germany was outside the path of totality, but the moon still obscured around 85% to 90% of the sun in much of the country.
The weather largely cooperated, with mostly cloudless skies providing good viewing conditions.
Authorities had warned people not to look directly at the sun without certified eclipse glasses. Demand for eclipse glasses had surged ahead of the event, with shops reporting strong interest.
World War II bomb disposal prompts Monheim am Rhein evacuation
An unexploded British bomb from World War II has prompted authorities to clear out a 600-meter area around Monheim am Rhein.
They were hoping to dispose of the five-hundredweight bomb on Wednesday evening. It was discovered on a business' property on Daimlerstrasse, not far from the Rhine.
"Because of a clockwork delay fuse located on the bomb, defusing it is not possible," town authorities said in a press release on the operation. "Therefore the bomb must be detonated in a controlled explosion."
Clockwork or mechanical delay fuses were used in the war to hinder firefighting and emergency recovery operations; they were designed to make a number of the bombs dropped explode only some time after landing, effectively targeting the firefighting and rescue crews dispatched to the scene.
Authorities posted a map showing a 600-meter-radius (roughly 2,000-feet) exclusion zone covering much of the northern half of the town center and a stretch of the Rhine River's right bank. They said around 2,600 people were affected, with some roads closed and shipping on the already-almost-impassable Rhine restricted.
Shortly before 8 p.m., they said that the area was cleared and the controlled detonation operation had begun.
Monheim is a town of just over 40,000 people, on the banks of the Rhine in western Germany between Cologne and Düsseldorf.
German team wins dressage World Championship gold in Aachen
Germany's dominant equestrian dressage team has added another World Championship gold to their tally at the 2026 FEI championships in Aachen.
Record-breaking rider Isabell Werth rode the fourth and final routine for the German team, scoring almost 80%.
Werth, 57, now has 10 World Championship golds to her name, along with her eight Olympic golds and six silvers spread across seven separate Games.
The German team beat Great Britain to gold by less than four percentage points, with Denmark in third position, two further adrift.
"That was super," Werth exclaimed after her run. "We really had a great team performance here."
Coach Monica Theodorecu praised all four riders for their performance on ARD public television.
After a particularly impressive ride from Katharina Hemmer and consistent scores from the entire team, the coach remarked that Werth "can now have a relaxed ride" in the final run — with Germany enjoying a comfortable lead going into the last ride. "She can do it very well under pressure, too," Hemmer said of her veteran teammate.
Bundesliga's '50+1 rule' can comply with antitrust laws, cartel office says
The Federal Cartel Office, or Bundeskartellamt, has said that the Bundesliga's famous "50+1 rule" need not breach German competition laws — particularly if it is applied in a "consequential" manner without any "factually unjustified exceptions."
The rule stipulates that a majority stake (50% of shares, plus one) of most football teams should be owned by the underlying club — and, by extension, the club's members and fans.
It's beloved by many in Germany and seen as a key guarantor of the league's authenticity, its comparatively affordable ticket prices and other fan-oriented considerations. But critics say it's a financial millstone weighing the league down, a reason German teams sometimes struggle to go toe to toe with the richest clubs in Europe.
Federal Cartel Office President, Andreas Mundt, said his organization's position on the rule was fundamentally unchanged since the last time it was asked to opine.
"The 50+1 rule can continue to be justified with the goal of securing teams' identites and ensuring the involvement of the membership," Mundt said. "The condition for this, however, is that it [the rule] is applied consequentially and without any factually unjustified exceptions."
Mundt also stressed in the statement that his office was neither conducting, nor even considering "an investigation that could ban the 50+1 rule." Instead, he said that the German Football League (DFL), which runs the professional Bundesliga competitions, had requested "a well-founded assessment of this complex issue under sports antitrust law."
What are the complexities and possible inconsistencies in the rule?

E.ON's chief executive has warned that Germany's energy grid could be attacked.

Cologne Cathedral association 'overloaded' by wave of applicants avoiding new entry fees
Cologne Cathedral's new entry fee has led to a boom in membership applications for the longstanding ZDV association — a voluntary club for supporters of the cathedral and the costs accrued maintaining it.
Since July 1, visitors to the famous twin-towered cathedral overlooking the Rhine have been asked to pay €12 (just under $14) per head, per visit.

Interior minister hails 'new era' for Germany's secret services
Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has praised newly approved measures that give the country's intelligence services new, broad powers.
The reforms, which we reported on earlier in blog, will give Germany's domestic and foreign intelligence services more scope in gathering and storing information and data, as well as operational powers to fight acts of sabotage and hacking attempts.
The German government says the reforms are needed to allow the country to better combat the growing threat from cyber and hybrid attacks, particularly – but not exclusively — from Russia.
"We are transforming our intelligence services into genuine secret services," Dobrindt told a press conference in Berlin on Wednesday, adding that the new measures, which include artificial intelligence tools, will "revolutionize Germany's security architecture."
Germany's intelligence services were set up after the end of World War II, when memories of the Nazi regime were still recent, while people in the former East Germany lived under the oppression and intense state surveillance of the notorious secret state police, known as the Stasi.
Because of that legacy, Dobrindt said Germany was "catching up with what is possible in other European countries" such as France or the UK, whose secret services have more and broader powers.
Rhine water level sinks further, stranding cargo vessels
The water level in the Rhine River has fallen further amid the current heat wave, with German companies reporting increasing disruption to their supply and operations as cargo shipping is reduced or blocked.
The inland navigation agency WSV said the gauge at Kaub near Koblenz measured 12 cm (4.72 inches) on Wednesday, down from 15 cm on Tuesday.
It is well below the previous lowest recorded level of 25 cm in 2018. 
The measurement indicates that the river at Kaub is now about 112 cm deep at its deepest point.
The low water at this chokepoint means that most vessels cannot pass through Kaub from either direction, effectively cutting the Rhine in two for commercial shipping.
Traders have told the Reuters news agency that sailings on northern sections of the river continue but are often only 20% full.
The Rhine is one of Europe's main arteries for transporting grains, fuels, minerals and manufactured goods.
Rights group files criminal complaint over Mega's AI glasses
A German digital rights group, HateAid, has lodged a criminal complaint against Meta and companies that sell Meta's "smart" glasses in Germany.
HateAid said in a statement that putting the glasses — which can record audio and video — on the market broke digital privacy laws.
"There's no place to escape from smart glasses. You have to expect at any moment to be filmed and then exposed on the Internet," said HateAid managing director Josephine Ballon.
The group said its complaint was based on a federal digital data protection law banning the sale of communication devices that can film people without their being aware of it.
Germany's digital communications regulator, the Federal Network Agency, issued a statement on smart glasses in late 2023, saying that connected devices for covert audio or video recordings were banned.
The glasses have earned the online sobriquet of "pervert glasses," with many fearing they could be used to take video particularly of unsuspecting women or children that is then turned into content of a sexual or hateful nature on the Internet.
Inflation rises to 2.8% as energy prices jump
Germany's inflation rate rose to 2.8% in July, a rise caused mainly by an increase in energy prices after a fuel tax relief scheme expired, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) confirmed on Wednesday.
The figure is up 5 percentage points on the inflation rate in June.
"Energy prices continued to rise at an above-average rate and thus remained the central driver of inflation," said Destatis head Ruth Brand.
In July, consumers paid 8.3% more for fuel and heating than a year earlier, compared with an increase of just 3.4% in June.
In May and June, the government had cut energy taxes on petrol and diesel by just under €0.17 ($0.20) per liter as the US war with Iran drove oil prices up.
With the scheme expired, gasoline now costs more than €2 (2.31) a liter in most places.
The oil price shock was the key driver in pushing the April inflation rate to 2.9%, the highest since January 2024.
Food prices, for their part, have seen only moderate rises over the past months. In July, they were 0.4% above the same month a year earlier, matching the two preceding months.
Economists say, however, that food prices are likely to rise more sharply as the high energy prices make transport, refrigeration and storage are all currently more expensive.
Heat and drought are also negatively impacting agriculture and could reduce harvests.
No accompanied drinking for 14-year-olds, Cabinet decides
The German Cabinet also on Wednesday approved a draft bill abolishing a previous law allowing 14- and 15-year-olds to buy and drink beer, wine or sparkling wine when accompanied by their parents or guardians.
According to the bill, the current exception to the general ban on under 16-year-olds drinking any form of alcohol "weakens the protection of young people from the considerable health and social consequences of alcohol consumption."
In Germany, under 14-year-olds are currently not allowed to buy or drink alcohol in any form, while 14-15-year olds are permitted to purchase and drink undistilled alcohol in public places in the company of their parents or legal guardians.
From the age of 16, people are permitted to buy and consume undistilled alchohol without accompaniment, while those aged 18 and over, as legal adults, can buy and consume all alcoholic beverages.
Cabinet approves child pension subsidy
Among the draft bills approved by the Cabinet on Wednesday is a plan for children from the age of 6 to receive €10 ($11.54) from the state every month for a pension deposit .
Under the plan, the child's parents or carers would open the account and be able to deposit money there themselves as well.
The state payments would continue until the child turns 18.
Pension payments from the account would flow only after the now-adult turns 65.
According to the Finance Ministry, the state subsidies would amount to around €2,200, which "could become around €53,000 by pensionable age without any additional payments."
With the plan, the government aims not only to guarantee better financial security in old age for the younger generation but also to educate it in financial matters.
"Someone who experiences the capital market already at a young age and has positive experiences with it develops an understanding of long-term investment and will tend to invest in the capital market during his or her life," the Finance Ministry said.
The bill still needs approval by both chambers of parliament to go into force.
Cabinet passes controversial intelligence agency reform
The German Cabinet has approved a more than 700-page package of laws granting much greater powers to both the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) and the foreign intelligence agency (BND).
The package will allow the agencies more latitude in the gathering and storage of information and data, along with new options to actively combat acts of sabotage and hacking attacks.
The government says the package aims to enable the agencies to operate more effectively in the face of a myriad of hybrid security threats.
"We will not look on passively as foreign interference, sabotage and threats to the pillars of our constitution and our free society continue to grow," chancellery head Nina Warken told the daily Rheinische Post.
"Our [intelligence] services can only take targeted action against these hybrid attacks if they have more liberties and up-to-date measures" at their disposal, she said.
However, the planned reform has also met with considerable criticism from those who see the extended powers as a threat to civil rights.
The leader of the Free Democrats (FDP), Wolfgang Kubicki, accused Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of "breaking a taboo."
"It can hardly be imagined that the Constitutional Court will not intervene here," he told the Augsburger Allgemeine daily.
"I do not want any secret police in Germany," he said. "I want full court control in the case of attacks on basic rights and a state that understands that you don't defend liberty by curbing it."
Ansah has 'no fear' of losing bronze despite looming doping ban
Sprinter Owen Ansah, Germany's 100-meter record holder, delivered his country's first men's 100-meter European Championship medal in 40 years, despite facing a potential doping suspension.
Ansah won the bronze at the European Championships in Birmingham, England on Tuesday night, to take the biggest win of his career.
The 25-year-old posted a time of 10.19 seconds, managing to shut out the considerable noise surrounding his looming suspension by Germany's National Anti Doping Agency (NADA), which accuses the sprinter of refusing to take a doping test on July 9.
But Ansah insists that he failed to provide a urine sample because the doping control officer arrived outside of the requested time slot and Ansah had to leave to travel to Monaco for a Diamond League event. He also says he had just used the restroom before the officer arrived.
He said he is "not afraid" of having his medal revoked. "I trust my team, which has my back. I can’t influence the other stuff. I can only influence how fast I am on the track. And I showed that well today," Ansah said.
The sprinter is now turning his attention to the 200-meter dash on Friday, where he is eyeing a second medal at the Championships.
Drone-related security incidents on the increase — military
Several hundred security incidents involvingdrones have been registered by Germany's armed forces in the past years, a military spokesman has said.
"Since the start of the illegal full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, reports on drone sightings affecting the Bundeswehr have greatly increased," the spokesman told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland.
"Over the past few years, several hundred suspected drone overflights in Bundeswehr-related areas have been reported," he said, adding that whole swarms of drones had been sighted on occasion.

Partial solar eclipse draws crowds across Germany
Millions of people across Germany have watched a partial solar eclipse, with largely clear skies offering good views as the moon covered around 85% to 90% of the sun.
Large crowds gathered at parks, observatories and viewpoints around the country, while many others stopped to watch from streets, balconies and open spaces.
In Munich, large numbers of people gathered in the Olympic Park to watch the eclipse.
Hundreds also headed to the Großer Feldberg in the central state of Hesse, while in Berlin around 3,000 people gathered near the planetarium in Prenzlauer Berg, according to police. The crowds caused some traffic disruption.
In the eastern city of Dresden, at least six hot-air balloons were spotted above the city, giving passengers an elevated view of the event.
Germany was outside the path of totality, but the moon still obscured around 85% to 90% of the sun in much of the country.
The weather largely cooperated, with mostly cloudless skies providing good viewing conditions.
Authorities had warned people not to look directly at the sun without certified eclipse glasses. Demand for eclipse glasses had surged ahead of the event, with shops reporting strong interest.
World War II bomb disposal prompts Monheim am Rhein evacuation
An unexploded British bomb from World War II has prompted authorities to clear out a 600-meter area around Monheim am Rhein.
They were hoping to dispose of the five-hundredweight bomb on Wednesday evening. It was discovered on a business' property on Daimlerstrasse, not far from the Rhine.
"Because of a clockwork delay fuse located on the bomb, defusing it is not possible," town authorities said in a press release on the operation. "Therefore the bomb must be detonated in a controlled explosion."
Clockwork or mechanical delay fuses were used in the war to hinder firefighting and emergency recovery operations; they were designed to make a number of the bombs dropped explode only some time after landing, effectively targeting the firefighting and rescue crews dispatched to the scene.
Authorities posted a map showing a 600-meter-radius (roughly 2,000-feet) exclusion zone covering much of the northern half of the town center and a stretch of the Rhine River's right bank. They said around 2,600 people were affected, with some roads closed and shipping on the already-almost-impassable Rhine restricted.
Shortly before 8 p.m., they said that the area was cleared and the controlled detonation operation had begun.
Monheim is a town of just over 40,000 people, on the banks of the Rhine in western Germany between Cologne and Düsseldorf.
German team wins dressage World Championship gold in Aachen
Germany's dominant equestrian dressage team has added another World Championship gold to their tally at the 2026 FEI championships in Aachen.
Record-breaking rider Isabell Werth rode the fourth and final routine for the German team, scoring almost 80%.
Werth, 57, now has 10 World Championship golds to her name, along with her eight Olympic golds and six silvers spread across seven separate Games.
The German team beat Great Britain to gold by less than four percentage points, with Denmark in third position, two further adrift.
"That was super," Werth exclaimed after her run. "We really had a great team performance here."
Coach Monica Theodorecu praised all four riders for their performance on ARD public television.
After a particularly impressive ride from Katharina Hemmer and consistent scores from the entire team, the coach remarked that Werth "can now have a relaxed ride" in the final run — with Germany enjoying a comfortable lead going into the last ride. "She can do it very well under pressure, too," Hemmer said of her veteran teammate.
Bundesliga's '50+1 rule' can comply with antitrust laws, cartel office says
The Federal Cartel Office, or Bundeskartellamt, has said that the Bundesliga's famous "50+1 rule" need not breach German competition laws — particularly if it is applied in a "consequential" manner without any "factually unjustified exceptions."
The rule stipulates that a majority stake (50% of shares, plus one) of most football teams should be owned by the underlying club — and, by extension, the club's members and fans.
It's beloved by many in Germany and seen as a key guarantor of the league's authenticity, its comparatively affordable ticket prices and other fan-oriented considerations. But critics say it's a financial millstone weighing the league down, a reason German teams sometimes struggle to go toe to toe with the richest clubs in Europe.
Federal Cartel Office President, Andreas Mundt, said his organization's position on the rule was fundamentally unchanged since the last time it was asked to opine.
"The 50+1 rule can continue to be justified with the goal of securing teams' identites and ensuring the involvement of the membership," Mundt said. "The condition for this, however, is that it [the rule] is applied consequentially and without any factually unjustified exceptions."
Mundt also stressed in the statement that his office was neither conducting, nor even considering "an investigation that could ban the 50+1 rule." Instead, he said that the German Football League (DFL), which runs the professional Bundesliga competitions, had requested "a well-founded assessment of this complex issue under sports antitrust law."
What are the complexities and possible inconsistencies in the rule?
One condition Mundt recommended was ensuring open access to all clubs for members and fans — which could be a nod to the Red Bull-owned RB Leipzig to open up for members.
He also said there was "room for improvement" in the proposed new regulations for the existing "sponsor clubs" with 50+1 exceptions.
That's a reference to Bayer Leverkusen and Wolfsburg — factory-owned clubs dating back decades belonging to chemicals giant Bayer and to Volkswagen in Wolfsburg — that are exempt from the model because of their roots. Hoffenheim used to enjoy a similar status but moved to meet the 50+1 ownership model as of 2023.
Hannover 96's patron Martin Kind, meanwhile, recently requested an exemption from the model but failed in 2018.
Bayern Munich's President Herbert Hainer controversially argued this year that the rule should be scrapped and each team should be free to decide its own ownership structure. Audi, Allianz and Adidas combine to hold a 25% stake in Bayern, while the club's 380,000 members own a 75% share. Counterintuitively, Hainer argued that scrapping the rule could enable other teams to better challenge Bayern's dominance.

Italy: Po River runs low amid prolonged heat and drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:30:08 UTC
16:30:08 KST

Italy's Po River is running unusually low in Turin after weeks of heat and little rain. The exposed riverbed is revealing rocks normally underwater, while algae and vegetation spread along the banks.
Italy’s longest river, the Po, is running unusually low in Turin amid prolonged heat and a lack of rainfall.
The Po crosses the city for around nine kilometres, but parts of its riverbed are now exposed, revealing rocks that would normally be underwater.
The low water levels are also allowing algae and aquatic vegetation to spread along the riverbanks, while wildlife is being affected by the changing conditions.
The Po is vital for agriculture and industry across northern Italy, making the falling water levels a growing concern for the region.
To boost water levels, authorities asked hydropower operators to release more water from Alpine reservoirs.
At Pontelagoscuro, near the mouth of the river, the flow has fallen to just 206 cubic metres per second, one of the lowest levels recorded this summer. It could soon drop below 200 cubic metres per second.
The lower flow is allowing seawater to move further inland. The salt wedge has reached more than 20 kilometres inland, making it harder to take water from the river for irrigation and putting crops at risk.

Israeli government accused of complicity as settlers demolish Jericho homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:28:48 UTC
16:28:48 KST

Israeli government accused of complicity as settlers demolish Jericho homes
Israeli settlers demolish homes in village, leaving rubble and fear among displaced Palestinian families in Jericho.
Jericho, occupied West Bank – Where Palestinian homes once stood among orchards and swimming pools on the southwestern edge of Jericho, there is now only flattened earth.
Somewhere beneath the packed dirt lie entire houses, dumped into pits and smoothed over. Only a few severed water pipes hint that anyone ever lived here – that, and the piles of rubble yet to be buried by an Israeli settler’s excavator.
“Why do you hide the crime you’re committing?” asked Khalil al-Razim, 60, a Jerusalemite who has spent his summers on a plot of land here in the area of Ein al-Duyuk for more than a decade.
Beside al-Razim’s house, a pile of rubble more than two metres high blocks the entrance to the home of his neighbour, Mohammad Salah. Next to the pile, Salah stood with one of his four children. He now climbs his own fence to reach his house.
Six months earlier in February, during the first settler attack to tear through the area – with homes demolished and damaged, and residents attacked and robbed – a settler arrived with a bulldozer and began demolishing fences and houses in the neighbourhood, including parts of Salah’s home. This summer, the same work resumed under the guise of “clearing” the ruins those earlier attacks had left behind – and in the process, the Israeli excavator dumped piles of rubble in front of Salah’s home.
“How am I supposed to get into my own house?” Salah recalled asking the settler.
“That’s not my problem, how you get into your house,” the man told him, according to Salah. “Can’t get into your house? Go around another way from here. This land is not coming back to you.”
Since July 19, settler-operated excavators have kept coming on a near-daily basis – for the supposed purpose of “clearing waste”, but doing far more than that. The settler behind the attacks, identified by locals and in legal filings from the Israeli state as Hanan Herbst, is escorted by soldiers on every visit. No order has ever been shown to residents – no paper a lawyer can hold up in court. “Not an official order,” Salah said. “It’s all thuggery. Just brute force, nothing else.”
What is unfolding here, according to residents, lawyers and the state’s own court filings, is a subversion of normal legal processes that have all but erased the line between settler ambition and state authority. In practice, Israeli authorities have given the settlers close to a free hand over an entire Palestinian neighbourhood.
“This is a state with no law,” Salah said. “No decency in it. A state of thugs.”
Al Jazeera reached out to Israeli authorities for comment, but received no response. Herbst was also reached by phone, but hung up after being told he was being contacted by Al Jazeera. He has not responded to further attempts at contact.
A minister and a pogrom
Herbst owns an Israeli settler outpost called Armonot Farm, built without authorisation on a ridge overlooking Ein al-Duyuk in the summer of 2024. It was initially illegal even under Israel’s own rules, but the Israeli cabinet formally recognised it as a settlement, under the name Daya, at the end of March.
The neighbourhood below, known locally as Stih, sits a few dozen metres from the ruins of the Hasmonean and Herodian winter palaces, an archaeological site Israel’s government has designated a flagship for a planned network of “Judeo-centric” heritage parks across the West Bank. On the morning of February 10, Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu posted a video of himself at the ruins, Israeli flag in hand. “Any place built on the heritage of the Jewish people,” he said, “we will destroy it.”
Within hours of the post, Palestinian residents said, dozens of masked settlers descended on the area from the Armonot settlement and other outposts in what activists and residents call an eight-hour “pogrom”. Two Palestinian communities sit side by side here, and both were hit that day: a group of Bedouins closest to the ruins, home to roughly a hundred people from the Kaabneh tribe, and the neighbourhood of mostly villa-style homes belonging to Palestinian families from elsewhere, including Salah’s and al-Razim’s.
Ali Kaabneh, 40, a Bedouin herder, was inside his house when the February 10 attack began.
“They started throwing stones at me,” he said. “They forced me and my wife out of the house. There were 13 families with me – they drove us out with stones and weapons. It was a threat: I’m going to die if I don’t get out.”
When the settlers withdrew roughly eight hours later, Kaabneh’s 150 sheep had scattered, and his licensed tractor was gone, driven up towards the settlement. Thirteen houses in the Bedouin compound were demolished that day, he said. In the neighbouring community, three homes were destroyed completely, according to Hussein Taha, a longtime resident.
Many of the Bedouin families have lived since then in the ruins of their partially destroyed homes, or without shelter at all, according to Kaabneh.
‘Clearing waste’
For months afterwards, “there was a kind of calm”, Taha said, during which settlers nonetheless carried out thefts of people’s properties and uprooted trees. “But whoever wanted to fix his wall, [Herbst] would come to him and stop him.”
But behind the scenes, developments continued. In March, the Israeli military issued a seizure order for a strip of Palestinian land for an access route to the archaeological site – an order not handed to affected residents until weeks after it was issued – part of a sharp increase in such orders that Israeli NGOs Emek Shaveh and Kerem Navot say now overwhelmingly serve settler rather than security interests.
That “calm” ended on July 19, at 8:30am, when Herbst arrived with a bulldozer – ostensibly to bury rubble from February’s attack, but soon damaging and destroying property well beyond it. The walls of four homes were destroyed or damaged in the first day alone, according to Taha. When residents and Israeli solidarity activists reached out to police, the military, the Palestinian District Coordination and Liaison Office (DCO) and the Civil Administration that day, they were told no one knew anything about it.
By afternoon, the official line had shifted, according to Yael Sela, a cofounder of the Palestine Solidarity co-op that has maintained a presence in the community since February: an unnamed “high-ranking” military figure, she was told, had authorised the work – to “clear waste”.
In the weeks since, residents and activists say, the bulldozers have demolished or damaged additional houses, alleys, orchards and gardens, and dug pits to bury the debris inside the residential area. Soldiers escort Herbst and keep activists back, citing an ambiguous “closed zone”; no official order has been produced for locals, though activists attempting to enter and document the site have been arrested.
Lawyer Tawfiq Jabareen filed for an emergency injunction at Israel’s High Court on July 23, then again, urgently, on July 29, when the demolitions intensified rather than stopped.
What came back, on the night of July 30, was the state’s own account of how Herbst came to be there – a filing, which Al Jazeera obtained, that revealed an extraordinary example of the state deputising settlers to carry out demolitions and land takeover.
The filing revealed that a state-backed arrangement granting Israeli settlers agricultural use of the land long predated February’s settler attack. According to the state’s account, a March 2025 agreement was reached between Herbst and the Settlement Division of the World Zionist Organization to cultivate “state land” for agriculture.
Following February’s mass settler attack that demolished the Palestinian homes in the area, in May, the Binyamin Regional Council asked the Civil Administration to let Herbst clear “building waste” from “previous demolitions”, without specifying that those demolitions were the settlers’ own making. Nonetheless, the Civil Administration approved the request. The Jordan Valley Brigade commander, Colonel Gilad Shriki, then approved a military escort for Herbst.
At least some of the Palestinian homes in the area have been under a longstanding Israeli court injunction protecting them from demolitions. The agreement instructed Herbst not to damage structures or trees and to stay within the allocated area – instructions that, residents and activists say, have been violated at every turn, under military escort.
“The settler has demolished, and continues to demolish, buildings and uproot trees, despite the existence of restraining orders from the court in Jerusalem barring the army from demolishing them,” said Jabareen, who filed his petition against the army, the settler and the state prosecution together. “That is: the army circumvented the court’s decision and sent the settler to do the demolishing instead.”
“The Prosecution claims the [Settlement Division of the World Zionist Organization] leased the land to the settler,” he said, “even though the Civil Administration itself had barred the settler from demolishing any building or any tree.”
“My analysis,” Jabareen said, “is that the army and the Civil Administration are now in the settlers’ grip, and there’s no longer any real difference between them.
“The law and court rulings mean nothing to them. They believe imposing facts on the ground is stronger than any court decision.”
‘Why can’t I go back to my home?’
Across the razed land, what remains standing is small strips of common-area vegetation belonging to no one in particular. The state’s initial response suggests Herbst plans to begin cultivating the razed land as early as this week. The state maintains the ground itself is state land, now allocated to Herbst for agricultural use – though, as Sela noted, no map or boundary of that allocation has ever been produced.
“The purpose of this act of destruction was to terrorise the Bedouin community, and to create the impression that this was an empty area with nobody living there – only piles of demolished concrete,” said Hussein Taha. “Then this ‘kind settler’ wants to come and ‘clean up’ the area, cultivate it, and benefit from it, because he supposedly loves agriculture and green gardens.”
For al-Razim, whose family bought land here more than a decade ago, what is happening feels familiar. He is from Silwan, in occupied East Jerusalem, where settlers have spent decades pushing Palestinian families out through a legal system that, he says, offers no real recourse. His own son’s rented home in Silwan was demolished by authorities. Due to the traditional system of ownership in the area, Palestinian-held land often remains undivided family inheritance, unregistrable under rules that demand proof no family can produce.
“They know there’s no tabu [land deed] for it,” al-Razim said. “But [they tell us to] bring proof. So they exploit that gap.”
Unable to safely reach their home and fearing settler attacks, Salah has moved his wife and four children into a rented apartment in Bethlehem, for 2,000 shekels ($667) a month, though he is unable to find work there. He goes back to what used to be his house, mostly alone, when he can.
“Any time I bring it up with my wife, she breaks down,” said Salah outside his blocked home. “She says to me, ‘We want to go back to our home.’ My kids say to me, ‘Why can’t we go back to our home?’ I don’t know what to say to them.”
Attempts to reason with the settlers have failed. “These settlers don’t try to speak with you,” he added. “They only speak in the language of power.”
He paused. “I feel like I’m weak,” he said. “In front of my son, I’m weak – I can’t protect him, I can’t get him back to his home. There’s no worse feeling than standing in front of your kids and your wife and not being able to protect your home.”
Salah glanced at his son accompanying him that day. “I always told my kids: If you don’t make trouble, nobody will bother you. If you don’t cause problems, the government won’t come after you. And my son says to me, ‘Dad, you’re a liar. Look – we don’t make trouble. And yet they came and destroyed our house.'”
He gestured at the razed land adjacent to their home, on the other side of the rubble. He looked up towards the hillside above – Herbst’s excavator visible on the slope of the now-legalised settlement.
“What am I supposed to say to him?”

Germany to Restore Five Former Military Bases for Soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:28:40 UTC
16:28:40 KST

Germany plans to bring five former military facilities back into operation to accommodate Bundeswehr personnel amid plans to increase the size of the armed forces.
The German publication Sicherheit & Verteidigung reports that the facilities are located in Sigmaringen, Kusel, Speyer, Soest, and Friedberg.
All five are planned to be transferred to the German Army.
The restoration of military infrastructure is linked to Germany’s plans to significantly increase the size of the Bundeswehr. By 2035, the country aims to increase the number of active-duty contract soldiers to at least 260,000, while expanding the reserve to 200,000 military personnel.
A key element of the army’s expansion will be a new military service model. It is intended to train a larger number of service members and build up a significantly larger reserve.
The increase in the size of the Bundeswehr is also creating a need for additional barracks, training centers, and military training grounds. That is why the Federal Ministry of Defence of Germany is assessing former military facilities that could be brought back into use.
As of June 2026, the Federal Ministry of Defence of Germany was assessing the potential reuse of 174 former military sites. In 2026, 27 sites were added to the list, while 40 plots of land were removed from further consideration.
Among the five sites planned to be returned to military use, the former U.S. military base Ray Barracks in Friedberg could prove the most problematic. Local authorities had planned to transform the approximately 74-hectare site into a residential, commercial, and mixed-use district.
Some of the former barracks buildings in Friedberg have already been renovated to accommodate refugees. The district authorities spent around €13 million on the renovations.
Meanwhile, the German government is seeking to accelerate the construction and modernization of military infrastructure. On July 1, the Cabinet approved a draft law aimed at reducing administrative procedures involved in implementing Bundeswehr infrastructure projects.
The increase in the number of active-duty personnel and reservists is being carried out gradually through the creation of new units and reserve formations.
Militarnyi reported that Germany plans to significantly expand its territorial defense forces and units responsible for protecting critical infrastructure. By 2035, the strength of the Territorial Defense Division (Division Heimatschutz) is expected to increase from the planned 6,500 to more than 10,000 military personnel.

Autism and war: Gaza families grapple with destruction and loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:27:42 UTC
16:27:42 KST

Autism and war: Gaza families grapple with destruction and loss
Continuous bombing disrupts routines, causing sensory shocks and behavioural relapses in Gaza’s autistic children.
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – Among the rubble of Khan Younis, 16-year-old Ahmed Hatem al-Mahabeel clutches his hand tightly under his chin – a repetitive movement he uses to calm his nervous system and cope with the memory of the sound of explosions.
Ahmed, who lives with autism, has had to face the loss of some of his favourite places – his bedroom, his school, the sports academy he would attend, all destroyed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Venezuela and Israel restore consular ties as relations warm
- list 2 of 3Rights groups launch new legal challenge to Trump campaign against ICC
- list 3 of 3Iran, US set new conditions during Hormuz talks: What does this mean?
Before the war, Ahmed was doing well. He was progressing through school under the supervision of a specialist. He was training at a football academy, as well as memorising the Quran and excelling in English.
But Israel’s war, ongoing since October 2023, has killed more than 73,380 Palestinians and destroyed vast swathes of the enclave. And behind those headlines is the disruption of the services and supportive environments needed by individuals like Ahmed who have autism spectrum disorder.
“Ahmed used to go to the mosque and the club on his own, making excellent progress, but the war destroyed everything we built,” said his mother, Umm Ahmed. “He suffers from extreme sensitivity to sudden noise; when explosions sound, he enters a severe panic attack, covering his ears and swaying. In cases of extreme terror, he resorts to self-harm, hitting his head against the ground to escape the sound.”
Beyond psychological trauma, severe malnutrition and protein deficiency caused his appendix to rupture.
“With food shortages, complications led to a wound infection, forcing doctors to perform a second surgical operation to open the abdomen and clean it until he recovered,” Umm Ahmed recalled.
Today, Ahmed spends his days confined indoors due to the lack of safety in Gaza, with Israeli attacks ongoing, despite an October ceasefire.
“All our hope is for Ahmed to get an opportunity to travel abroad for treatment and rehabilitation, to reclaim what the war took from him,” his mother said.
Shelling and sensory overload
Continuous bombardment poses a direct threat to the nervous systems of autistic children. In Gaza, constant explosions have driven severe behavioural relapses, including total sleep deprivation, wandering from tents, panic attacks, and self-harm.
“A child with autism relies entirely on routine and calm to feel safe,” explained psychological specialist Diaa Abu Aoun, who has worked with Ahmed. “When forced to live in a tent amidst continuous explosions, their brain receives a sensory shock it cannot process. This fear translates into insomnia, digestive issues, and severe screaming fits where the child completely loses control.”
In Nuseirat camp in central Gaza, 19-year-old Muneer al-Haj has exhibited elements of those behaviours. When he hears air strikes, he squeezes his hands tightly into fists, pacing back and forth while making sounds to block out the noise.
Before the war, Muneer followed a promising rehabilitation path under specialists. He attended school, and displayed strong communication skills and a talent for drawing.
With the onset of Israeli shelling during the war, and medication shortages that were caused by Israel’s blockade of Gaza, his condition regressed to screaming fits and seizure-like symptoms.
Muneer’s treatment protocol was reduced to half a tablet daily of a sedative due to the shortages.
His father, who did not wish to give his full name but preferred to be called Abu Muneer, described the shift.
“He used to communicate and express himself clearly, but the war consumed everything… this safe space dissolved facing hardship and fear,” Abu Muneer said. “He now asks urgent questions we cannot answer, entering severe attacks if unresolved. We try to reassure him during shelling, saying ‘God will protect us’, but he realises what is happening, expressing his anguish by saying: ‘I am without shelter or a homeland.'”
“The absence of a safe space and the depletion of sedatives turned our attempts to calm our children into individual efforts fraught with fear and confusion,” Abu Muneer said.
Medication shortages
The interruption of specialised treatments directly threatens dozens of children, experts say.
“The sudden interruption or forced reduction of psychiatric and anti-convulsant medication doses… creates severe disruption in brain chemistry,” Abu Aoun said. “When a child is deprived of medication or receives only half a dose, the nervous system enters a severe rebound effect. Violent fits and acute convulsions increase, driving self-harm and preventing response to behavioural training.”
Medicine shortages and the collapse of specialist services have left autistic children without consistent treatment or suitable alternatives. The World Health Organization says no rehabilitation equipment entered Gaza between May 2024 and April of this year, while all facilities faced severe constraints.
The Palestine Center for Special Education was also destroyed, and its former director, Arij Abu Sultan, was killed, forcing parents to increasingly assume greater therapeutic roles.
Reem Jarour, the head of autism programmes at Gaza’s Dolphins Association for Education and Community Development, emphasises that individuals with autism rely on predictable environments for emotional stability.
“An autistic child cannot survive without a predictable ecosystem; routine is a neurological safety valve,” Jarour said. “What we witness today in Gaza is the total destruction of the behavioural foundations built over years. Sudden displacement turns environmental triggers into acute threats, leading to massive regression in linguistic and social skills.”

US allies question Trump’s Middle East leverage after Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan - report

- i24NEWS

- US allies question Trump's leverage in Middle East after Netanyahu’s rejection of Gaza plan - report
US allies question Trump's leverage in Middle East after Netanyahu’s rejection of Gaza plan - report
"Netanyahu's move is a sign that the American strategy towards Israel is wrong"
US allies are increasingly concerned that Prime Minister Netanyahu’s rejection of the Peace Council’s 15-point plan for Gaza could weaken confidence in the council and raise broader questions about the Trump administration’s ability to influence developments in the Middle East, according to a report published Wednesday by Politico.
The report, citing several diplomats and officials familiar with US strategy in the region, said there is growing concern that Washington either lacks the leverage needed to advance its objectives in Gaza or is unwilling to use it.
Diplomats told Politico that the issue could have implications beyond Gaza, potentially complicating U.S. efforts to advance negotiations elsewhere in the region.
“The rejection of the peace plan by Netanyahu carries significant implications for long-term regional stability and for Israel’s security,” an Arab diplomat familiar with US Middle East policy told Politico. The diplomat said President Trump remains the only figure with the potential to influence the situation, arguing that he could seek to restore his political leverage by pressuring Netanyahu to reconsider his position.
The diplomat also warned that Arab and other regional leaders could be forced to balance their interests against a rapidly changing political landscape.
The Peace Council declined to comment directly on the report. However, a source familiar with the organization’s work said its efforts were continuing “at an accelerated pace” and with Israeli cooperation.
The source pointed to a logistical support area currently under construction that is expected to support hundreds of troops who could be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilization force.
“The roadmap is between the Peace Council and Hamas,” the source said, emphasizing that separate discussions are being held with Israel. According to the source, Israel is not being asked to take irreversible steps or rely solely on assurances before verified developments occur on the ground.
A Western diplomat familiar with Middle East policy offered a more critical assessment, saying Netanyahu’s rejection indicated that the US strategy toward Israel may be failing.
The diplomat argued that repeated attempts at reconciliation with Israel had resulted in increasingly maximalist demands, and said Netanyahu’s position did not necessarily spell the end of the Peace Council but demonstrated that Israel remained an obstacle to achieving a sustainable two-state solution.
Netanyahu has rejected the 15-point document, saying Israel will not agree to an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza before Hamas is genuinely disarmed.
The Trump administration, however, does not appear to view Netanyahu’s position as a threat to the broader peace effort. A Trump administration official told Politico that the White House believes Netanyahu’s rejection is primarily political and aimed at a domestic audience ahead of Israeli elections.

German Cabinet to discuss intelligence service reforms granting more powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:27:02 UTC
16:27:02 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The German Cabinet is set to discuss reforms to the country’s intelligence services on Wednesday that would introduce new and broader powers.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt will present the reform to the Cabinet, which aims to transform the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution into a full-fledged intelligence service with far-reaching powers, daily BILD reported Tuesday.
The Office for the Protection of the Constitution has reportedly been primarily responsible for collecting and evaluating information, with interventions reserved for police and security authorities since its founding.
With the reform, Dobrindt aims to turn the office into a more offensive actor.
"The hybrid threat situation, attempts to destabilize through sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and covert actions by foreign powers are receiving a new response. We are turning our intelligence services into real secret services," he told BILD.
The draft law would allow the office to disrupt ongoing operations by terrorists, saboteurs or foreign agents, redirect data traffic and specifically interfere with technical systems. It could also be authorized to render means of attack harmless or replace bombs intended for attacks with nonfunctional replicas.
The agency will also receive completely new digital tools and will be allowed to infiltrate computers and smartphones, conduct online searches and gain broader access to communications and video data.
"It is high time that we make ourselves competitive and operate on an equal footing with our partner services around the world. This requires operational capabilities and active powers to act more effectively against modern state terrorism and extremist groups," Dobrindt further said.

Nigel Farage and Count Binface: a visual guide to their electoral careers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:26:45 UTC
16:26:45 KST

Nigel Farage has been standing in British elections since 1994, when he narrowly beat Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony party into fourth place in a Commons byelection. He was elected five times to the European parliament before achieving his goal of abolishing his seat.
Finally, after 30 years of trying, he was elected to the Commons as member for Clacton in 2024. He resigned that hard-won seat in July after a parliamentary inquiry was launched into a £5m gift he accepted from a Thailand-based businessman shortly before the general election, but is standing again in the resulting byelection on Thursday. The other major parties are not putting up candidates, so the chief contenders, according to the limited polling, are Farage and Count Binface.
These charts show the respective electoral histories of the two main runners.
Count Binface, or rather, his earthling avatar the comedian and writer Jon Harvey, has had a shorter and, so far, less successful electoral career, although he has stood against four prime ministers. On Thursday, he will face Farage at the ballot box for the first time, alongside his longstanding electoral adversary Laurence Fox, standing for Reclaim.
Over the years, Nigel Farage has stood against dozens of British politicians, including in 2006 a young Labour candidate by the name of Rachel Reeves.
In her capacity as chancellor a few weeks ago, it fell to Reeves to accept Farage’s resignation as MP for Clacton. There was some speculation at the time that she was not obliged to do it, but she accepted the resignation on the basis that “if he [Farage] wants to spend summer arguing with a bin, I won’t stop him.”
Thursday’s contest will, of course, not be the first time that either Farage or Binface has faced a novelty opponent. Riding high in the polls in 2015, Farage was so confident of winning Thanet South in that year’s general election that he pledged to resign as leader of Ukip if he did not take the seat.
This led Al Murray, a comedian whose main persona is the Pub Landlord, a straight-talking conservative patriot, to stand against Farage. Even without the resulting split in the straight-talking conservative patriot vote, Farage would have lost the seat. Ever a man of his word, Farage resigned, and then unresigned three days later.
Harvey’s first electoral foray was not as Count Binface at all, but rather as the similarly behatted persona of Lord Buckethead. He was moved to adopt the Binface persona when a man got in touch claiming to hold copyright in the Buckethead character. In 2019, having failed to prorogue parliament, the then prime minister, Boris Johnson, called an early general election. A roster of novelty candidates – and Boris Johnson – ran in Uxbridge and South Ruislip, among them for the first and only time, both Count Binface and a copyright-approved Lord Buckethead.
Voters in Clacton on Thursday can, of course, choose to vote for neither Binface nor Farage. In fact, there are 34 candidates in all, including three from the Monster Raving Loony party.

Coffee exports from Colombia have been largely halted after a powerful earthquake
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:25:45 EEST
16:25:45 KST

Coffee exports from Colombia have been largely halted after a powerful earthquake
Kyiv • UNN
The earthquake disrupted operations at the port of Buenaventura and blocked key roads, suspending coffee exports. The head of Asoexport reported that operations had been halted and that there was uncertainty about the timeline for their resumption.
Coffee exports from Colombia have largely been put on hold after a devastating earthquake disrupted operations at the country's main port and caused road closures on key highways, the head of a coffee exporters' group said, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
Buenaventura, Colombia's main coffee export port, is effectively inaccessible because of several blocked roads, especially around tunnels along the Cali-Buenaventura highway, a key route to the country's Pacific coast, Gustavo Gómez, head of Asoexport, said in an interview.
"Coffee operations are currently suspended. Some individual operations may be possible, but at this point coffee export operations are halted," Gómez said. "At this point, there is no specific official information on when the road will be fully reopened," he added.
Port terminal operators are assessing the damage and have suspended or limited coffee-receiving operations. Other ports in Cartagena and Santa Marta on Colombia's Caribbean coast have not reported serious disruptions, but redirecting coffee north has been complicated by a severe shortage of trucks.
The disruptions are being exacerbated by the concentration of transport companies and processing facilities in the country's coffee-growing region near the area affected by the earthquake, where operations have also been disrupted.
Arabica coffee futures in New York fell sharply from multi-week highs to slight losses as traders assessed the potential impact on supplies and logistics of the earthquake that struck the world's second-largest producer of premium beans. Colombia's coffee production reached 13.4 million 60-kilogram bags in 2025.
Although Colombia produces coffee across much of the country, the timing of the disruptions is particularly problematic because the harvest is currently concentrated in the southern regions, including Cauca, Nariño, Valle del Cauca, and Huila. Much of this coffee is normally exported through Buenaventura.
"Processing facilities are still assessing the damage. So far, there have been no reports of serious structural damage to coffee mills, but operations are being affected by power outages, communications problems, and the personal consequences for workers, including people who have lost their homes," Gómez said.
Even after roads and facilities resume operations, exports may face further delays as accumulated coffee begins moving again, potentially creating congestion and bottlenecks at ports. Colombia exports around 1 million 60-kilogram bags of coffee per month, meaning that each day of disruption could delay significant volumes of shipments.
"This will ultimately lead to delivery delays and also put pressure on the supply chain once everything begins to recover and operations resume," Gómez said.

Two-thirds of Poles support deportation of unemployed Ukrainian men
A proposal by Poland's opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party to deport Ukrainian men of conscription age who do not have legal employment has received broad public support in Poland.
Source: the latest IBRiS poll for Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita
Details: The poll found that 67.2% of respondents support the deportation of Ukrainian men without legal employment, while 23.4% oppose it.
The data show that support for the proposal increases with age. Among respondents aged 18-29, 43% support it, compared with 80% of those in their 50s. Religious respondents were also more likely to support the PiS proposal than their non-religious counterparts.
The survey was conducted on 7-8 August 2026, immediately after PiS unveiled the proposal, and polled more than 1,000 respondents.
Law and Justice has presented a new migration policy plan, one of the key proposals of which is to deport Ukrainian men of conscription age (25-60) if they do not have legal employment in Poland. The proposal has sparked widespread debate among politicians and the public.
"Law and Justice's plans to deport Ukrainians of conscription age are populism," said Karolina Gałecka, spokesperson for Poland's Ministry of the Interior and Administration. She also said that 95% of Ukrainian men in Poland are legally employed.
Background: On 30 July, the Council of the EU approved, by written procedure, an extension of temporary protection for Ukrainians in EU countries, introducing a new provision under which newly arrived Ukrainian citizens liable for military service will be eligible for the status only if there are no issues with their military registration documents.

The Fire Services Department said it received multiple reports of a blaze that broke out near a minibus terminus in Po Toi O village at 8.33am on Wednesday. It was classified as a No 1 alarm fire, the lowest in Hong Kong’s five-tier system.

Po Toi O is known for its seafood restaurants. Its sheltered bay is also a popular lunchtime stop for people arriving by boat.

France swelters in new heatwave as water restrictions tighten

16:24:35 KST

Seventy-eight departments, including Rhône, Hauts-de-Seine, Calvados and Finistère, are on orange heatwave alert. Weeks of drought have led the authorities to impose successive restrictions on water use.
France is facing another spell of intense heat. On Wednesday, the heatwave is spreading across much of the country, with 78 departments placed on orange alert. In several regions, temperatures will climb above 35°C, while in some areas, such as Corsica, the mercury could exceed 40°C on Thursday.
This prolonged heat is making everyday life harder for residents. In Bordeaux, as elsewhere, some people have no choice but to keep their windows closed during the day and limit their movements to the coolest hours. Nights are also proving difficult, with temperatures struggling to drop, particularly in the west of the country.
In these conditions, the authorities recommend drinking water regularly, staying cool and paying particular attention to vulnerable people, such as older people and young children. A diet rich in fruit and vegetables and cool showers can also help people cope better with the high temperatures.
But the heatwave is not the only cause for concern. The lack of rainfall (source in French) is worsening the drought. Soils remain extremely dry and small rivers are in a particularly worrying state. Nearly 1,400 waterways are thought to have run dry, according to the OFB, the French Office for Biodiversity. (source in French) Restrictions on water use now affect a very large majority of the population in mainland France and in Corsica.
This succession of heatwaves, which are becoming more frequent and more intense in the context of global warming, highlights the growing difficulties France needs to prepare for. A return to more bearable temperatures is not expected before the weekend.

Power was restored at Global Funeral Parlour in Hung Hom on Wednesday, with lights and air conditioning returning across its five floors and large fans and air coolers deployed to further cool the premises.
But the burning of paper offerings, a traditional ritual in Chinese funerals, remained limited as the building’s exhaust ventilation system had not been fully restored, with repair work still ongoing, according to a staff member.
“We try not to burn too many paper offerings for now, because the exhaust ventilation is still a bit weak,” the staff member told the South China Morning Post.
Funerals proceeded inside two halls, while notices about the power situation remained posted near the passenger lifts.
Cheng Chi-kit, chairman of the Funeral Business Association, said the outage hit the parlour on what was already the hottest day in the city’s recorded history, with multiple lighting failures on about half of each impacted floor.
The biggest impact, he said, was the loss of air conditioning and ventilation in the mourning halls.

India, 5 southern African nations agree to open trade talks
India and the five countries that make up the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) have agreed to begin negotiations on a preferential trade agreemen (PTA).
South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Eswatini are members of SACU.
SACU and India held five rounds of trade talks between 2002 and 2010, but negotiations stalled.
The move comes as India looks to secure lower tariffs on its exports, including vehicles, pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery, the Reuters news agency reported Wednesday.
Under President Donald Trump, the US has imposed a range of tariffs on many of its trading partners, including India. Washington and New Delhi are currently negotiating a bilateral trade agreement.
After the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in July, the Trump administration turned to another law in a bid to make the tariffs stick.
Cockroach founder hints at new wave of protests
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) , has suggested that a new wave of protests could be imminent.
The movement led weeks of protests and hunger strikes calling for education reform, which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25.
Thousands of protesters camped out at the Jantar Mantar observatory in central Delhi.
"Many people were commenting on Instagram when Season 2 of 'Jantar-Mantar' will begin. I want to tell them that Season 2 of 'Jantar-Mantar' is going to start very soon," Dipke said Wednesday.
It was not clear when or where the next phase of protests would begin.
Similar demonstrations and rallies have since spread to other parts of the country.
The movement has emerged as one of the most serious challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.
Tata Sons' chairman will not seek reappointment at end of term
Indian conglomerate Tata Sons' Chairman N Chandrasekaran said on Wednesday he would not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.
The 63-year-old, who has led Tata Sons since 2017, cited a lack of board support amid tensions with the charity arm, Tata Trusts, which controls 66% of the conglomerate's holding company.
Chandrasekaran said uncertainty over the leadership situation had remained unresolved for six months and that a decision was important for employees, investors and other stakeholders.
Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata opposed Chandrasekaran's reappointment at a February board meeting, Reuters reported.
Seven killed, more feared trapped after landslide in Mumbai
At least seven people were killed and several injured after a landslide hit Mumbai's Kurla area early Wednesday following heavy rain, the Hindustan Times reported.
According to the report, the landslide occurred around 3 a.m. local time, with more people feared trapped, Deputy Commissioner of Police Ganesh Shinde said.
Rescue operations are underway, with teams from various emergency agencies deployed.
Mumbai has experienced heavy monsoon rain in recent weeks, causing waterlogging and disruptions to air and road traffic.

Supreme Court urges faster adjudication of West Bengal SIR appeals
India's Supreme Court on Tuesday urged tribunals handling appeals against voter deletions in West Bengal to speed up their work, saying the process could not drag on indefinitely, a report in the Times of India said.
Nearly 3.4 million appeals are pending before tribunals set up to hear challenges to deletions from electoral rolls during a Special Intensive Revision (SIR), according to the court.
"The process cannot be so slow that the next assembly elections would be due by the time the appeals are decided," Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said, according to the report.
India's election commission conducted the SIR of electoral rolls in several states and territories ahead of state election, including West Bengal, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party recently won state elections.
The commission said the "intensive revision" was needed to remove the names of deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."
Critics of the SIR say it is skewed against marginalized and minority communities.
IN DEPTH: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat
For generations, India has lived by the rhythm of the southwest monsoon. But with the country hit by dry spells, cloudbursts and deadly floods, climate swings now expose the costs of building for yesterday's weather.
Food safety, hygiene issues plague India's quick commerce firms
India's quick commerce sector, especially grocery delivery services, is in the doldrums as authorities flag serious food safety and hygiene violations.
Authorities in the southern Karnataka and western Maharashtra states sealed a Zepto warehouse on Tuesday and suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after inspections found serious violations, reports said.
In Karnataka, a Zepto warehouse near Bengaluru was sealed by the food safety department after finding unhygienic food handling and storage conditions, improper labelling and misbranding.
Zepto said in a statement that it had cooperated with officials and was taking steps to address their observations, the Hindustan Times reported, adding that it remained committed to food safety and hygiene standards.
In Mumbai, authorities suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after finding a large-scale cockroach infestation, improperly stored food and expired or tampered products.
Food was also found on rusted racks, while cold-storage areas lacked adequate cleanliness.
The facility has been barred from selling or distributing food or conducting any food business during the license suspension, authorities said.
Air India pilot tests positive in drug test
The captain of an Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.
The Airbus A320neo, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew, lost about 300 feet of over Odisha before landing safely in Delhi.
The plane stabilized and landed safely. India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the incident as serious.
The incident had left 13 passengers and four crew members injured, and led to India's aviation ministry summoning Air India CEO Campbell Wilson on Tuesday.
Emergency at Chennai airport after IndiGo plane suffers engine failure
Late on Tuesday night, Chennai airport declared a full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, media reports said.
This came only a few hours after reports emerged that the captain of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week, injuring crew and passengers, tested positive in a drug test, further plunging India's aviation into turmoil.
On Tuesday, the pilot of an IndiGo plane, flying from Kolkata to Chennai with 224 people on board, noticed that the left engine had failed while the plane prepared to land, reports said Airports Authority of India (AAI) officials.
Airport authorities activated emergency response measures, which remained in place till the plane landed safely. The declaration of full emergency was withdrawn soon after.

Romania Blows Up Two Gerbera Drones Drifting Near Black Sea Gas Platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:19:48 UTC
16:19:48 KST

Romanian military forces destroyed two Gerbera-type drones on Tuesday that were drifting within the country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, near a gas platform operated as part of the Neptun Deep project.
Romania’s acting Defence Minister, Radu Miruță, reported the incident on August 11.
The drones were detected by one of the vessels carrying out work in the area of the gas platform. A Romanian Coast Guard vessel carrying bomb-disposal specialists was dispatched to the scene.
The drones were located approximately 90 nautical miles east of Constanța. Several other pieces of debris were also found alongside them.
Romania’s Ministry of National Defence contacted the Ukrainian side, which confirmed that the drones did not belong to Ukraine.
“Two drifting drones and several other pieces of debris were found. Romania’s Ministry of National Defence contacted Ukrainian officials, who confirmed that the drones did not belong to Ukraine,” Miruță added.
To ensure the safety of ships and workers operating near the platform, the Romanian military decided to safely destroy the drones by detonating them in a controlled explosion.
The Gerbera UAV was primarily designed for use as a decoy target. These drones force air-defense forces to spend time and resources detecting and intercepting them, while also helping Russian forces identify the positions of Ukrainian air-defense systems.
Later, Russian forces began equipping Gerbera drones with warheads, turning them into strike UAVs. The drone can also be used for reconnaissance and intelligence gathering.

Amit Shah says 'ready to sit through, take notes and respond to anything' in Parliament.
NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Wednesday offered to sit in Parliament from "3pm today till 3pm the next day" to hear the opposition's concerns and respond to every point, amid protests over his "absence" from the Houses. Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, however, rejected the offer saying they "seek answers, not lectures."Shah's offer came amid opposition protests demanding that he make a statement in Parliament on the police action against students during their July 20 march over the NEET paper leak issue.Speaking to reporters, Shah rejected opposition allegations that he had been absent from Parliament and said the government was ready for a detailed discussion on the issue."First of all, terms like 'laapata', 'bhaag gaye' are the kind of language increasingly being heard in India's public and parliamentary life. I have been coming to Parliament regularly since the session began; I sit in my chamber, but since the opposition is not allowing Parliament to function—in either House—what is one supposed to do?" Shah said.He said Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju had already made it clear that the government was ready for a full discussion on the student protests.
"We asked for a time to be fixed and for the Opposition to be ready. That was their initial demand, and we agreed to it. I, too, have stated that I am ready to answer any question in Parliament, yet they simply do not want the discussion to take place," Shah said."Now, let the public decide who is running away. Let them submit a letter to the Speaker by 3:00 pm today. We are ready for a discussion on all aspects from 3:00 pm today until 3:00 pm tomorrow. I will sit in the House; I will listen to everyone and respond to every point. The government has nothing to hide," he added.Shah said he was even willing to discuss why the opposition had not allowed the debate to take place. "The NDA government—under Modi ji's leadership is ready to discuss anything; they just need to let Parliament function," he said.Elaborating on his offer, Shah said, "I want to tell the opposition: submit a letter to the Speaker by 2.00 pm, we will start the discussion at 3.00pm, and I will provide answers to everything by 3:00 PM tomorrow.""There are established rules and procedures for parliamentary discussions. Yet, some ask me to simply make a statement. Such a serious issue cannot be discussed in that manner. That may be your method, but it is not the parliamentary way. In Parliament, discussions are held at length," he said."In Parliament, discussions are held at length. I am ready for the debate to continue from 3:00 PM today, sitting late into the night and continuing until 3:00 PM tomorrow; I am even prepared to suspend the Question Hour if the Speaker grants permission," Shah said."I am ready for the discussion to go on until 3:00 PM tomorrow. I will sit through it myself, take notes on everything, and respond to every point so that the entire matter becomes clear to the people of the country—so that the truth is fully revealed. Now, the Opposition must decide whether they want to engage in a discussion or create an uproar," he added.
Rahul Gandhi hits backCongress leader Rahul Gandhi rejected Shah's offer, saying the opposition was seeking answers on the alleged police action against students rather than a lecture from the home minister."The opposition has clearly said that we are not interested in Amit Shah giving us a lecture. When I say 'we', I mean the younger generation of this country. Who shot the students? Who gave the order to beat up the students with lathis with nails? Did Amit Shah give this order to shoot our children? If he did, then he should resign. For the last 20 days, Amit Shah has been missing. The Home Minister of India has no courage; he cannot come to the House," Rahul said."Did home minister Shah give orders to shoot our children or not; if he did, he is culpable and if he did not, he is incompetent," he added.
The leader of opposition also took to X, sharing a video of his remark saying "When a man lacks the courage to speak the truth, his silence speaks for him. Amit Shah’s silence is his confession."Centre vs oppositionThe opposition has been demanding Shah's presence in Parliament and a statement on the "police action" against students during the Jantar Mantar protest.Earlier in the day, opposition MPs, including Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and party general secretary Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, staged a protest in the Parliament House Complex over the alleged theft of donations at the Ram temple in Ayodhya and the alleged police excesses against student protesters.Priyanka also questioned the government over the alleged use of force against students.The INDIA bloc has been protesting for more than three weeks, demanding Shah's presence in the House and a statement from him.Earlier on Monday, Kiren Rijiju said the government was ready for a detailed discussion on the student protests and urged the opposition not to disrupt proceedings when Shah responds."The offer made by the government is very clear that it is ready to have a full and detailed discussion on students' movement and activities related to it," Rijiju said.
"My only point made to the opposition is that while the discussion and a reply are being made, the opposition should not create disturbances to prevent the statement of the home minister," he said, adding that, "They must listen to the reply of the home minister and the government. Once discussion begins, we must have a threadbare discussion."Rijiju's remarks came after Rahul criticised the Centre over the alleged police action during the July 20 student protests at Jantar Mantar and demanded a court-monitored probe. Parliament proceedings have repeatedly been disrupted during the Monsoon Session, with several Bills passed by the Lok Sabha amid the continuing deadlock.
